PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. WITY is John Bigger's boy larger than his father ?—Because he is a little Bigger! Wm' is a whale like a brickbat 2—'Cause lb can't climb an apple-tree. WHY should a man, when he's eating salt fish on a Good Friday, take no egg-sauce with it I—For fear his appetite should get egg-sauce-fed (exhausted). —Punch. A FAIR EXCLIANGE.—The mistress of a dame school, speaking of her pupils, honestly declared, "It is but little they pays me, and it is but little I teaches them.' SOMETHING NEW "UNDER THE SUN."—Mrs. Partington junior, asked a daguerrotypist the other day if he could daguerrotype a picture from recollection 1 A LITTLE girl was told to spell ferment and give Its meaning, with a sentence in which it was used. The following was literally her answer— " F-e-r-m-e-n-t, a verb signifying to work—l love to ferment in the garden 1" NEWS rnom SPAIN—The press has been abol- ished by a single order of the Court. It is expected that the next decree will, in addition to this, formally abrogate the mischievous invention of printing. —Punch. A POOR man who had a termagant wife, after a long dispute, in which she was determined to have the last word, told her that if she spoke one more crooked word, he'd heat her brains out. "Why then, ram's•horn, you rogue," said she, "if I die for it."

_ A FEW days ago Mr. B. was walking down St. James's Street, and on meeting the witty Mr. H., expressed deep regret at the severity of the weather, complaining that it made him hobble. "Oh !" says Mr, H., " if it only continues a little longer, you will jump from winter to summer with- out spring." WE ALL HAVE OUR TROUBLES.—Sister Mary: "Why, Charley, dear boy, what's the matter? You seem quite miserable! Charley: Ah ! ain't I just I Here's ma says I must wear turn-down collars till Christmas. and there's young Sidney Bowler, who's not half so tall as I am, has had stick-ups an white chokers for ever so long. A SMART young man saw, with blushing pride, a pretty actress watching him, and, growing bold too soon, he was thus repulsed: "Oh, you need not apologise for speaking to me. I did notice you; but the fact is I am studying a big silly boy's part, and wanted a good lay figure to look at.' *Amin BOTH WAYS.—An astronomer Once con- fidently announced that a big comet that was approaching the earth would not destroy it. How do you know?" he was asked. "I don't know," he replied; but in either case lam safe. If it does not knock the world to pieces, I shall be considered a prophet. If it does, they can't blow - me up in the nefespapers." A LITTLE boy had his long curls cut off the other day, and way annoyingly reminded of the fact by the remarks of all his friends. Going a ith his family into the country, soon after his arrival, he came running into the house in great sorrow, crying: "Mamma, mamma, even the hens laugh at me; they all say: 'Cut-cut-cut-got-your-hair- cut." AN honest farmer was invited to attend a party at the village squire's one evening, when there was music, both vocal and instrumental. On the following morning he met one of the guests, who said, " ‘Vell, farmer, how did you enjoy yourself last night? Were not the quartettes excellent ?" " Why, really, sir, I can't say," said he, "for I didn't taste 'ern ; but the pork chops were the finest I ever ate," VIOLATING A RULE. —A man who had climbed a chestnut tree, had hy carelessness missed his hold of one of the branches, and fell to the ground with such violence as to break one of his ribs. A neigh- bour, coming to his assistance, remarked drily, that had he followed his rule in these cases, he would have avoided this accident. "What rule do you mean?" asked the other.—" This," replied the philosopher, "never come down a place faster than you go up." A LADY asked a minister if she might pay atten- tion to dress and fashion without being proud. "Madam," replied the minister, whenever you see the tail of a fox out of a hole you may be sure the ox is there also." Dotramess a custom-house officer would be able to see the meaning of the following from the Boston Transcript :—Since the liquor law came into force in Maine, great quantities of bottles, labelled "Day and Martin's Blacking," have been imported into that State, and yet it is not observed that the boots are cleaner than before. THE Boston Tran.script says that the doctors, for two years, treated a child of that city for pulmon- ary difficnlty, and just found out that the trouble was caused by two buttons in her nose. The pro- fession has found out by this that two buttons in the nose are as unpleasant as two buckles (tubercles) on the lungs. "Joirlf," said a clergyman to his man, "yea should become a teetotaler—you have been drinking again to-day."—" Do you never take a drop your. eel', meinister ?"—" Ah, but, John, you must look at your circumstances and mine."—" Varra true, sir," says John; "but can you tell me how the streets of Jerusalem were kept so clean?"—" No, John, I cannot tell you that." —"Weal; air, it was just because every one kept his ain door clean." A YOUNG gentlemen, a short time since, was about making an excursion for fish, and on one of the thoroughfares to the lake he met and made the acquaintance of a lady, Mary Pike by name with whom he became very much pleased, and from whom he could not part without some pangs of sadness. He expressed a hope that he might hear from her occasionally. To which she replied, that "if he was not successful in taking fish at the lakes, she had not any objection to his dropping a line to her." A CONTRAST. Matrimony: Hot buckwheat cake—warm beds, comfortable slippers—smoking coffee—round arms—red lips _(ahem shirts exulting in buttons—redeemed stockings boot jacks—happiness, &c.--Single Blessedness Sheet-iron quilts—blue noses—frosty rooms—ice in the piteber —unregenerated linen—heel-less stock- ings—coffee sweetened with icicles—gutta percha biscuits—fiabby steaks—dull razors—corns—coughs —oholics—rhubarb—aloes—miaery, Ste—American Paper. Dean Swift had occasion one day to unite a rustle couple in the bonds of matrimony. The ceremony over, the husband began to "sink in rusolution,land falling into a fit of repentance, he said: "Your reverence has tied the knot tightly, I fancy, but, under favour, may I ask if so be you can untie it again?' "Why, no," replied the dean, "we never do that on this part of the conse- crated ground," " Where, then ?" cried the man, eagerly. "On that," said the dean, pointing to the burial-ground.

A COMPROMISE. —A lady was recently waited on by a poor woman, who lived in the neighbour- hood, and who solicited charity, urging that she had named her child after the lady. "I had understood that the little one was a boy," said the lady.—" So it is," said the other—" Certainly, then, you could not have given it my name."—" I know it," said the other, "but your name is Augusta, and I named my boy Augustas, which is so near it that I thought you would give me a new fro& for him; and I will do without the hat on account of the difference in the last syllable." crup-rasurosen I-I al =..rf. amnia ago, two aged men, near 111d.rshalton, traded—or, according to Virginia parlance, swapped horses, en this condition—that on that day week, the one who thought he had the best of the bargain should pay to the other two bushels of wheat. The day came, and as luck would have it, they met about half way between their respective homes. "Where art thou going ?" said one—" To thy house with the whet," answered the other ; "and whither art thou riding!"—" Truly," replied the first, "I was taking the wheat to thy. house."—Each, pleased with his bargain, had thought the wheat justly due to his neighbour, and was going to pay it.

The Villa Palmieri, where the Queen will shortly take up her residence, is two miles north-east of Florence, whence it is approached by a narrow road known as the Via Boccaccio, which was widened on the occasion of the Queen's last visit so as to permit of two carriages passing one another. It is also lined with lamps. The villa stands conspicuous, backed by a steep and wooded hill and close to the road. It is a large, low, flat-roofed edifice, quad- rangular in form, with a beautiful courtyard and frescoed walls. From the terraced garden near the house only the north-western part of Florence can be seen, but better views of the fair city by the Arno with its domes and towers, may, of course, be had from the adjacent heights. Florence is scarcely less interesting than Venice, not only for its glorious works of art, but also for its associations. The neighbourhood of the Villa is also rich in these, for apart from its connection with Boccaccio, it was here that Lorenzo the Magnificent loved to live, and here in a villa that he built Cosmo del Medici died.

The Marquess of Huntly, on whom Aberdeen Uni- versity is to confer the degree of LL.D., is hardly a bookish man, but he has rendered considerable ser- vice to the educational institution which has just lost the brilliant Professor Minto. Lord Iluntly is one of the handsomest of the Scotch peers—tall, well-built, fair, with regular features, and a pleas- ant smile. He looks best in the kilt, and when he is at Aboyne, the family place on Daeside, he is very food of wearing it. His lorship is the titular head of the Gordons, who once were an exceedingly powerful clan in the north. So, of course, there is a Gordon tartan, and certainly it is much prettier than the Duff tartan appertaining to the chieftain- of the Duke of Fife.

That rising hope of the Tories, the Hon. George Nathaniel Curzon,M.P.,is back in London after a tour through Corea, Annam, and Siam. Since he ceased to " orate " at Oxford, as President of the Union, Mr. Curzon has been mightily fond of making Asiatic tours, and writing about them. It was largely duo to the popular superstition that he had conquered the whole science of foreign affairs that the young member for Southport was viven the Under-Secre- taryship for India at the tail-end of the late Govern- ment. He sadly disappointed his friends in that capacity. The one incident of his brief reign wes a wordy duel with Mr. Swift DlacNeill, in which there was no doubt, even in the minds of the Tories, as to which way the fighting went. But Mr. Curzon is young yet ; lie is only thirty-three, and has seen but six years' Parliamentary life.

-- The Queen will travel by train to Portsmouth, where she will go on board the royal yacht Victoria and Albert, which is .commanded by Rear Admiral Fullerton. The Queen is on excellent sailor, and it will take more than an ordinarily rough passage to inconvenience her. The port of arrival is Cherbourg, from whence her Majesty will proceed by special train to Paris. At Paris the special train will be put on to the circular railway, and so will proceed to the Southern line. Dijon will be one of the places where a brat will be made for refreshments. The further route lies through the Mont Cents T•anael to Genoa, and thence to Florence. At the station the royal carriages,which have been sent on in advance, will meet her Majesty and conduct her and the ,uite to the Villa r almieri.

There has just died at the monastry of the Grande Chartreuse a man whose history was a romance. This was Brother Anselm, the night porter. M. de Brecourt, for such was his real name, was three times married. His first two wives had no children. The third had one child, a daugh ter,who lived to be nine or ten years old. One day the father was out shooting, and discharged his gun through a hedge. The unhappy man heard a shriek, and on going to the spot whence it proceeded found his child lying dead, killed by his own hand. M. de Br6court,it it said,literally never smiled after the event. He went into the convent as a porter,and to the very last he fulfilled without complaining the most menial d uties.

The death of Madame GrOvy, the wife of a famous President of the French Republic, is an event that has attracted little attention on this side the Chan- nel. Yet her life was not without romance. The daughter of a tanner at Narbonne, on the death of her father she came with her mother to Paris, where they lived for some time in a very humble way. The extreme beauty of the daughter struck the future President, who in tho.t days was nearly as obscure as the girl whose hand he sought. But so poor were his prospects that his offer was declined. Some sears later, however, when M. Grevy had attracted some attention in high quar- ters, he renewed his offer with success. But to the I last Madame Grovy remained what she had always been—of a singularly retiring disposition, avoiding publicity, distrusting politics, and not in the least implicated in the faults with which M. Grevy and his son-in-law have been charged by their enemies.

Sir William Harcourt is not the only man in the House of Commons who can claim to be the des- cendant of kings. Sir H. Meysey-Thompson, who the other day introduced that blessed word bimetal- lism to a languid house. can boast of direct descent in the female line from the first Henry and the first and second Edwards. This is due to the marriage t,f his father, the first Sir Henry Meysey-Thompson. with a daughter of the late Sir John Croft,in whose veins flowed the blood of all the Percys, the De Cliffords, and the Mor- timers. But Sir Henry Meysey-Thompson is too busy with bimetallism to worry about his pedigree, and hi A utterances lack the regal solemnity of Sir William Harcourt's.

The Hon. Duncan Gillies, who, according to the cable, is coming to London to fill the port of Agent- General for the Colony of Victoria, is a typical specimen of the Scotchinan who succeeds in the colonies. He landed in Melbourne in his twentieth year, but, unlike a good many young Britons who hang about Melbourne and sink into incurable vagabondage, he courageously started up country on foot, and earned his first ss. in Australia by breaking stones on the road-side. That humble beginning of his colonial career contrasts curiously with his coming back to London as the ambassador of his colony at a salary of £3,000 a year.

He was one of the first of the adveaturous young men to arrive on the famous Ballarat goldfields, sixty miles from Melbourne, and there he laid the foundation of his fortune. He worded as an ordin- ary red-shirted gold digger, but he also soGn stepped to the front as a spokesman of his brother diggers, then ground down by a despotic Government with an arbitrary ex-captain of the Royal Navy at its head. He achieved so much local celebrity as a speaker at the monster open-air meetings which the Ballarat diggers held to ventilate their wrongs that, when the battle was won and the diggers were authorised to return members to the Victorian Parliament, it was only natural that he should be one of the first of their chosen M.P.'s. Ever since, for close on forty years, he has sat in the Victorian Parliament, and of these forty years fifteen were spent on the Treasury bench. When last in office it was as Prime Minister, and it is quite likely that the danger of his becoming Prime Minister was one of the reasons that impelled the new Victorian Government to offer him the tempting bait of the colony's ambassador in London.

By the death of Mr. George Graham, of Yardley, we have lost one of the most prominent agricul- turists of the Midlands. The son of a Scotch farmer, and born at Bannockburn, he came south with his family when quite a child, and was brought up in Oxfordshire. His original profes- sion was that of land surveying, but he did not pursue it after he completed his articles, turning his attention to grain dealing, in which he and his brother established a very wide connection. In 1858, however, he struck out a fresh line by raising a herd of Shorthorns, which by careful breeding from pure strains of Knightly and Bates blood be- came one of the most celebrated in the country, fancy prices being always obtainable at periodical sales of the stock. He was equally successful fifteen years later in raising a flock of pure-bred Shropshire sheep, and as much as three hundred guineas has been paid at times for his rams. The Yardley stud has also a name on the turf, its fame commencing with Whisper. Her third foal was Sterling, the greatest handicap horse of the century and from him have sprung a wonderful succession of equine celebrities, including Isonomy, Energy, Paradox; Enterprise, Hurvester, Fernandez, and Enthusiast, with Common in the third generation. Mr. Graham married the daughter of a German baron, and leaves five children, all girls.

How to extinguish fire in a chimney. Throw some powdered brimstone on the fire in the grate, or ignite some on the hob, and then place a board or something in front of the fireplace to prevent the fumes descend- ing into the room. The vapour of the brimstone as- cending the chimney will then effectually extinguish the soot on fire.

Gingerbread. Two cups of brown sugar, one cup of butter, mixed to a cream. Add two well-beaten eggs, a cup of sour milk, a teaspoonful of soda, the same of ginger, a pinch of salt, and flour enough so you can roll out the dough and make into a sheet half an inch thick. It will take about three pints of flour. When baked, glaze the top with a mixture of molasses and water or the beaten white of an egg. French Pudding. • One quart of milk, ten tablespoonfuls of flour, eight eggs. Beat the eggs very light, and add them to the milk with the flour. Butter a pan, pour in the mixture and bake it. Serve it hot, with sweet sauce.

Baked Custard. Beat four eggs very light, or until they do not string, and stir them into a quart of rich, sweet milk ; add sugar to taste, and a teaspoonful of extract of vanilla, or whatever flavour is preferred. Either bake in cups or in a pudding dish set in a pan of water in a moderate oven. Be careful to remove before the custard becomes watery. Try it by thrusting a spoon in one of the cups; if not firm, bake a little longer.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
DIARIST NELLIE.

As I said last week, hats and bonnets are for the most part law, made in straws of two colours, the crown being of the lighter shade—brown an 4 straw, brown and pink, green and black, pink and red. The leading spring flowers are :. violets, polyanthus, auriculas, cowslips, and tulips ; they are most effective in velvet. Upstanding feathers are still much worn, but these having been in favour during the past winter, flowers are fresher and more spring-like. A hat of black satin had the brim edged with a narrow ostrich feather trimming, and around the crown petunia. coloured velveteen was arranged in vandyke points. At the one side were two upright black plumes and right in front a small flat black satin bow.

Spring materials are showing their crisp and fresh faces, and not a few summer materials may already be seen in the leading houses. Oi course, nothing is definitely chosen yet awhile, and will not be for at least another fortnight. Spring goods are nearly every one shot or shaded, and plain materials other than thin cloths or thickly-ribbed aerges— and even some of the latter are woven in two colours—appear to be somewhat tabooed, although plain twills in greens, soft browns, beige, and stone, and the evelpopular though somewhat fatiguing petunia or n,hlia tints, are still amongst the early season's selections for morning or walking dresses. Greys and "mastic "or putty tints there are in abundance, shot with soft pretty colours either in silk or wool; spongy and other cropons following suit. Some of the ex epons have a narrow stripe of silk and an intervening one of crinkled crepon ; others, again, have the silken line embroidered with dots er tiny flowerets. Speckles, dots, checks, and fine stripes, dotted or speckled over, are amorlgst the newest designs, both on woollen goods or soft measseline-de-laines.

Coming to walking dresses a very dainty frock was of heliotrope diagonal cloth, made in the usual gaffe pplaifl skirt with a triple band of golden otter fa- The bqioe was of cloth, made quite laced tilt& hick, frill in the same shade of Bengikhe hifining_a kind of ca e, edged with fur; high EmpireTelt-EV s;ik gathered in at the elbow la.& utak nt tur ; rot. thene tight aleeigi to the wrist, Anislea off with a band of fur. Hat of a rich shade of prune- coloured velvet toning with the heliotrope; high, upstanding hnlys of velvet at a7:iiicie. the nal i_kc2,llllrikags of t e oco ou . 1 Tv-ad- is still fo the fore lii Thed gie _de wit iti checks, laFge "Find small, all made in the 1830 style, narrow at the waist and full at the hem, with velvet yokes and sleeves. Another charming dress was of silk cri3pon, and Was accompanied by a short cape of black lace and jet. A full crown of soft grey silk to the hat was the only lighten- ing note to this costume.

In Paris I am told that the Empire style has lived. With the exception of robes d'interieur, or tea gowns, and mantles, the short.waisted frocks have bad their day. The very moment fathers, husbands, brothers, and cousins, not only set their face against, but turn into ridicule some pet fancy, there is no gainsaying the fact the vagary is doomed Women have gone home and pondered and have rapidly concluded that the men have this time—just for once—judged a fashion rightly. Hence its rapid d•sappearahce. The jaunty and dapper Louis Philippe, or 1830 and thereabouts, fashions are first favourites in the field, not only for day, but evening gowns also, although the Ann of Austria or Louis XIII. style, with its iiitiler fall skirts and handsome collars of Mazarene guipure, are perhaps prettier, or, more properly speaking, more picturesque and ornamental. I have seen a charming Recamier jacket. This style of jacket fouhd the greatest favour in my eyes when composed, of a rather dull chestnut cloth, with a velvet cape in the bright ruddy shade of the same colour, and bordered around with an edging of black ostrich tips. The hat worn with this is of the same shade of chestnut-brown velvet as the cape, and lined underneath with black vel- vet. The sole trimming is a large butterfly bow of black velvet, seemingly held in place by a rosette.

You will, I am sure, be glad to hear that blouses will be as much worn as ever this summer. We are too sensible, I hope, to discard a pretty, simple, and thoroughly comfortable garment, than which nothing better for summer morning wear in town or country could possibly be devised, on such a ground as this. As a matter of fact, a well. made blouse is perfectly distinguishable from a cheap, ready-made article. I can certainly con- ceive no garment that could possibly replace it in the favour of women of all classes. Yours ever, JENNIE.

div.head: STONES THAT WILL BEND.
div.p: STONES THAT WILL BEND.

Of most stones rigidity is one of the most marked characteristics, and it is hard for uninformed people to believe that there are any stones that can be bent. There are soi.,e, however, that are more flexible thin wood and bend readily under slight pressure without breaking. The most abundant of these is itacolumite, of flexible sandstone, which is found in large deposits in Brazil. This stone is composed of separate grains of sand cemen- ted together with a mineral closely resembling mica or sericite. The minerals being quite flexible in themselves confer the same property upon the stone as a whole. The way in which the cementing material was introduced into the itacolumite is rint easy of explanation. Mica and sericite are not soluble and could not have been deposited by water like calcite or silica. It is most prob- able that they were originally introduced in the form of clay or some similar material and afterwards metamor- phosed by heat, pressure, and superheated steam into micaceous mineral. Instances of a similar change of one material species into another are very common.

div.head: CROCODILES.
div.p: CROCODILES.

Major F. J. N. Ind, of Miley, is anxious to (Lacer- tain,it possible, what are the greatest sizes to which crocodiles and sharks have respectively been known attain, and furnishes to the " Field " a few notes and reminiscences. On one occasion, he says, I killed a crocodile which was reported to have caught at diffe- rent times and eaten no less than seven men, among them a tappal-runner (postman) with the mail bag. The beast was described to me beforehand by natives of a neighbouring village as having a peculiar flesh mark on one side of his head, and by this he was clearly identified after capture. The news of his death spread rapidly. and I was escorted to my jungle quarter 4 be the whole of the available population, inchltlie,k man musicians of great power. As an itlance of the vora- city of the crocodile I may Menl that two of my old brother officers—the la"— Major Pelly and Captain Bur- ton (brother of the traveller) were once crossing a small river in Ceylon on horseback, when Pelly, who was in front, hearing a shout from his companion, looked back , and saw a crocodile head and shoulders out of the water in sharp pursuit, as he thought, of a horse. To save time, Pelly jumped off and scrambled to land as fast as he could, but the reptile landed also, and actually ran after him for some little distance on terra firma. I have never heard of a parallel case to this.

div.head: DOWN THE MOUNTAIN TO DEATIL
div.p: DOWN THE MOUNTAIN TO DEATIL

At four o'clock on the morning of November 8th,1875, an express train on the Lehigh Valley Railway in America, was on the top of a mountain, eighteen miles above the city of Wilkosbarre. Among the passengers were the President of the United States and several members of his Cabinet, in a special coach. From this point the grade was very steep, and the road full of curves. It was the custom to keep the brakes sat all the way down. If they failed, disaster was sure to follow. Within a minute after the train started, the driver noticed that something had suddenly gone wrong with the brakes. The train .kept pushing the engine. He reversed,but without checking the speed. Seeing this, the guard and one or two other train men jumped, and escaped with only slight injuries. The train now ran faster and faster, and a horrible death seemed wait- ing for all on board. The driver blew the whistle con- tinuously to warn trains at the foot of the mountain of his alproach. -When ,the runaway passed Nescopeck station it was goingst rate of nearly seventy miles an hour, and the faithful driveretood at his post,bareheaded holding on, and still blowing the •whistle. At the foot of the mountain all the trains had got out of the way except the rear end ot a coal train which was just shunt- ing. Into this the paisenger train train dashed with a crash that was heard for miles around, knocking the coal cars in all directions. The passengers were badly shaken, and some were bruised, but none were killed. But where was the brave driver ? From under the wreck of the overturned engine he was taken an hour afterwards, crushed and dying, but still able to speak. "Is the Pres;dent safe ?" he gasped. " Yes, and every. body else," was the answer. " Thank God for that," he said, and never spoke again. A splendid deed, truly, yet there is not a driver in a hundred who would not have stood to his duty with the same fidelity. Exposed to all sorts of weather, to con- stant danger, and laden with responsibility, the engine drivers have a commendable record, and deserve higher appreciation both by the companies and by the public. "I am an engine driver," says Edward Roberts, "and have been for eleven years. My health was always good until July, 1885. Then something came over me that I couldn't account for. I felt tired, sleepy, and languid. My stomach felt sour and cold, my mouth tasted awfully bad, and my tongue was thickly coated. A disagreeable fluid came up into my mouth, and my appetite failed. No food, however light, agreed with me, and I had great pain after eating anything at all. In ten minutes my stomach would be all in a ferment, and swell like as a balloon does when the gas is running into it. I had also a miserable tightness around my chest and sides. Later on I had awful pain in the kidneys. I could not rest at night; I had dreadful drea ms, and would turn and turn in bed, but found no ease.

" As time went on I got weaker and weaker until I could scarcely crawl to my work, but having a large family to support I struggled on as best I could, when many another would have been confined to bed. As it was, my sufferi ng,was so great that I went to bed as soon as I returned from my work. For over four years

I went on in this fashion, about half alive and half dead obtaining no relief from the medicines the doctors gave me. I took six bottles of pepsine, but it did no good, neither did the seven bottles of a medicine we sent over and got from Dublin.

" In May, 1890, a lady who called at my house, told me of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Syrup, and re- commended me to try it ; so I got a bottle from Mr. Wile on, at Drug Hall, Holyhead, and began taking it; In a week I felt better, my stomach was easier, and my food digested, and I gradually gained strength. By the time I had taken six bottles I was strong as ever. I could eat anything and have kept well ever since. I have told of my recovery everywhere, and many of my
friends have used the Syrup with benefit. I wish my experience to be published, and will reply to inqtilrles about my case.
(Signed) " EDWARD ROBERTS, No. 9, Tyn Pwll-road, Holyhead." What originally brought on this wretched attack of

indigestion and dyspepsia—which through lack of the proper remedy became chronic—Mr. Roberts does not say, even if he knows. Probably the cause was ex- posure, and a hasty and irregular habit of eating. At

all events he was fortunate in learning of Mother Seigel's Syrup before it was too late. We congratulate him on this point, and are confident his frank statement will be of use to others of his honourable and responsible calling. For one, the writer of these lines never lies comfor- tably back r,n the cushions in a first class carriage on the excellent North-Western Railway without hoping (selfishly enough, to be sure) that all is well in mind and body with the man who drives the iron horse.

div.head: l''CrT TO TIIE PROOF
div.p: l''CrT TO TIIE PROOF

Gwen was standing at the drawing-room window, screened by the soft falling lace curtains, when Ronald Chilton rode up and dismounted at the side' 1 porch. She watched him idly, a flush kindling and clespelin7., on her cheeks. She saw Mrs. Quillet meet him respectfully and conduct him into the house, while a stable lad led away the horse. Still Mr. Chilton did not enter the drawing-room as she expected, and the sound of the library door closing informed her that he had been shown into that apartment. What could it mean? Had the butler sought private speech with Mr. Chilton. Gwen asked herself these questions in an odd tremor and suspense. She had waited a month for an answer from Squire Markham to the letter of the Quillets, but no one had come. During these weeks she had changed greatly. The communication with the housekeeper had made to her concerning her origin, had not crashed her as the Quillets had expected; had not broken her high spirit. She seemed to have gained a new hauteur. Her pure, proud, high-bred face had gained in all these characteristics. The Quillets said to themselvees how well she bore the revelation nf her true history. They never dreamed of the sleepless, sorrowful nights, of the hidden anguish, of the bright young life poisoned at its spring • they never suspected how heavy was the burden ;hey had laid upon her, nor how she sickened of her existence, and wished that she had died in her mother's arms in that wild storm of nearly seventeen years ago. With all her added pride, despite her increased hauteur, Gwen exhibited a strange humility in the presence of the Quillets. She felt grateful to them for all they had done for her, and begged Mrs. Quillet to give her work to do, and to allow her to give up her present rooms; but the housekeeper, colder and more severe than ever, bade her continue to occupy the house, and wait patiently for a letter from the squire. The Quillets, connecting her with all the trouble their lives had known, felt harshly towards her. And they made her life doubly bitter to her, when a little sympathy might have lessened her load. _ _ .

Driven back upon herself, suffering as only a great and sensitive nature can suffer, Gwen bore all her horrible torture with an outward calmness and cold- toss. But under that ice a great fire was burning. The Quillets, scorning more like enemies than friends, and avoiding her, Gwen's only gleam of cgmfert during thesQ Weeks had been the visits of lir. Chrit'ini. _

She had never thought of him as a lover. He had come to Lonemaor almost daily; had talked to her of art and literature; had brought much sweetness into the bitterness of her life, and she had grown to look for his coining as one in darkness looks for the sunshine. . .

_ . tat can Mr. Quinot be ksing to him?" she asked herself, uneasily, withdrawing from the window to a sofa. "Can he he telling him not to come here again 7" She took up some embroidery, making an effort to work upon it, While her thoughts flew to the liorary, and speculated as te what was passing therein. .
But even her wildest speculations never came near the truth. _ _ _ . .

For Mr. Quillet, in the grim, hard way, was tel- ling her story, with but one reserve, to her admirer. "Mr. Chilton," he said, when they bad entered the library, "you will wonder that I should ask a private interview with you; I, who am only a butler —a servant in this house. But in Squire Markham's absence I and my wife are in charge here. And we are Miss Winter's actual and only guardians. I want to speak to you of her. Ronald Chilton bowed gravely. He was too true a gentleman to show surprise at this address, even from a butler.

"You visit Lonemoor very often, Mr. Chilton," pursued Mr. Quillet, in some embarrassment. "You are in truth, Miss Winter's only visitor. But that she has no friends or acquaintances here, and that she is newly come from school, I think I should not have allowed your visits. But in view of her lone. unoss and your credentials, A have been glad to have you come." Mr. Chilton again bowed. "I am not a gentleman," continued the butler, still greatly embarrassed; "but I have my own ideas of honour. And it has seemed to me that you ought not to see Miss Winter again until I have spoken to you about her. The people here. abouts speak evil things of her. Have you heard them ?" - -

Ronald Chilton's blue eyes flashed. "No one has dared to speak disrespectfully of Miss Winter," he exclaimed. "No one has ever spoken her name to me." The butler drew a sigh of relief. "Let me tell you what is said," he remarked. "The bailiff's son—young Mr. Orkney—wants to marry Miss Winter. She has refused him. Ile persecutes her with his attentions. His family are greatly opposed to the match, and have set afloat vile stories to the effect that she is a foundling, a beggar, and all that sort of thing." Mr. Chilton's face flushed, but he did not speak. "There is some foundation for their stories, sir," said Mr. Quillet reluctantly. "Miss Winter is a lady. You hardly need that I should tell you that. Her mother was a lady before her—a lady born.and bred. Her life had a sorrowful—an awful—ending. Let me tell you how she died." Simply and briefly the but'er told of the terrible storm in which the mother of Gwen had come to LonenAaor. He spoke of her youth and beauty. He told that she was insane. Then he told how a month later, leaving behind her the infant to which she had given birth at Lonemoor, she had gone forth in storm and terror to her death. Mr. Quillet made no attempt to gloss aver his opinion of the dead girl. He told of the headstone at her grave in Penistone, and of the name be had caused to be cut upon it. He mentioned without boasting what he had done for Gwen, how she had been educated and cared for, and concluded— " Now you know all, sir. Miss Winter is refined and accomplished—a lady, whatever her parentage. It was my duty to tell you the truth. She is likely to be sent away from here any day. I have nothing more to say. Shall I order your horse, sir 1' He moved towards the bellpull secretly anxious and trembling. "Certainly not," replied Mr. Chilton quietly. "I came to call upon Miss Winter. I will join her now. Gwen was busy with her embroidery when he came in. She arose, and he noticed how she had changed sinoe that day of their first meeting upon the moor. The change had come so gradually that he had not observed It till now. He went up to her, exchanged greetings, and sat down beside her. He seemed in an unusually merry mood this morning, and Gwen's smiles returned to the lips they seemed to have deserted. It must not be supposed that Ronald Chilton was insensible to the advantageS of birth and connec- tion. The story told him by the butler had wounded him to the quick, for he had grown to love Gwen with all the ardour of a fervent and impetuous nature. But he was noble and chivalrous in the highest degree. Gwen would be only Gwen if she were a duke's daughter. And with her burden of sorrow and possible disgrace, lonely, poor and friendless, Gwen was Gwen still, peerless among women—the only woman he had ever loved I His heart yearned over her now in her desolation, He knew what she must suffer. He longed te gather her into his arms and shield her from Oat whole cruel world. His tongue ceased his pleasant jests and silence fell between them. Gwen looked up in surprise, and met his gaze, full, tender, and worshipping, fixed upon her. She blushed and trembled.

"Gwen," said Mr. Chilton softly, "I love you. We have not 'known each other a long time if we count by days and weeks; but we have learned to know each other well, have we not? Will you be my wife?" The passionate tenderness with which this state. ment was uttered went to Gwen's heart. A greai answering tenderness awoke in her soul. She could not answer.

He seized her hand, and in quick impetuous worde he urged his suit. Her silence, her blushes, her downcast eyes, her very trembling, all betrayed to him that she returned his love. The truth, too, rushed upon Gwen's heart in a flood. "Tell me that you love me,' he whispered. And Gwen told him, not in words, but in blushes. He caught her in his arms, and bestowed upon her a lover's embrace. And then Gwen remem- bered. She disengaged herself, and said, des. perately— " Ronald—Mr. Chilton—l forgot—l cannot bt your wife !" "And why not, Gwen ?" "I cannot tell you, except that I am not what you think me. I am not a relative of Squire Mark. ham. I have no right here. I have no name even," said Won Gwen, hanging her head.

7 "Irr. Quillet has told-ine all that you know your- self of your own history, Gwen," said her 16ver. "And there is no reason why you should not become my wife. No false notions shall stand between you end me, Gwen. I shall not give you up. I shall not heed your scruples!' " But your friends ?" "I have no mother," said Mr. Chilton. "The only friend I have to consult is my father, Viscount Chilton, who is now at our country home in Berks. I shall write to him this evening.' The title, "Viscount" Chilton, struck upon Gwen's heart like a blow. If Ronald's father were noble he would never accept her, as a daughter. in- law. Ronald read her thoughts. "My father has no other child," he said. "and regards my happiness above all other considerations. He would love you, Gwen. I shall insist upon a speedy Marriage, and take you home to Chilton Park. This is no place for you." "Lord Chilton will never consent to our marriage, Ronald. It will be better so. You ought to marry a lady of family—" "Whether I will or no?" interrupted Ronald, smiling. "No, Gwen, I shall marry for love and love only." He emphasized the declaration, after an auda- cious fashion, with!). kiss. _

The girl Lew little of the world. She but vaguely comprehended how, by reason of her birth, she was set apart from other people. She knew herself worthy of even the Hon. Mr. Chilton. and she could see no reason why, if he also deemed her worthy and loved her, she should not marry him. Yet a foreboding of trouble came upon her even in her joy. "I think Lord Chilton will refuse his consent," she said. "And until you gain his consent I will not allow you to bind yourself to me by an engage- ment. No, Ronald, you shall be free and unfettered until you have his answer. Don't urge me. I know I am right." She would not turn from this resolve.

"I shall claim the eights of an engaged lover," said Ronald. "I will come over and see you again in the morning. May I not ?" "You will always be welcome. But I shall not expect you. Mr. Quillet has told you my history. It is all fresh in your mind. You are sorry for me, end have spoken on impulse. Think over the matter to-night, Ronald, and if reflection brings change of purpose I shall not blame you. I shall not expect you.,, When he went away an hour later she repeated these words to him.

And yet when morning came she did expect him. She dressed herself prettily for his eyes, and took her place in thn drawing-room, watching the moor eagerly anit Ten o'clock struck, and he did not come. Eleven chimed, and still he did not appear. Had reflection liwought a change of purpose? Had he been eadied away by impulse on the previous day, and since regretted his precipitancy? "If he isn't here by noon I shall give him up," thought Gwen. Eitt noon Passed, and still he wag missing. The whole dreary day wore away, and no message came from him. "He has taken me at my word," the girl said to herself. "I shall never see him again. 1 have lost my lover, and lost him for ever I"
CHAPTER XV/I. DuNaoLm CASTLE.

The Darkwood estate in Shropshire comprised nearly a score of valuable farms, a magnificent park, and extensive home grounds, laid out in the high- est style known to modern landcsape gardening. A streams: of water known as Dark river ran through Its domain. Dnnholm Castle was situated in the midst et the park upon the summit of a hill, and commanded a prospect for miles in every direction. This was one of the "stately homes of England" which art and wealth had combined to render a very Paradise. And it was this home that had fallen so uunex- pectedly to the inheritance of Captain Tollisb. The late Lord Darkwood had enjoyed his title. and honours for about ten years, having inherited them from his father. The late marquis had spent little time in his ancestral home, seeming devoured by a secret unrest. He had cared nothing for society, and had lived a lonely bachelor existence on board his yacht, in the Highlands, or in London. In his early manhood he had been intimate with his cousin, Fabian Tollish, but they had long since become estranged, and during his later years they had seen nothing of each other. Lord Darkwood and Captain Tollish had been as unlike as day and night. Lite former had been noble, brave, and truthful, the very model of an English gentleman. In his young years lie had hen frank and unsuspecting, ot a joyous and confiding nature; but long before his accession to the mar- quisate he had become grave and stern and silent, a man upon whom some secret sorrow brooded heavily, or who had tried the world, and found its best pleasures all unsatisfactory. He had been adored by his tenantry, and honoured by all who knew him.
Such was the man whom Captain Tollish was to succeed as lord of Dar kwood.

It wai late in the afternoon of a pleasant October day when the new Lord Darkwood and Mr. Sutton alighted from the train in the Shrewsbury station. The Duckweed carriage was in waiting, with coach- man and footman all in deep mourning. The mar- quis and his lawyer entered the vehicle, Pietro mounted beside the driver, and they set out briskly for Dunholm Castle. When the town had been left behind the new lord thrust his head from the carriage window, and surveyed the landscape with eager greedy eyes. ' "We have some miles to go before we come in sight of the Darkwood property, my lord," said Mr. Sutton. "Yes, I know," said the marquis, impatiently. "I know the estate thoroughly. I spent much time there in my boyhood. I know every copse and dingle, every nook in the great park, every turn and bend in Dark river. I never suspected that I should one day be master here." 1 "No—how could you suspect it?" said Mr. Sutton. "The thing would then have seemed impossible. Who could have foreseen that the late lord would never marry? Who could have foreseen that his ' younger brothers wopd die young and also tunne.r- ried ? Why, in your boyhood, my lord, the old marquis, your uncle, was living. He was a stern, hard man, with a will of iron. He kept his sons in subjection to him until the day of his death. But under his rile the property doubled in value. You, my lord, will reap the benefit of his wise out- lay of care and money.' The marquis laughed, his round, fat face expres- sive of a malicious delight. "I wonder my uncle don't rise from his grave to resist my succession," he exclaimed. "He never liked me. His younger brother, Fabian Charteris, married a great heiress Miss Tollish, and changed his own name for that Of his wife, an act which my uncle never forgave. And he seemed to regard me with peculiar dbilike because I bore the name of Tollish instead of Charteris. I hope that he knows that Fabian Tollish, his hated nephew, is now lord in his stead. And my cousin who has just died j kated me also. We had long been enemies."

Mr. Sutton did not answei:. In truth he felt a sense of disgust for his new employer. When they neared the boundaries of the Dark. wood property the marquis became wrapt in his observations. He had keen eyes for the farms and ho,:ses they passed. He saw some of his tenants. They looked contented and prosperous, "They'll bear having the rents raised," thought Lord Ds.rkwood. "They have got no easy landlori low, I can assure them. The income is already lrincely ; but I can double it, and I will." They passed through the little village of Dunholm, a pretty little place, set on the edge of the park, with brick houses in the midst of gardens, a feu shops, including a smithy, an inn, and a post-office, and they then turned aside into the park, proceed. lug by a wide, winding avenue, bordered with stately trees, to the castle. A drive of over two miles brought them in sight of the castle, and they were then within a few rode of its door. Upon the broad, slightly wooded slop that stretched before the extensive buildings a few fallow deer were browsing. The carriage whirled up the drive and entered the porch. The gentlemen alighted and slowly entered thc dwelling. . . .

The servants were marshalled to receive them, headed by the butler and housekeeper. The mar. quis spoke to the two latter—he remembered them well —nodded to the rest, and passed into the drawing-room. "At last," said Lord Darkwood, with a dark jubi- lance that impressed the lawyer unpleasantly, "1 stand at the summit of my ambition. I am a peer of the realm. lam rich beyond my wildest dreams. I have nothing to wish for save one thing." "And that 1" "Is a wife. I ought to marry," and Lord Dark- wood began to swell himself, and to walk up and down the room importantly, feeling every inch his grandeurs. "All this great castle needs is a mis• tress. The rustle of woman's garments in these rooms— these big apartments filled with guests— laeople 01 the terracee-z-these would take away the

dreariness n-630 only too apparent. A big fiousi should be well filled." "It is strange that you never married, my lord," said Mr. Sutton. Lord Darkwood's face clouded. "I have been married," he said briefly. wife is dead 1" The lawyer looked surprised. "I had never dreamed of your being married, my lord," he exclaimed. "I always supposed you, like the marquis, a bachelor. I remembered your entanglement with Miss Markham. Was it s'ne whom you married ?" A gleam of passionate regret appeared in Lord Darkwood's eyes. "Miss Markham was the only woman I ever loved," he exclaimed. "The only woman, Sutton. I ever cared for. Her memory will haunt me to my death. But let her name be buried, as 4 has been for years. I thought you had forgotten it. Never speak it again. Miss Markham died, and I married the orphan daughter of a fellow officer. She brought me a fortune, which melted away somehow. She was extravagant, and so was I. The money went and she died several years ago." "Did she leave any children, my lord?' " One—a girl, now fifteen yea:s old. She is in Malta." Your daughter is your heiress, and will succeed you as owner of ill these estates, unless you should marry and have a son," said the lawyer. "The succession runs in the distaff line the male heirs
"My

failing." "My daughter would scarcely make a suitable lady of Dunholm," said Lord Darkwood. "She has grown up as a weed grows in a straggling fashion. I never had much money to spare upon her, and her advantages have been few. She has been for years in a cheap boarding house in Valetta, and is forward, tawdry—a perfect hoyden," Mr. Sutton looked shocked. "You see," continued the marquis, "I never expected this windfall, or I would have educated. the girl properly. But it is not too late. She's only fifteen. I'll send her to school somewhere. I won't} have her here, at least until after my marriage, r shall look me up a wife without delay, and settle. down to my new life as a peer and a landowner." Lord Darkwood made a brief investigation of the- rooms opening out of the drawing-room, and then, s. reposed that they should seek their own rooms to- r 0 for diaper. y The hutlee was called to show them upstairs. 1 Dinner was Retired at seven o'clock, and Lord Darkwood did the honours with a grace that be- trayed in him a fitness for the mode of life. Mr. Sutton remained at Dunholm Castle a day or two, going over the title deeds and various other documents with their new owner, and then he. refurnecrio town. Lord Darkwood and his valet settled easily into' an aristocratic existence, Pietro sharing in his masters prosperity to a remarkable extent. Ile was a " gentleman s gentleman" indeed. He had an under valet to do the most of his work, and be as promoted to be a sort of confidential friends with oculjar iflifnunities and privileges which' were the wander and envy of his fellow-servants. But though Pietro knew his master's very' thoughts, Lcird Darkwood was not so well ac- quainted with the tortuous workings of the valet's' mind. The master was secret and reserved ; the map was more so. ... The Maltese had various schemes for his future self-aggrandisement, of which 'the marquis had no conception, and one of these—the most important —has already been revealed to the reader. Pietro remained at the castle a month in perfect contentment. Then he expressed his desire to go up to London on business. "Business 1" echoed the marquis. "What business have you in London?' "I have a brother there," was the answer, "and he is ill. He has written me to come to him, and as the new valet begins to understand his duties, I can easily be spared for a week, my lord." "You can go," answered the marquis. "That brother of yours is always unfortunate, it seems to me. I should hope he would die, if I were you, Petro.'.- • - ' , . The Maltese shrugged his shoulders and depauted. He went straight up to London by mail train, but he did not stop there to visit his relative. Ile spent a night at.a lodging-house in Leicester.tquare frequented by his compatriots, and the next day journed to Yorkshire. "I'll go to Lonemoor," was his resolve. "11l inquire if the girl is living. I'll see her, if she is. And servant or no, I mean to marry her 1 lam the first to search out Miss Markham's child. And when she is in my hands I shall command a for- tune.," With high hopes and vaulting aspirations he was Lorna swiftly onward to his destination.
(To be continued.)

div.p: SOMNIA.

In this stirring age of ours Len—and wolneEll too—are so much intellecrnally worked, or 8' emotionally disturbed, that their brains have 1110 to do than they can accomplish and yet preseqe their normal balance. Mental work, whether it 11 simply preceptional, intellectual, emotional, Off volitional, requires that an increased amount blood shall flow to the brain; hence during men,,tr4 exertion of any kind the cerebral vessels become tended owing. to the increased volume of blood to" 4.118 . . .

contain, and they remain in this condition as long as exertion is continued. It it is too intense, or if be Prr, severed in for too long a period without them 19'3°4 alternations of rest, the vessels lose their contractibility', and remain in a permanently enlarged state. The are,theretore, not able to contract so as to procure slee4. A state of cerebral congestion is established, and ic,1".„6 fulness is the result. Such persons go to bed pernarir feeling as if they would sleep, but no sooner do tilerr heads touch their pillows than their minds become_lor ordinately active, and they lie awake hour after to:be recalling the events of the day, or else indulging itg, !nest preposterous thoughts. The blood vessels will ne empty themselves, simply because they have lost wd, power to do so. They are like the india-rubber bari,pa that we put around big packages and leave undisturu;e for a long time. We try to use them again, and find that the elasticity which they once possessed gone.

THE LATE MR. MORLEY. The MAYOR said : Since our last meeting in this room, a figure familiar to all of us, has departed, never to return. In the death of Mr. Chorley we may deplore the less, not only of an officer of the Corporation, but 4lso ef a personal friend. The name and presence of Mri Chorley have been so long associated with our =Mei- Pal life that there is only one amongst us (Mr. Alderman Holmes) who can remember his coming into the service Of the town. For 45 years Mr. Ci orley has served the • Corporation, acid almost the whole of that time he has l'eld the responsible position of borough treasurer. It Is not saying too much that we in a great measure owe Our firm financial position to the , judicious and careful Management of our treasurer. We can safely say that' ths credit of the Corporation has never suffered in his hands. Mr. Chorley has been a true and faithful ser- 'ant. He has laboured almost unceasingly in his duties with marked fidelity and zeal. He possessed the confi- illence of the Council, and we cannot part from one who as long been familiar to us without expressing our heartfelt sorrow of the loss. I therefore beg to propose: " That this Council deeply regret the loss of so effi- cient and valuables public officer as Mr.Cliarles Chorley Who has for unwards of 43 years discharged the impor- tant and responsible duties of the office of Borough Treasurer to the entire satisfaction of the Coancil, and 9esire to place on record their sense of the zeal and strict integrity which always distinguished his services ; and that the Mayor be requested to convey, to the relatives af Mr. Chorley the expression of the deep sympathy of this Council with them in their bereavement." His private character was inevery respect equal _e his official and public character, and on whatever grounds they met him, they had felt the better for his !zilla.intance, and the better for contact with him. 2,Without question he gave a certain elevated tone to the utricial life of the Corporation. The Committee had therefore drawn up this resolution: "That the tender of Mr. William Morton to fit up and connect with telephones and wires the two intercepting depots at Howley and liardv-street, and the depot at Longford, at 235 be accepted ; subject to Mr. Morton maintaining the same at an annual charge of £1 per annum so long as the Corporation shall require him to do so." Conncillor BONNELL seconded, and the minutes were adopted.

PAVING AND SEWBELOR COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following restflutions :—" That the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 200 tons of 4-inch granite cube setts at £1 per ton, delivered at Whitecross wharf, and the tender of Messrs. John McCollough and Sons to supply 200 tons of setts at 19s. 6d. per ton, delivered at War- rington be accepted."—" That the tenders of Mr. Samuel Hutton, of Peel Causeway, for the forming and paving of Forshaw-street, at £684 45., and for the forming and paving of Henry-street, at £195 12s. 9d., be accepted." The estimates of expenditure by the Committee for the year commencing 26th March, 1893, was as follows : Paving department, £5,200; scavenging department, £3,200 ss. ; total, £8,400 ss. Councillor HEATON moved and Councillor Huxcumsox seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were carried.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that 22 cases had been taken before the Magistrates, and fines inflicted in 18 cases, three boys sent to the ship" Clio," and one girl ordered to attend school. Forty cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the Public Elementary Schools, during the month of January, was 7,917 ; corresponding period last year, 7,743 ; increase 174. The following resolution was also submitted: " That the following estimate of expendi- ture, by this committee, for the year commencing 28th March, 1893, be approved.:—Salary of Inspectors, £305 ; maintenance of boys at Industrial Schools,£2oo ; contribution to ship " Clio," £3O ; sundries, £2O ; total, £555 10s. Councillor /Imam moved the adoption of these minutes and in doing so, pointed out that their ex- penses were something like £lOO in excess of last year's expenses. This was accounted for by the fact that they had only estimated for 110 boys at the Industrial Schools, whereas they had been compelled to provide for 180. Then they had to increase the contribution to the ship " Clio " from £2O to £3O which made up the excess, with a few other extra items of expenditure. He had te mention that last Saturday an examination of children for labour certificates was held, and out of 189 appli- cants 31 passed, and there were 31 absentees. He thought the result was very satisfactory. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SHAW-GREEN seconded the adoption of the minutes, and stated that he saw the children at the ex- amination named by Councillor Fleming. He considered the result of the examination was satisfactory, and the large number which took part 'in it emphasised the great necessity for the test. He thought that more would have passed had it not been that they considered they were free, and had not been kept up with theii les- sons for some months. The minutes were adopted. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, &C. COMMITTAE. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the adoption of this Committee's minutes which contained the report of the following gilts :—Bronze cell and ring, found at Win- wick, bronze cell found at Rixton ; Mss book containing botanical notes, by Dr. Kendrick the elder, 1808, from Mr. B. Kendrick ; nineteen specimens of moths, from Mr. E. E. Lowe. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion which was carried.

-- -- This committee reported that the number of inter- ments for the past month were :—Adults 47 ; minors 38; stillborn and premature 14. Corresponding period of last year—adults, 53; minors, 47; stillborn and pre- mature 12. Councillor HUTCHINSON moved the adoption nf the minutes, and in doing so said there was nothine ef im- portance in the minutes ; everything was all right. Councillor flEavox seconded the adoption and Councillor ROBERTS said everything was not all right as Councillor Hutchinson had said. He wished to com- plain about the condition of the church at the Cemetery. When attending the funeral of the late Borough Treas- urer there on Saturday, the condition of the seats and floor was simply disgraceful. He was sorry to have to complain but Councillor Shaw Green and other members of the Council could bear out the statement. The minutes were adopted, it being decided to take Councillor Roberts's complaint into consideration.

TOWN HALL, 'PARE, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. There was nothing of importance in the minutes of this Committee which were moved and seconded by Councillors BOLTON and HILTON. Before the minutes were adopted Councillor Pinurrow said :—I should like to know if the bandstand which recently cost £390, is—(cries of " No, no," and" out of order.") The MAYOR : You are out of order. The subject is not on the minutes. Councillor DIXON considered it a very unfair thing that they could not mention anything that was not on the minutes. fie wanted to know wouldn't they answer him if he asked were they going to open the new baths. (Laughter.) Councillor BOLTON said they intended to open the new baths in two or three months. (Laughter.) The minutes were then adopted.

MARKETS COMMITTEE.--FAvocexnu SIGN. The minutes of this committee contained this notice : "The total income from all sources for the past tour weeks was £292 7s. 11d. Corresponding period last year, £262 2s. Bd. ; increase, £3O ss. 3d." Also the fol- lowing resolution :—" That the tender of Messrs. James Smith and Company, of Derby, for the supply of the un- dermentioned clothing be accepted r 2 Inspectors top coats at, £2 each ; 2 dress coats at, £2 2s. each ; 2 vests , at, 7s. each; 4 trousers at 17s. per pair. ' The MAYOR in moving the adoption of the minutes mentioned that he was happy to state that during the ' recent hard times the income of that Committee had not suffered. Be considered it a very favourable sign. Alderman BLACKIIIIRST seconded the adoption of the minutes which were adopted.

TME GAS CONIMITTRB. The Gas Committee's minutes contained the fellowing : "The average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 19.9 candles at both works."— The Town Clerk submitted a letter from the Local Gov- ernment Board dated the 6th February, 1893, with reference to the proposed loan of £20,000 for Gas Works purposes and it was resolved "That in accordance with the terms of the above letter the Town Council do hereby undertake to repay the sum of £lB,OOO, being part of the said loan of £20,000, within the period of 30 years from the date of the borrowing of such loan, and also to repay the sum of £2,000, malting together with the sum of £lB,OOO the propesed loan of £20,000, within a period of ten years from the date of tbe borrowing thereof." There was also a communication from the Local Goverment Board sanctioning the loan. The adoption of the minutes was moved by Council- lor FAIRCLOUOU , seconded by Councillor HEPHIGID, and carried. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE.—NO FRICTION! Contained in this Committee's minutes were the following resolutions :—" That the following estimate of , expenditure by this committee for the year commencing 28th March,lB93,be approved £442. Also "That in f uture no fire hydrants be fixed by the Water Department with- out a written order from this department as to the situa- tion of same." Councillor HUTCHINSON in moving the adoption of the minutes drew the attention of the Council to the expendi- ture for clothing. He said they were compelled to pro- cure the clothes because the brigade had not had new tunics or trousers for several years. Councillor MUIR seconded the adoption of the minutes and Councillor Sismv GREEN wanted an explanation about the resolution to prevent the Water Committee fixing hydrants without a written order from the Fire Engine department. It seemed to him to be rather an unjust kind of thing; it appeared to be casting a reflection upon the Water Committee. Councillor FLOOD said that he believed there had been a considerable amount of friction existing between the Water and Gas Committees for some time. ("No ! no !") This affair about the hydrants was an outcome of it. The Fire Engine Committee were quite justihed in asking that the resolution be passed. The hydrants fixed by the Water Committee were of half a dozen different kinds and were placed in positions which were not always found convenient by the firemen, and conse- quently caused much delay at the time of 8 fire. , Councillor HICATON said bethought there was no fric- tion existing now between the two Committees. It , was only right that the Water Committee should con- sult the Fire Engine Committee in laying these

hydrants. Councillor ROBERTS remarked that it would have afforded him much satisfaction had the Fire Engine Com- mittee made some provision in the estimates for a new steam fire engine. (Hear, hear.) The management of , the brigade and its condition was much superior to what it had been in the past, and he believed that every- one was well satisfied with its condition. The town had, however, much extended, and the property had in- creased greatly in value since the brigade was estab- lished, and he considered that the time was at hand when a further adoition should be made in the shape of another engine,in order that the efficiency of the brigade should be assured. Possibilities of the most grave character were to be faced, and it was for the Corpora- tion to be prepared for any emergency. Had the com- mittee made provision on their estimates for a fire engine, he was confident that they would have met with the approval of the Council if only on the score of pru- dence and economy. The MAYOR concurred in the views expressed by Councillor Roberts. Councillor R. T. Fenter.ouda spoke of the excellent manner in which the brigade was managed on the occa- sion of the fire at Mersey Mills. He said that ten minutes after telephoning to the station, the brigade was on the scene, but twenty minutes had elapsed be- fore steam was up, a delay which was probably due to

the fact of the high wind blowing down the chimney and thus creating a back draught. He advised that a gas jet should be kept continually burping under the boiler at the station' in order that, steam might More easily be raised. Had that precaution been in force steam would have been raised before the mills were reached, and the hose immediately turned on. i Every minute n the early stages of an outbreak of fire was precious, and at the Mersey Mills, at the outbreak, on February 10th, every minute wasted might have meant a loss of 23,000 • in fact; had the brigade been three minutes later he believed that the mill would have been a total loss. 7 Councillor Mom said that the question of the provision of a new fire engine was discussed at the last meeting of the Fire Engine Committee, but it was thought advis- able not to approach the Council at the present juncture as it was felt that the borough could nol well meet tho heavy expense of the fire engine—Zsoo. Councillor Dixon said that he disagreed with the pro- position that a new engine was desirable, for during the last 34 years there had only been two serious fires. Councillor ROBERTS pointed out that several large fires had occurred, and the Corporation ought not to allow the industries of the town to be jeopardized for the sake of the cost of a properly .equipped brigade. Councillor HUTCHINSON, in replying to the various comments which had been made by members of the Council,said there was a great need of another steam fire engine, as the old one had been in use for a considerable number of years. Considering,however,the great expense to which the borough had been put to this year, it was thought advisable to wait until next year. The committee had a little money in reserve, and they hoped next year to ask the Council to grant them a few hundred potinds,and they would then be able to procure a steam fire engine and thus place the brigade in a most efficient state. The minutes were then agreed to. WATER COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained a resolution that the General Purposes Committee be requested to trans- fer to this committee the duty of attending to the public fountains in the borough: Alderman Fast:comma moved the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Fmairro seconded the motion which wag carried. PENNY POSTACIE, RAILWAY RATES AND CHARGES. The General Purposes Committee recorded that the estimate of expenditure for the ensuing year by the committee is £B3B 7s. 4d. on behalf of the borough rate accounts and 488 7s. 4d. on behalf of the improvement rate account. A memorial was forwarded to the -Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Post-master Gen- eral pointing out, the popular demand which exists for the introduction throughout 11. M's. dominions of the Penny Postage. The Committee also adopted a resolu- tion on the question of railway rates. The MAYOR moved, and the DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor DIXON asked if it was wise to memorialize on the subject of railway rates and charges since the various railway companies had expressed their intention to make reductions, the Great Western Railway Com- pany in particular. He should be sorry if the Council were the means of causing further irritation. The MAYoa : We are acting in concert with other municipalities, who say that it is useless to appeal to the railway companies. If anything is done it must be done by law. Councillor DIXON : Had you memorialized at the end of January or February I would have supported you, but since that time a great change has occurred in the position of affairs. As I have already said, I should be sorry for us to cause irritation. Councillor R. F. Famownon : Not yet ; no reduction has been made yet. Councillor DIXON: The Great Western Company re- funded me without a word. The minutes were then passed. "ALL YIDDLE-DE-DE."—A "SCENE." Councillor Snew had given notice of his intention to move the following resolution :—" That the Chairman of the Gas Committee be required to state the basis of the charges for lead service pipes, and the profit charged on material." Councillor TINSLEY asked if the motion was in order. The Towe CLERIC replied by reading the following extract from the Act :—** A mereber of the Council shall not vote or take part in a discussion of any matter before the Council or a committee in which he has, directly pr indirectly, by himself or by his partner, any pecuniary interest.' I take it that the motion refers to a personal matter, and, therefore, Councillor Shaw will be out of order. Councillor Siraw :I am quite surprised to hear the Town Clerk make the remark that this is a personal , matter to me. Originally it was, but I have abolished 1 the matter in that form ,and I have taken another course. Councillor REPHEIRD (interrupting) : Is Counciller Shaw in order after the ruling of the Town Clerk? • The TOWN Cum : Councillor Shaw is in this particu- lar line of business, and whether the question is answered or not I don't think it advisable, in the in- terests of the town, for it to be put. Councillor SHAW If you rule that the motion is out of order I shall be very sorry, because there is sontething that ought to be known. The TOWN CLERK Refer the matter to the Gas Corn-

mittee. Councillor &tor : It is all fiddle-de-de talking about a committee. The MAYOR: Is it the wish of the Council that Coun- cillor Shaw should be heard? Several Voices: No, no. The MAYOR (to Mr. Shaw) : We cannot hear the motion. Councillor SnAw : It is not out of order. Councillor HIPIIIIRD : You must go on the ruling of the Mayor. THIS MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT CHURCH. ' The MAYOR announced his intention to attend the ser- vice at the Parish Church on Sunday morning (Hospital Sunday), and he would be pleased to be accompanied by as many members of the Corporation as could make it convenient to attend. TBZ APPOINTIOM OW BOROUGH TRBASURNR. It was decided to hold a special meeting of the General Purposes Committee on Monday afternoon to appoint a Borough Treasurer to succeed Mr. Chorley. The Town Clerk said it was necessary by law to fill up the appoint- ment within 21 days. The Council then rose.

RUGBY. LANCASHIRE RUGBY CUP -COMPETITION. WARRINGTON v, SALFORD. The first meeting of these clubs in the above competi- tion took place on Saturday at the New Barns enclosure. The first arranged meeting of the clubs was postponed,Sal- ford tearing the smallpox epidernic,and it may be interest- ing to note that Warrington's latest conquerors are due at Wilderspool on Monday, April 17. The fine afternoon accounted for a large attendance, and different estima- tors put down the gate as being between 8,000 and 9,000. Both clubs had strong teams up, the Salford team having two new additions in • Paul, of Swinton fame, whilst a place was found for Smith, of Radcliffe, at three-quarters, though *here the latter's qualification came in is an open question: It was nearly 3.35 when Craven kicked off, and Boscow's response saw Kent making his mark. The latter gained a little, but from the first scrimmage found the Bates were too smart for Walsh and Harley, and half-way was the scene of operations. Headway was made by Brierley and Roberts, but judicious tackling by Webster and James Bate sent play to the " Beds'" quar- ter-flag, where the tackling propensities of the Warring- ton forwards did not allow the Salford backs any chance to clear the dangerous attack. Eventually the home forwards cleared smartly, and Myles got a fine opening, but failed to account for Evans, Lawless was next to the fore With a tackle of Smith, but a concerted movement by Jolley, Donohue, and Ashton almost upset •the calculations of Paul, the Swintonian just saving. A rush, headed by Turner, was met by Smith, but, not to be denied, Thorniley and Berry each led the way, and now the Salford backs showed up with capital punting. By degrees the oval was worked to the Warrington quarters, and both John Bate and BoscoW were tackled. Higham and Jolley relieved slightly, whilst the first- named was again responsible for Paul being grassed at half-way. Smith got his side out of difficulties and from the renewed attack a smart passing movement between the, Radcliffe man, Barrett, and Myles saw Webster easily drawn, and the Salford captain got in amidst a scene of the wildest excitement. Paul made a good attempt with the place. This reverse stirred the visitors to renewed exertions, for in the drop-out we found them attacking in strong force, Webster punting to Paul, who failed to gather, and the Warringtonians had the hardest of luck in not equalizing. The visitors maintained the attack, and from a scrimmage James Bate passed splendidly to his companion half, who got in neatly, but to the astonishment of the Warringtoniaps the point was annulled. This .let-Iff saw Haslam coin- ing through a scrimmage, when Nevins and Webster blocked the way, and the former made one desperate rush which Paul could not account for. Fortunately for Salford their defence was sound, Barratt and Smith I showing up well. A series of exohanges by. Harley, Myles, and Boscow, ended to the advantage of the War- ringtonian, whilst in another raid an excellent dribble by Jolley was seconded by Fair. Turner and Ashton, and Warrington again appeared certain scorers, when Walsh saved daringly. Webster was next held on the line, and Paul appeared in a new departure when he came through a scrimmage, and reached the half-way, where the oval remained at the interval, with Salford in a majority by a try. Turner Re-started, and Lawless having a kick charged, the Warrington 'line was early threatened, Boseow saving grandly. The Iforwards packed in fine style, and Salford were over- played, for in one scrimmage the Warringtonians swept the Reds before them, Donohue Nevins, Ashton, and Berry being in the van. James Donohue, next threw across Ito Webster, but the pass was a trifle too high, and the ' Warringtonians forced their way in the Salforl quarters by superior footwork. Barratt essayed to clear, but Webster floored him in fine style, whilst Smith was up- set by Evans a minute later. The visitors were now having considerably the best of it, and a series of rushes were seconded by cross-dribbling, and when within a few yards from the line Ashton crossed to James Bate, but Roberts intercepted, and a dribble three-parts the length of the field saw Webster saving well within his own 25. The two Bates, Jolley, and Donohue were I loudly applauded for some capital short passing, and then the second penalty kick of the match fell to John Bate for a foul tackle by Walsh. Turner punted to Paul. who regained the lost ground, and another Grand Passing Display, in which the Bates and Evans shone, saw Lawless miss- ing a grand opening. Forward play claimed attention for the next few minutes, whilst just before "no side" Nevins made a desperate effort along touch, but a hasty call for a pass, spoiled an excellent chance, and the , final came with the score—Salford, a try ;Warrington nil. Teams :—Warrington • J. Boscow, back P. R. Lawless, J. W. Evans and H. Webster, three-quarter backs ; John Bate and James Bate, half backs ; H. , Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, J. Jolley' W. I Nevins, T. Donohue, J. Berry, J. T. Thorniley, and J. Bigharn, forwards. Salford: A. Paul, back; F. Myles, A. Barratt, and J. Smith, three-quarter backs; S. Walsh and C. Harley, half backs ; T. Kent, T. King, T. Craven A. Knowles, F. Knowles, J. Roberts, J. Brierley, G. Cartwright, and S Haslam, forwards. Mr. Simpson officiated as referee. WARRINGTON "A" T. SALFORD" A."—A vast amount of interest was taken in this fixture, and a crowd of several thousands assembled to witness tke fray. Both teams were very strong, and turned out exactly as selected. Salford started against the wind,and one of the fastest matches seen for some time commenced. Lally's I smartness forced the visitors to defend in the first minute, and,the quick Warrington forwards made mat- ters look exceedingly lively for the visitors, who con- ceded three minors in quick succession. Playing with tine dash the home men, headed by Holmes, Bailey, Randles, and Davies, made a grand rush right to the 25. Salford improved their position, but Rowlinson made a mess of a kick,and the Warringtonians quickly swarmed round him. These fierce onslaughts fairly roused the enthusiasm of the spectators, and many times the War- rington men were almost over, but the stubborn defence Was equal to all demands. At length Rowlinson got away, and the visitors dashing onwards forced the home teatte to defend. Not for long did the play stay in this vicisrity,•for Hampson made a fine dribble past half *v. and Barnes and Ashurst kicked cleverly to the line. While the game was raging about the quarter flag Ashurst seized possession and bluffing his opponents got a remarkably clever try. Salford showed some excellent passing,and the game settled for a few moments in mid- field. The striped jerseys were then seen heading to- wards their opponents' goal, Lally, Monks, Edwards,and Teare performing splendidly. The leather was kicked to Ashton, and before he could return Barnes closed with turn, preventing any return, and directly afterwards
