ped) ; Crompton, nothing. Barber restarted the game, which was centred at midfield. Johnson picked up and passed to Clarke, who was pulled in touch near home. A scrimmage took place, when Broome picked up for the visitors and got safely home from almost the whole length of the field. Stott took the kick, but failed to improve. Until from now to the finish the game was simply a series of scrimmages. Final result : Widnes, 4 points ; Crompten, 2 points. ASSOCIATION. WARRINGTON V. Sr. HELENS JUNCTION.—This match was played at Sutton on Saturday, before about 150 spectators. Warrington won the toss, and elected to defend the railway goal. From the kick off the home team slightly pressed, but soon found that the Warring- ton defence was good. The visitors now played up, and experiencced hard lines. From a combined rush of the Junction forwards, they were enabled to notch their first goal, owing to a mis-kick by the Warrington goal- keeper. Soon after they were credited with another. There was no further score up to half-time, the game being evenly contested. From the restart Warrington pressed, but were rather faulty with their shooting. For the next 25 minutes play was of a give-and-take charac- ter, and both goals were visited in turn, but the score remained unaltered. The Warrington team, five of whom were new players, played very well, but Bannon was slightly off form. WARRINGTON CRICKET V. LYMlL—Played at Warring- , .ton on Saturday. A strong wind was blowing across the ground, which made the play at times uncertain. Lymm kicked off, having, if anything, a disadvantage as regards the wind, but it soon became apparent that the home team was by far the better lot. They at once took the ball up to the Lymm goal, and Connor had two or three shots which went over the top. At length he registered the first goal with a strong low shot. Shortly after this Fennelly added a second. Result: Cricket club five goals to nil. WARRINGTON S. ELPHIN'S V. LIVERPOOL VICTORIA ATHLETIC.—These teams met to play their return match at Walton Bank, on Saturday, before a good gate. The homesters won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. Doughty set the ball in motion for the visitors, and assumed the aggressive only to be repulsed by Cook, who transferred play to the other end, Taylor having a shy, which the goal-keeper easily cleared. Colley scored from a scrimmage, and had hard lines. A minute or two later, Clayton had an opening, but shot wildly, and then It. Colley sent a shot against the bar, Clayton doing the same a minute or two later. Hickinbottom and Colley then showed up with a good run, but the visitors' backs were in grand form. Scarisbrick scored number two in the second half,. followed with Clayton scoring number three, Scarisbnck bringing the total up to four goals, and the whistle sounded shortly after with the result St. Elphin's, four goals ; Athletic, nil. The teams after the match sat down to a knife and fork tea, the remainder of the evenjng being enjoyably spent. RUNCORN ASCOCIANKRi Y, WWNr, CZURCIL— This match was played at Widnes, On Saturday. The first fixture between these teams on Runcorn ground resulted in a draw of two goals each. The ground was quite unfit for play, there being pools of water in several places, scrimmages in which, caused great amusement among the spectators. The home team won the toss, and placed Runcorn with wind and sun in their faces. Widnes pressed. Meiklejohn, who had been greatly bothered by A. Richards at centre half, scored a good goal for Widnes. At half time the score stood—Widnes one goal, Runcorn nil. On resuming' Runcorn with the wind now in their favour pressed considerably, and after abbut five minutes' play, the right wing forward fouled Mainwaring, and blows were exchanged. Run- corn then decided to leave the field, a procedure with which many of the spectators a greed.

Ashurst intercepting a pass ran over, and the signal for refreshment sounded. Upon the resumption, the speedy and clever Warrington forwards came swooping dawn the field, and within a few minutes Lally ran clean through the thick of his opponents, and planted the leather safely over the line. Then Salford showed up with some clever passing, and danger threatened, as a free kick sent the fray right to the line. Edwards,Eden, and Davies dribbled past midfield, but again Salford by pretty passing attacked. A fine run by Ashurst from Hampson's pass resulted in a severe struggle on the visitors' line. The visitors tried to break away, but the smart tactics of the home forwards frustrated the at- tempts: 'After Heesom had put in some splendid work aampsoni 'Barnes, and Massey passed neatly, and the last-named taking the chance ran in splendidly. The red jersey brigade then dashed away, and Rowlinson was getting clear when Heesom effected a grand tackle. Ditchfield showed up to a grand run and kick,but Ramp- son, Barnes, Massey, and Holmes regained all the lost ground,and with the game hovering in the Salford quar- ter a splendid bout of passing by Hampson, Lally, and Ashurst gave Barnes a chance, and in a cool manner he dropped a goal amidst great enthusiasm, Warrington retiring winners after a splendid game by 1-4-4 to nil. Teams :_Warrington: Heesom, back ; Potts, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarters ; Lally and Ashurst, half- backs ; Davies, Holmes, Teare, Randles,,(Bailey, Ramp- son, Eden, Monks, and Edwards, forwards. Salford: W. G. Oswald, back; E. Barratt, C. Bowker, G. Ashton and J. W. Rowlinson, three-quarters ; Ditchfield and C. Oswald, half-backs; Rawson,Hohnes, Campbell,Horrox, Davidson, Wilson Hagal, and Flindshaw, forwards. IN WARRGTON 2/6'Y. LEIGH SHAMROCKS IST.—Played at Leigh on Saturday In grand weather, and before a good attendance. Leigh started, and Daniels had a good chance, but failed to take it. The Shamrocks at- tacked, but the visitors' forwards rushed them back to halfway. A pretty piece of work by Mannion took play on the hotne goal line, and Warrington experienced hard lines in not scoring. After a spell of give-and-take play the home team forced a minor. The remaining portion of the first half was chiefly confined to the forwards. Half time arrived without any score. Warrington re- started, and at once pressed, but Shoyelton took play to the Warrington quarters, a good bit of play by Page, Coffey, and Price ending in the latter being pulled up on the line by Bolesworth. The Shamrocks continued to press, but Bolesworth was again to the front by a splen- did run and kick. The Warrington forwards again rushed up the field. Smith picked up from a scrimmage and after eluding his opposing halves passed to Mannion, who in turn passed to Gibson, who had hard lines in not scoring, being tackled on the line. Warrington were now having the best of the game and Rowe made a splendid run up the field, but nothing came of it. Coffey next had a chance, but Buckley tackled him. This brought about time, a pleasant game ending in a draw, neither side scoring. For Warrington, Bolesworth, Mannion, Gibson, and Rowe were the pick of the backs, whilst the forwards to a man played a good gam _

ARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S V. PORT SIINLIIIIIIT.-I"layed on the Saints' ground, on Saturday. Sunlight playing with the wind in the first half could not break through the home defence, whose backs played a good game. The Saints,hotvever,rushod the ball towards the visitors' line, Bennett scoring'. Helsby failed to convert. The home team still continued to have the best of the game, and pressed the soapmen severely. Half-time—St.Marys', one try and two minors; Sunlight, nil. Restarting, the visitors managed to get in the home 25, but Roughley sent them back again with a nice kick in touch at half- way. The home forwards were now quite outplaying their opponents,Hampson and Burton having hard lines.' However,after a spell of passing between the home backs Hampson got hold, and dodging through nearly the whole team scored a splendid try near touch. Burton failed at the difficult place. Sunlight now tried hard to score, but could not break away, the tackling of the home team being good all round. Towards the close of the game,Hampson getting possession handed to Burton, who dashed over the line, Thomas failing at the place. Final result—St. Mary's, three tries and four minors ; Sunlight, nil. Rl:Neoax v. ROCHDALI3 nontiErs.—The ahnital Meet. ing between these old rivals took place on the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, on Saturday, in spring like weather and before 3,000 spectators. Runcorn were short of several of their usual combination, Crompton having gone to Leeds, as first reserve centre for England, Lock- wood, who was originally chosen, not being able to play, owing to an injury to his knee. Morris was also absent from the threequarters, and W. Faulkner, Williams, and ' Davies amongst the forwards. The Hornets had, also several men away. The teams faced each other as follows :—Runcorn : S. Houghton, full back; A. Abrams T. Warden, and Rev. G. H. Kingston, three-quarter backs ;G. Robinson, and J. Faulkner, half-backs ; P. Riley, A. Hampson, H. Farmer, J. Langley, S. Derby- shire, J. Evans, L. Dolan, J. Stubbs, F. Gayter, forward. Rochdale Hornets :—Woods, full back ; Smith, Jackson, and Isherwood, three-quarter backs ; Howard, and Dex, half-backs.: Lord, Leach, F. Renshaw, E. Renshaw, Sunderland, Horsfiel,i, Melledew, Simpson, and Binns, forwards. The visitors won the toss, Runcorn having to face a powerful sun. Riley started, to which there was no return. Robinson got hold from a scrimmage, and passing between Faulkner, Warder, and Kingston, enabled the latter to put in a useful run, Isherwood pushing him into touch. Warder was next prominent with a tricky run and kick, which removed hostilities to the Hornets quarter flag. Lord and Melledew came finely through with the ball, and strong forward play by the visitors took the ball to the home lines. Heavy scrimmaging followed, until Lord got a mark, from which Midgeley placed a splendid goal. the Runcorn forwards combined splendidly, and with an Irresistible rush took the ball over the Hornets' lines, Farmer scoring. Ward took the place and easily kicked a goal. The game was now very even for some minutes until Howarth and Leach initiated a passing movement, but Isherwood was held when seeming dangerous. The home team regained the ground with some excellent footwork, and Kingston, getting a pass from Faulkner near the centre flag, rounded his opponents with a magnificent run, and planted the bail between the posts, Warder having no difficulty in placing a goal. Half- time : Runcorn, two goals (ten points) ; Hornets, one penalty goal (three points). Upon resuming, the game was hotly contested at neutral ground for some time. The homesters gradually got the upper hand, and at times screwed the scrimmages in fine style. Runcorn attacked strongly,Hampson eventually scoring. Warder kicked a goal. The home lines were hotly assailed. A free kick brought relief, but they were soon back, until Kingston cleverly intercepted, and dribbled beautifully to the other end, and scored a brilliant try. No goal resulted. Following this reverse, the Hornets made another spirited attack, their heavy forwards using their weight to great advantage. Houghton, however, was in his best form, and repelled each attack in his well-known style. The game eventually ended in a well deserved victory for Runcorn by 3-1-0 (17 points), to Hornets 1 penalty goal (3 points). WIDNES V. Cnomwroth—The above teams met on Saturday, on the Lowerhouse-lane ground, to play the return match. There was a large number of spectators. The visitors kicked off with the sun shining brilliantly in their faces. Play was of an uninteresting character' for some time, until Hughes picked the oval out of a scrimmage, handed to Drummond, and he to Barber, who dropped a fine goal. The remainder of the first half was evenly contested, but the home forwards were very weak. Half-time score : Widnes, one goal (drop-

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

MONDAY. In the House of Commons on Monday evening, on the order to gi into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, Sir. .7. Goan moved an amendment declar- ing that no person should in Her Majesty's naval estab- lishments be engaged at wages insufficient for a proper maintenanCe, and that the conditions of labour as regards hours, Wages, insurance against accidents, provision for old age, &c., should be such as to afford An example to private employers throughout the country. Colonel LLOYD seconded the amendment. Mr. CAMPBELL- BANNERMAN said no one could dispute the principle contained in the amendment; it was only when they came to the interpretation of its somewhat vague terms that difference of opinion might be expected to arise. The Government were unable to embark on any daring scheme, but were most anxious to remove anything that might be quoted by employers seeking justification for ungenerous dealing with their men. After some discussion the amendment was adopted.

TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. MosontLe, answering a question stated that the dispute in the cotton trade had now lasted 17 weeks, that 410 mills and sheds had been suspended, and that 30,000 operatives were directly affected by this state of affairs. Mr. Amon% in reply to Mr. H. HOBROUSE, gave some figures relative to Welsh benefices which are in English dio eses, and to English benefices which are in the diocese of St. Asaph. In Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates Sir U. KAY-SHUTTLEWORTH made the statement respecting the navy. He said the amount pro- posed to be spent on construction was as near as pos- sible £3,000,000, including the expenditure for the year on the contract ships. Adding the armaments,the expen- diture would be about £4,400,000. Lord G. IlAmiLTou considered that the estimates were too low, but had no fault to find with the new construction programme. At the evening sitting Mr MACARTNET moved a resolution in favour of the compulsory slaughter of foreign cattle at the port of debarkatiou. Mr. GARDNER, on behalf ot the Government, opposed the motion, which was re- jected by 186 to 151.

In the House of Lords the Lord CruNcELLoses Hill on the law of inheritance was rejected by 61 votes against 56. The rejection of the measure was moved by the young Earl of DUDLEY, Wh3 complained that it" struck directly at the law of primogeniture." WEDNESDAY. In the House of Commons on Wednesday Mr. HOLLAND moved the second reading of the Rating of Machinery Bill. He denied that it was a measure for exempting machinery from rates, and said its object was to prevent the over-rating of machinery. Mr. FOWLER said the Government thought that the time had arrived when the law should be made clear, and that the question of rat- ing was emphatically one for the unbiassed opinion of the House. On a division the numbers were—for the second reading, 27; a gainst, 134 ; majority for, 153.

THURSDAY. lii the House of Commons on Thursday evening a pro- posal by Mr. PICKERSGILL that it be an instruction to the Committee on the City and South London Electric Rail- way Bill that they should insert a clause reserving to the London County Council, power to purchase such under- takings after the expiration of a limited period, was de- feated by 242 to 129. In reply to Mr. Brand, Mr. GLAD- STONE said the question of the appointment of county magistrates was under the consideration of the Govern- ment. In the course of a statement on the business of the House the right hon. gentleman said the second reading of the Home Rule Bill would be moved next Thursday.

In the House of Lords a reference to the subject of ap- pointments to the county magistracy gave the Marquis of SALISBURY an oppmrtunity to accuse the Lord Chan- cellor of having issued a circular to the lords lieutenants of counties impressing upon the desirability of recommend- ing for appointment gentlemen whose politics were the same as his own. Lord iIERSCIIELL said that if the noble Marquis had accurately represented the information which had been given to him he had been grievously mis- informed. No .one was more desirous than he was not to introduce politics into this question.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED AT ST. HELENS.
MORE WORKS STOPPING.

On Monday abont 200 men employed at the Greenbank Works, St. Helens, of the United Alkali Company, Limited Ceased work for an indefinite period in consequence of the fall of the large chimney connected with the salt cake, black ash, and vitriol de- partments on Thursday morning last week. Although the notice is for an indefinite period, the men consider that the company will re-start the works as soon as pos- sible. The erection of another chimney will occupy about three months, but temporary provision for the working of the plant will be made. A number of men are engaged to finish the caustic at present on the works. The caustic plant, which is worked to another large chimney now undergoing repairs,cannot be carried on without the other processes and that will also be stopped. Regarding the bsttlemakers' strike,there is no change, and no overtures have been made by either masters or men. An official of the Bottlemakers' Association stated on Monday,that the men were as firm as ever,and would not for some time to c.me make any overtures to the masters. The association has decided to apply for sup- port from other trades. The London and Manchester Plate-glass Company have given notice to their employes engaged on the old process at the Sutton glassworks. The notice, which will terminate in three weeks, will probably affect about 100 or 150 persons.' The opinion is that the machine hands will be employed on the yard while this portion of the works is being fitted with the new process.

div.head: CONCERT AT TIM DRILL HALL.
div.p: CONCERT AT TIM DRILL HALL.

A grand evening promenade concert of the War- rington Association of Amateur Bands was held on Saturday night, at the Drill Hall. The Mayor (Alderman (ireenell), presided, and among those present were Mr. R. Pierpoint. M.P., Aldermen Wright, and Francomb, Councillors Bolton, Heaton, Smethurst, Muir, Hutchinson, and Shaw, and Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town Clerk), T. Longdin (borough surveycr), John White und T. J. Downs. Mr. Joseph Taylor was in charge of the arrange- ments. The Mayor said that he had been requested to preside over the meeting by Mr. Taylor, and it gave him great pleasure to do so. The bands associated with the Warrington Amateur Bands Association, num- bered 10 and there were three hundred members. The object of the association was to provP.e bands sufficient to play In the park from May to September. He could say on behalf of the Corporation that they had made the band stand sufficient for all requirements. He hoped that the arrangements would be for the benefit of the people of Warrington. SATURDAY. MARCH 11,.1893.

CAT°rY THE Conservative Party met to- enclave. gether in conclave on Wednesday, and, it is said, at the very corn- ant of the proceedings every 4: member Pledged his word that he would not lieCe anything that took place at the meeting. seelh'itbstanding this ominous preliminary, which t° be borrowed from the repertoire of stage titti-l'lN tors, it is pleasing to learn that the bus- NttBe,,of the meeting was not of a treasonable det 7e. It did not consist of arrangement of the opt4;18 Of that much-talked-of amateur military it -hatien, known: as "lining the ditches," nor was tlt (heckling of whether the embattled host of 11tr. Bt,t,' Bneuld be led by COLONEL SAUNDERSON, bbr. RUSSELL, or Mr. JOHNSTON, of Ballykil- of `Z in fact the real busineas of the meeting was s erY prosaic and inglorious character—it wa the devising of methods by which the 008:able work of obstruction in the House of Ter,:n° Th tis may be more effectually carried on. vet; Party in the House of Commons has been b, ranch demoralised lately. They have been I,4l4i'eha in almost every division by majorities tb;,-e" are far heavier than what is supposed to be ihde ziaealinal majority of the Government, and, as one of their own leading newspapers car; the Government "have been allowed to tribY, rYthing before them." This has been at- repe'hed to bad leadership, but no doubt the the 4ted shocks which the Liberal victories in tor 4 c°estituencies have administered have had the ethiag to do with that " looseness in PhreZank of file " which is the euphemistic ehee used by some Tory scribes. Strict adher- -09., pledges is not a strong point amongst f_r"osetr.vative members of Parliament, and there- auecreie Is not surprising that, despite the vow of Y,lnost of what was said and done at the

meeting was very quickly made known to the public. The Marquis of SALISBURY, as might be expected, was emphatic enough in his condemna- tion of the Home Rule Bill, and, strange to say, he made a special point against the Legislative Council, which is to be elected on a property franchise of twenty pounds, and which to a great extent has been devised for the protection of Lord SALISBURY'S particular proteges, the landlords. There are a fair number of Radicals who will not feel specially aggrieved if the noble] marquis's criticisms result either in abolishing or "demo- cratising "the second chamber in the Irish scheme of government. Lord Salisbury's address con- cluded with the amiable advice to his party to vote for all amendments, "so as to inflict as many
- --- -- wounds on the Bill as possible." Another result

of the meeting was to disclose the fact that the Tory party in the House of Commons are already face to face with the question of a divided leader- ship. Mr, BALFOUR is, of course, nominal leader, but Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL is again being regarded in some quarters as the real chief, and at the meeting on W ednesday he was very much in request. He protested his great regard for his friend and political chief, and Mr. BALFOUR on his side, was very profuse in his thanks to Lord Ranilolph for his " kindly speech," but it is quite evident that ere long there will, between the two, be some pretty complications.

Ma. CLEVELAND was on Saturday Protection Condemned. for the second time installed President of the United States. The inaugural ceremony was one of great brilli- ance, and the immense crowd of spectators which gathered at Washington gave the new President an enthusiastic reception. A great deal seems to be expected by his fellow-citizens from Mr.CLEvis- LAND during his term of office. The elections which resulted in placing in power the party of which he is the head, were an emphatic condemna- tion of the policy and the methods of the Repub- licans, and particularly of that part of their policy which reached its culmination in the notorious McKinley tariff. In his inaugural address Presi- dent CLEVELAND takes note of this, "The people of the United States have," he says, "decreed that on this day the control of their Government, in its legislative and executive branches, shall be given to the political party pledged in the most positive terms to the accomplishment of tariff reform." Protection of the most resolute kind, and with many circumstances of an exceptional kind to favour it, has been tried in the United States and it has proved a failure. It has added burdens to the daily life of the people, and, says Presid- ent CLEVELAND, "when we tear aside the delusions and misconceptions which have blinded our countrymen to their condition under vicious tariff laws, we but show them how far they have been led away from the pathsof contentment and prosperity." What an exposure is all this of the unwisdom of those English politi- cians who have advocated, and, in fact, still advo- cate with a kind of hysterical pertinacity the imposition of a Protectionist tariff in this country. ( Such would-be leaders of the people should now hide their diminished heads and give up the advocacy of their discredited nostrums. President CLEVELAND also reads a useful lesson to another class of persons who are wishful to make a change which would not be a reform. As he says, no- thing is more vital to the supremacy of a nation and to the beneficial purposes of a Government than a sound and stable currency. "It's exposure to degradation should at once arouse to activity the most enlightened statesmanship, and the danger of depreciation in the purchasing power of the wages paid to toil should furnish the strongest incentive to prompt and conservative precaution." These are words which may very profitably be pondered by English people who are plied with 1 the arguments of self-styled "currency re- formers." Bi-znetallism if adopted in England, would undoubtedly—and, indeed, it would not answer the purpose it is intended to serve if it did not—" depreciate the purchasing power of the wages paid to toil," while it would not, as Mr. GLADSTONE very clearly demonstrated last week, provide the country with a "sound and stable cur- rency." President CLEVELAND is equally emphatic in his condemnation of that other form of protec- tion and class favouritism which takes the shape of bounties and subsidies to ill-advised and languishing enterprises in which the mass of citizens have no concern, and his allusion to the excesses of the pension and the " spoils" systems, and the " conspiracies against the interests of the people" under the guise of trusts and combina- tions, seems to indicate a determination on his part to lift the Government of the United States from the vicious grooves into which it has in some respects fallen.

THERE seems to be a growing fashion of dealing' with political affairs in very sanguinary language. The Ulster members are, perhaps, to some extent, responsible for this, but the publicans do not dis- play any disposition to be behindhand. A placard which the Licensed Victuallers' Protection Society of London have pullout with reference to the Government's Liquor Traffic Bill, is headed with the words "A Declaration of War," and it makes an urgent appeal for the "sinews of war with which to carry on the "campaign." At a meeting of publicans, which was held in London this week, one of the speakers completely eclipsed Colonel SAIINDERSON and other North of Ireland fire-eaters. Their martial ardour not only contem- plates "lining the ditches," but the belligerent publican in question declared that he wowld "place his back to the wall and give his life's blood" rather than that local option should be conceded. Another speaker described the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER as "The Barabbas of 1893." A disposition was even shown to round upon the Church, and the clergy were reminded in not very considerate terms, that they might need the help of the publicans when Disestablish- ment and Disendowment come to the front. This insolent insinuation that the Church and the liquor trade must stand or fall together can hardly be relished by those for whose benefit it was made.

According to a writer in a London newspaper/. there is one industry which does not show any symptoms of decline in these days of depression, and that is the growing of flowers for London and other large towns. It is gratifying to learn that there is an ever-increasing demand in crowded towns for those floral "things of beauty which tend to embellish and sweeten the homes of the rich and poor alike. In the neigh- bourhood of London enormous glass houses have been erected for the culture of the flowers which are most in request, and many men who have begun in this line with little but experience and aptitude for the work are now in receipt of hand- some incomes. Specialism is beginning to prevail in this branch of market gardening as in other in-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 11, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 11, 1893.

dustries, and, speaking generally,th at man appears to be most successful who devotes his undivided attention and skill to the raising of only one or two kinds of flowers. Under one enormous expanse of glass alone there are something like a quarter of a million roses in pots, while other structures on a somewhat similar scale are devoted to lilies and carnations and geraniums, and pelar- goniums. Of lilies of the valley, one large firm can at the present time show no fewer than two mil- lions and a half in all stages of growth. When the London market is glutted with any particular class of flowers from these immense propagating establishments the overplus is hurried off to the great provincial towns—to Birmingham,and Man- chester and Newcastle.

NELSON-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. On Monday the scholars of the above school were the recipients of a free tea, given by Mr. and Mrs. Henry Dodd, who sympathize with the work carried on at the school. The junior scholars took tea at five o'clock, and the adults at six. Afterwards they were the recipients of fruit. Various games were engaged in. An enjoyable evening was spent. MARINERS' CHURCH, RUNCORN. On Tuesday evening a temperance entertainment took place, in the above church under the presidency of the Rev. Dr. Preston. There was a good attendance. Interesting addresses were delivered by Mr. Gill and the Rev. A. Riley. Master Timmins played two piansforte solos, Miss Huhn° gave a song in character, and Mr. Gill gave two selections. Co to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have.—Advt. FATAL FALL FROM A SCAFFOLD AT RUNCORN. Yesterday morning Wm. White, of Irwell-lane, Run- corn, brother of Mr. Henry White, was painting a house in Bentinct-st., when part of the scaffold on which he was working fell, and he was precipitated to the ground a distance of thirty feet. His head came in contact with the kerbstone' and he sustained such serious injuries to his head that he died in a litte over an hour. A strong wind prevailed at the time.

THE RITNCORN CENTRE THREE-QUARTERS. In connection with the international match at Leeds on Saturday, the " Yorkshire Evening Post" gave photographs of the team. They also had one of J. H. Crompton, the Runcorn and Cheshire centre three-quarter, and the English reserve, respecting whom they wrote—He is 22 years of age, and started his football career with the Runcorn Recrea- tion Club six years ago, and played with them one season. He then joined the Runcorn Club, and has remained with the Cheshire champions ever since. In making his debut with them his play was of a somewhat sensational character, for in the match against Sale he dropped five goals, and obtained one from a free kick—a veritable record. During the second season, in 1889, he secured his highest average, namely, 61 tries and 10 dropped goals. He has all along represented his county in every match, played. He was one af the 'members of the team Rest of England against Yorkshire three years since, when he secured one drop goal and one try; and he participated in the competition between the same organizations last Saturday. He has displayed excellent form in the last few matches, and has rejoiced the hearts of a large circle of friends. He played a champion game against Bradford on the 18th February, when amid excitement he land3d safely after a run nearly the whole length ' of the field, cleverly evading all his opponents. He is one of the finest centre three-quarters in the country." And yet the English Committee by a most unfair and dishonourable "shuffling of the cards" caused Crompton to "stand down " after they had chosen him as reserve centre three- quarter.

Yesterday an inquest was held at Runcorn, on the body of Elizabeth Woodward, aged four years, daughter of Wm. Woodward, of Union-st. It appeared that about half-past seven the girl struck a match and set her nightdress on fire. Her screams attraoted the attention of Mary Ann Bebbingion domestic servant, who with commendable presence of mind, wrapped the young sufferer in a blanket and extinguished the flames. The girl was terribly burned about the head, face, and body and she died at 10 o'clock. A verdict of " Accideital Death " was returned.

LECTJRE ITT MR. C. A. TIMMINS, AT RUNCORN. In aid of the repair fund of Holy Trinity Church, Mr. C. A. Timmins, on Thursday evening delivered a lecture in Bethesda Lecture Hall, entitled " A thirteen days scamper through the Norwegian Fjords." There was a large and appre iative audience and the Rev. Dr. Pres- ton presided. Mr. Timmins gave a most interesting ac- count of his voyage to the land of the midnight sun and the 120 photos shown by the lantern were veritable works of art, and as some exceptionally lovely effect of sea, sky and mountain, was unfolded, the audience broke into rapturous applause. The pleasure of those present was enhanced by the vocal selections of Mr. G. Platt (Liverpool), and Mr. R. Morris (Runcorn), the musical performances of Mr. W. Burnett, Liverpool, Masters C. and A. Timmins, Runcorn. Mr. J. L. Mackrell, Liverpool, manipulated the lantern with great success.

On Tuesday evening a public meeting was held in the Union Ball, Runcorn, for the purpose of distributing certificates of merit, awarded to the successful boys and girls from the various day schools in the town, for ex- cellence of a written report of a lecture on " Alcohol and digestion," delivered in the schools by Mr. J. J. Jakeman, of Liverpool, some little time ago. The Rev. J. Pulford Williams presided, and was supported on the platform by several members of the Runcorn Women's Temperance Association, Mrs. Walton kindly distributed the certificates, which numbered 168. During the even- ing several pieces of music were efficiently rendered by the scholars and friends. Miss Kilburn was present from the Board Schools, and did yeoman service. The hall was crowded in every part with a most appreciative and attentive audience, and a very interesting and en- joyable evening was spent. EXORBITANT INTEREST BY A RUNCORN MONEY LENDER On Tuesday, at the Runcorn County Court, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes,John Henry Harrison, money lender, Waterloo-road, brought a claim against John Cardus, 2, Wlckston-hillV and Wm. Antrobus, 25, Granville-at., Runcorn for £2 10s. 4th due on a promis- sory note. Mrs. Antrobus appeared, and admitted £1 195. sd. to be due, but disputed the remainder of the debt, alleging that interest had been charged twice.— Plaintiff denied this, and pointed out that he was not in fact claiming the full amount of interest to which he was entitled under the note, which originally was for £6, from which 19s. 2d. was deducted for interest and ex- penses. There was an agreement far payment by in- stalments, and in case of default, to pay interest at the rate of 0. in the shilling per week.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for £2 93. 7d., and remarked that the rate of interest was over 200 per cent. He had frequently pointed out the folly of people borrowing money at such exorbitant rates of interest, and added that if they entered into such agreements he was unable to assist them. They must pay for their foolishness.

THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDOR OYER THE MERSEY A conference of representatives of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils and of the local authorities at Widnes and Runcorn was held on Tuesday at the Isling- ton Court-house, Liverpool, for tho purpose of consider- ing the necessity of providing a bridge for vehicular traffic over the river Mersey between Widnes and Runcorn. Alderman W. W. B. Hulton presided over a large attendance. The proceedings were private, but we learn that the representatives of the local authorities which are the principal contributors (they having offered £30,000 each to the cost of the bridge) gave further information as to the volume of traffic and probable cost. This Information was carefully considered by the joint committee, but, as it was considered incomplete, it remains for the promoters to supply further information before the county council representatives can report to their respective oounciis at the quarterly meetings in May next. • When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, Hlgh-st.—Advt.

• . _ SERIOUS ACCIDENTS ON THE SHIP CANAL. Several accidents of a serious character have occurred during the past two or three days on the Manchester Ship Canal works, in the vicinity of Runcorn. On Tues- day, at an early hour, John Slinking, aged 18 years, whilst following his employment near Weston Point,was so badly injured that he was removed to the Latchford Hospital. It was considered that he was suffering from a fracture to the base of the skull. On Wednesday an- other patient was taken to the same institution, in the person of Thomas Lundey. of Inca Huts. He sustained contusions and wounds on the legs, at Weston Poiat, by the breaking of the bucket chain of a steam navy. On the afternoon of the same day a youth named John Bar- ker, who lodged at 19 Hut, Big Fleld, near Runcorn, was taken to the Infirmary. He was engaged as roperunner to the locomotive "Winsford" driven by John Heslop,and whilst uncoupling waggons at the Old Quay, he fell. The engine came back, and three empty waggons ran over him. - - RUNCORN BURIAL Bonin:). The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery on Wednesday. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi pre-lided and there were present Messrs. Thomas Handley, H. Coleburn,and W.F.Salkeld (secretary). The monthly report stated that the interments to Feb. 25th (11 months) were 429, cor- responding period last year 484 ; decrease 55. The fees received during the same period amounted to £4lO 18s. 2d., last year £416 6s. Bd., decrease £7 Bs. 6d. The Finance Committee reported that they had passed for payment of ordinary aecounts amounting to £25 145., and for interest falling due amounting to £76 2s. 11d.— The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. T. Hand- ley, seconded by Mr. Coleburn. It was resolved to give the overseers notice to call a meeting of ratepayers for the the purpose of appointing two persons not being members of the Burial Board, to be auditors of the accounts of the Board to the 25th March, 1893. The tender of Mr. Thos. J. Kirkham of Greenway-road for cleaning and repairing the churches and the mortuary was accepted.—The Secretary said there had been two deaths from smallpox at the hospital ; he did not know whether they were Ship Canal people or not, but he understood that they ware strangers. Percival, the sanitary inspector came to the Cemetery and said he must have a grave opened directly. The question of " who will pay" was asked, and Percival replied "I will see you paid." It now appeared that the officials were not quite certain whether the Overseers or the Commissioners should pay. At all events he had not yet got the money, which amounted to nearly £3. If he had not received it before neat meeting he would men- tion the matter again. The Board agreed to this course.

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORIIESPONDENT.

The coming grand performance of St. Paul, by the Runcorn Musical Society i 3 arousing great in- terest in musical circles in the town. It will be the first performance of the noble work in the neighbourhood, and it speaks highly far the Com- mittee that they should have included such a diffi- cult and classical work in their season's programme. The work will be given in Runcorn Public Hall, on Thursday, the 23rd. Interest, will be further en- hanced by the first appearance of Miss Clara Taylor our clever local contralto, who recently won the bronze medal at the Royal Academy London. The rehearsals are being prosecuted with great vigour and a really fine performance is sure to result under the able direction of Mr. Crossley.

On a trivial technicality the Board of Commis- sioners last week declined to peaition in favour of the ballot and purer elections by asking that com- missioners shc uld be included in the Local Author- ities (Voting and Qualification) Bill. The following letter shows that the desired end will be attained without their help. " 9 Ennismore Garden. S. W. March 6th 1893.—Dear sir,—ln further reference to your letter of the 25th ult. re the inclusion of Boards of Improvement Commissioners in the Local Authorities (Voting and Qualification) Bill. I am desired by Mr. Brunner to inform you that he has given notice of amendments in Committee to that effect and that he has received a communication from Mr. Fowler stating that tht Government will include them in their measures. Yours faithfully, Colin H. Browning, John Clarke, Esq."

At the quarterly meeting of the Cheshire County Council, on Thursday, Col. Dixon was elected chair- man by 41 votes against 29 recorded for Mr. Lister. Mr. T. W. Killick was appointed vice-chairman. The committees were alsoselected at the same meet- ing, and Mr. P. Speakman, member for Runcorn south,was much in request. He was made a mem- ber of the Main Roads and Bridges Committee, Finance Committee, Parliamentary Committee, Standing Joint Committee, Railway and Canal Rates and Charges Committee. Polling Districts Committee, Technical Instruction Committee, Upton Asylum Committee, and Committee as to Bridge over Mersey at Runcorn. Major Hazlehuret member for Runcorn north, occupies a place on the following committees :—County Rate Basis Com- mittee, Finance Committee, Boundaries Commit tee, Weights and Measures Committee, Small Holdings and Allotments Committee, and Committee as to Bridge over the Mersey. Mr. Francis Greg objected to the re-appointment of the last named committee on the ground that the proposal affected nobody but the two towns concerned in the matter.

div.head: BANKRUPT POULTERER AND HIS GEESE.
div.p: THE BANKRUPT POULTERER AND HIS GEESE.

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Samuel John Francis, for whom Mr. Unwin ap- peared, and who was a fish and poultry dealer at 01, Widnes-road, Widnes, came before the Court for public examination, his statement of affairs show- ing liabilities £374 and assets £4B. In the course of examination by the official receiver the bankrupt stated that he attributed his failure to loss on a con- signment of geese last Christmas time and to the costs of a lawsuit respecting them. There were 104 geese, which cost him £33 75., and being bad they had to be destroyed. fie therefore lost not only the geese, but the profit he would have made on them, and he not only lost the lawsuit, but had to pay the lawyers' cost. The official receiver, in the course of further examination, elicited an admission that the bankrupt had known himself to be insolvent for about two years, and had been carrying on business in the names of his wife and daughters. The bankrupt further admitted that he was a joiner by trade, and that neither he nor the members of his family who carried on the business for him knew anything about it. He assured the court that at the present time, after the experience he had gained, he personally knew very little about the business except that " the geese brought him to the bankruptcy court." He hoped to be able to make an acceptable offer to his creditors. The examination was ordered to be closed.
RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND THE PROPOSED PURCHASE OF RUNCORN WATERWORKS.

On the first March, the following letter was ad- dressed to Mr. F. Wiswall, Chairman of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners by Messrs. J. Clarke and A. Riley secretaries, to the District Liberal Association "Dear Sir,—We are instructed by the Runcorn Liberal Association to ask your Board to be good enough to sup- ply them for their own use all information and-reports re- lative to the proposed purclaase of the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Water Co.'s concern, a week before the next town's meeting to be called to authorise such purchase in accordance with a resolution accepted by you on be- half of the Board at the recent meeting. We trust your Board will find no difficulty in complying with this re- quest, as the tone of the discussion preceding the adop- tion of this resolution did not indicate any feeling of mistrust, or yet any desire to embarrass the Board in delicate negotiations. It is simply intended to elicit in- formation in time to allow the ratepaying public an op- portunity of mustering the details of any bargain your Board may have to recommend to them before being asked for their formal assent." Under date March 2nd, Mr. E. Marshall, secretary to the Commissioners replied,—" Dear Sir,—l am directed by. the Chairman of this Board to acknowledo.e the re- ceipt LA your letter of the Ist inst., and lam to say that the matter therein referred to will have his considera- tion."

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

MR. EDWARDS AND HIS LIGHTING RATE.—A rule has been obtained by the overseers calling upon Messrs. C. Reynolds and A. Thomas, magistrates, to show cause why they have not issued a distress warrant against Mr. Thomas Edwards for 13s. 2d., the amount, of a rate for lighting. The matter will be argued in the county of Queens Bench on Thursday next. rHE UNION CHURCH MOTHERS' MEETING.—In connec- tion with this institution the members had their annual tea on Tuesday. A miscellaneous enteitainment was afterwards given, which was presided over by Mr. T. A. Rigby, and consisted of songs, recitations, dialogues, Rtc.

RELIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the Frodsham branch of the above society was hold in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening, when the Rev. W. J. Wilkins, association secretary of the society, attended, and gave a'inost interesting descrip- tive lecture (illustrated by dissolving views) on "Christ and the Religions of India." Thore was a very large audience, and Mr. Thomas A. Rigby presided.

TRH PAROCHIAL COHHITTERS.-At the monthly meet- ing, held yesterday week, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., in the chair, letters were read from the Local Government Board, in which it was intimated that a public inquiry would be held at Frodsham with respect to the Frodshana water scheme, and the application of the central author- ity for urban powers for the township. A report on the analysis of water taken from the borettole was read, frQm which it appeared that the water was very suitable for domestic purposes, but it was decided to await the receipt of Dr. Carter Bell's report on the same water and the Clerk (Colonel Ashton) was asked to mite to Messrs. Timmins to obtain the report from the county analyst as early as possible, and to point out that his de- lay is unreasonable. Messrs. Timmins' account for the trial boring for the water amounting to £205 was passed for payment by the Central Authority, as was also an account from the Town Hall Company for £2 25., for one year's rent for committee-room. Directions were issued for certain repairs to the sewers in Bradley-lane and near to the Ring o' Bells. The attention of the com- mittee was called to the Church-street brook, which had recently become quite a nuisance, and it was decided to , ask Mr. Diggle, the road surveyor, to see to its being I put right.

div.p: ORGANIST OF BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN.
Mr. Clifford Le Conteur has been appointed to this position in succession to Mr. J. Clough.
SITCOMS OF A RUNCORN_ ARTIST.
Miss Pierpoint, of Halton-road, Runcorn, has been successful in getting two pictures hung at the Spring exhibition of the Liverpool Walker Art Gallery.
RUNCORN AND DISTRICT PEERS' EcoNONIIC BUILDING SOCIETY.

A ballot meeting in connection with this society has just been held, Mr. I. H. Annett presiding. N 0.184 was the winning number entitling Mr. Royle Garnett to an advance ol £2OO for 18i years without interest. Joaria PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladies' silver and sold watches in the town.—Advt. THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE.

The boy Tl;;;a-s Fisher was again remanded on Wed- nesday, on the charge of stabbing a playfellow named Albert Royle. Superintendent Atherton said the in- jured boy would be able to appear in a fortnight.

div.head: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

. _ The service of song entitled " Christie's dd organ," was given in these schools on Monday evening in aid of the prize fund. The music was rendered by a choir cf 100 voices under the conductorship of Mr. W. G. Buck. nail, and the narrative was read by Councillor F. Neil. Mr. Stuart Deacon presided. JOSEPH PRITCIURD is prepared to wind and keep in repair. private clocks from 10s. per anoufn.—Advt.

div.head: CHILD DRINKS CARBOLIC ACID AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A CHILD DRINKS CARBOLIC ACID AT RUNCORN.

On Monday morning about half-past eleven, Percy Walter Booth, aged one year and ten months, son of P.C. Booth, of Percival-lane, obtained possession of a bottle of carbolic acid, which was in the house for dis- infecting purposes, and drank a small portion of it. The liquid burnt the mouth, lips and chin of the child, who was immediately taken to Dr. MacLennan, and under his care is progressing satisfactorily.
PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN.

The house and shop 56, High-st., Runcorn, in the occupation of Mrs. McQuinn, was offered for sala at Wilson's Hotel, on Monday evening. The property which is subject to the yearly ground rent of £2 11s. 10d., was withdrawn at £650, the reserve not being reached. The solicitors were Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, and the auctioneer, Mr. Mainwaring, of War- rington. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PRITCHARD'S.—Adrt. Sr. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN.

A very successful commencement has again been made wifh the classes of this association. The male of 30 has been fully made up, and there also attended the first lecture a considerable number of old members who have obtained the first, and in some cases the second, certificate, and who desire to be examined a second or third time. The Secretary, Mr. Epps, would call the attention of those who are desirous of being re- examined to the fact that it is necessary for them to attend the lectures as the attendance register has now to be forwarded to London. Two MONTHS FOR POACHING NEAR RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Chas. Stubbs, a young man, was charged on two informations with' killing game on Sunday, Feb. 26th, on land ía the oc- cupation of John Baguley, Hallwoud farm, Halton, and also with having on the same day used snares for taking game without having a game certificate. In consequence of finding some snares laid on the Saturday night, a gamekeeper named Knight watched the land, and at noon on Sunday he saw the defendant take up three , snares and a hare, which had been caught and put them in his. pocket.—The prisener who had been previously convicted, was fined and costs 9s. 6d. in each case, or in default two months ,hard labour. The defendant went to gaol.
Both PRITCHARD'S Shops are under personal superrisien.and customers may rely upon receiving every attention.—Advt.

- MORE ROBBERIES FROM THE WIDNES MARKET. At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman F. H. (iossage) and Mr. H. Deacon, a married woman named Eliza Roberts, ef Tarbuck, was brought up on two charges of larceny from stalls in the Widnes Market on Saturday night. Police Constable Almond, who was on duty In Widnes Market, saw the prisoner take a shoebrush from Mr. MlGnley's stall shortly before seven o'clock. When he was searching her at the police station he found an eggstand and a meat dish in her basket, and she would give no satisfac- tory explanation of how she obtained them. The pris- oner denied both charges, but the bench fined her ss. for each offence, with the alternative of fourteen days imprisonment with hard labour. - -

'JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51. High- it.. and 4, Bridge at.. Runcorn.—Advt. THE VICAR OF WIDNES ON HIS DEPARTURE. At a gathering in Widnes Parish Schools on Monday night, Mr. Stuart Deacon referred to the fact that they were soon going to lose their good vicar. Of course they knew when Mr. Garrett came they would not be able to keep him, and although they were sorry to lose him, yet they would congratulate him upon his appointment. Not only members of the church, but everyone who had the religious welfare of the town at heart regretted that Mr. Garrett was leaving Widnes and they would watch his future 'career with interest and pleasure. Ho ven- tured to indulge in the hope that they would yet see Mr. Garrett raised to the dignity of the episcopal bench. The Vicar thanked Mr. Deacon for the kind words he had spoken, but he thought the prophecy he had made would never come to pass. Neither Mrs. Garrett nor himself were seeking position merely for position's sake, but they were willing to take 'any position which might be given them in the providence of God, where they could be more useful in furthering the work of God.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY PUBLIC-ROUSE Row AT _RUNCORN..
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY PUBLIC-ROUSE Row AT _RUNCORN..

--- --- Mary Eliza Santley, keeper of the Union Vaults, Union-street, was summoned before Mr. H. Reynolds aid Mr. A. Thomas at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Mon- day to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness.— Mr. J. Burton depended. The evidence showed that on the night of the 22nd February two women named Allman and Leach, entered the bar of the Ship Inn, Mill Brow, and called fcr three gills of beer in a bottle, and the order was supplied. Two men, named John Daniels and Fred Griffiths emptied the contents of the bottle into the glasses and drank the liquor. A boy, fourteea years of age, named Edwin Henry Davies was in charge of the bar, and the woman Leach called him "young four eyes" in allusion to his wearing spectacles, and upon the boy making a retort, she became enraged and threw five glasses and four pint cups at him. The men ejected the woman and the boy fetched P.S. Woolley and P.C. Ridgway and together they went in search of the woman. They found Leach near the front door of the Union Vaults, vomiting, and inside they discovered Allman and the two men drinking together, and there was a glass of beer on the counter which Leach informed the police was hers. The police testified that the women were unmistakably drunk, and the boy Davies said they were the worse for drink. The defence was that Griffiths and Daniels when they entered the house were only accompanied by Allman, whom several witnesses stated was not drunk and that they were followed by Leach, who immediately she entered upset a glass of beer which was on the eounter and had to retire in consequence of sickness. She was never served. It transpired that eighteen months ago Mrs. Santley had married a man named Joseph Young, a worker on the Ship Canal, and during that time she had carried on the 1 house without notifying the police of any change. After hearing the evidence, the Bench dismissed the case.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. ISAAC SPEAKMAN,
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. ISAAC SPEAKMAN,
OF RUNCORN.

The funeral of Mr. Isaac Speakman whose death was recorded in this journal last Saturday, took place on Monday. There were universal signs of mourning. The tradesmen throughout the town partially closed their establishments, and the win- dows of numerous private houses were darkened. Flags were flying half-mast in various parts of the town. The mournful procession started from the late residence of the deceased gentleman shortly after eleven o'clock, and was watched by large numbers of spectators. Preceding the hearse were Messrs. J. E. Meredith, W. Timmins, E. Gregory, R. Abel, and W. Crosby, representing the Parish , Church, of which the late Mr. Speakman was a sidesman ; Messrs. B. Trevitt, A. Price, P. Bolton, J. Yates and C. Woolley, representing the Parish Church Bible Class and the following tradesmen, &c., Messrs. G. Moss, W. Handley, T. Handley, W. Hankinton, J. Bate, B. Kniveton, C. Dutton, J. Poole, W. Kay, R. W. Pierpoint, T. Jones, F. Beck, T. Cooke, S. Coventry, J. W. Woodland, W. B. Brimelow, J. Connor, J. Byrne, W. Mutch, R. Hampson, W. Bankes, and S. Mason. 'Through the glass sides of the hearse, it could be seen that the coffin was covered with choice floral tributes, many also being placed on the top of the vehicle. On each side walked the bearers namely, Messrs. Thomas Jones, Inn. Shields, Fred Dutton, L. Peacock (employes) Joseph Clark, J. Fearnett, William Dudley, and Joseph Barker. In the first carriage were Master Percy B. Speakman (son), Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., Mr. Joseph J. Speakman, and Mr. Abraham Speakman; second carri- age, Messrs. Thomas Speakman, John Speakman, and Frank Speakman (nephe vs) and Mr. Reid; third carri- age, Messrs. Eric Speakman, ',red Widders, E. Marston (flelsby), and W. E. Lea. The first part of the burial service was conducted in the Parish Church by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, who read the lessons in an im- pressive manner. The service was choral. The choir under the conductorship of Mr. James Littler, chanted the 39th psalm and the congregation sang the hymn When our heads are bowed with woe," and as the , congregation left the sacred edifice, Mr. A. Savage, organist at Holy Trinity Church, played the Dead ' March in " Saul " on the organ. Afterwards the e,rtege reformed and proceeded to the railway station, where the mourners and their dead were conveyed by ' the 12.18 train to Liverpool, where the remains of Mr. Speakman were committed to the earth in Smithdown Cemetery, in the grave where his wife and infant lie buried. The body was encased in an oak coffin, with brass mountings and a shield bearing the inscription " Isaac Speakman, died March 3rd,1893, aged 43 years." At Smithdown Cemetery, the cortege was met by Mr. Pewker, Mr. Newall, Mr. White (of Liverpool), and Mr. E. J. Reid, of Preston. Mr. W. H. Rogerson, of Bridge- St., efficiently carried out the duties of undertaker, and the coaches and hearse were supplied by Messrs. F. and W. Yarwood. The wreaths included the following To my dear father from his affectionate and loving son, Percy ; Mr. and Mrs. Philip Speakman ; in tender affec- tion to our dear brother, fromJ. J. and M. J. Speakman; in loving affectio., to our dear brother, from Abraham and Lydia Speakman ; in loving affection to our dear brother, from William and M. J. Reid ; from Mr. and Mrs. A. J. Reid, with deepest sympathy ; with love and sympathy from Mrs. D. Speakman and his loving neice, Annie ;a tribute of love from Emily to my dear uncle; a tribute of love from Harold and Bessie ; in loving memory of dear Isaac, from his sister Mary, and nep- hew, Fred Widders ; to our dear uncle, from John, Frank, Eric, Albert, Bessie, Eva, Gladys, Fanny ; from Mrs. Nellie Kirkham, Blackpool ; with deepest sympathy and respect from Mary ; from the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Maitland Wood, with deepest sympathy and truest es- teem ; from his fellow members of the Vicar's Bible Class, with sincerest regrets; from the wardens and his fellow sidesmen of the Runcorn Parish Church, in sad recollection of staunch and loving friendship ; Arthur Dutton ; Mr. and Mrs. Charles Dutton ; Mr. and Mrs. Jno. Knowles, Liverpool ; Mrs. Earp, Colwyn Bay; Mr. Ed. Marston, Liverpool; Mr and Mrs. W. E. Lea, Runcorn ; Miss Nellie Speakman, Rut bin ; and one from Pembroke house School, Lytham, and with the sentiment, " the master and boys join with Mr. and Mrs. Lightwood in sincere sympathy with Percy Speakman."

div.head: WEAVER NAVIGATION TRUST. --- MR. BRUNNER DEMANDS AN INQUIRY.
div.p: THE WEAVER NAVIGATION TRUST. --- MR. BRUNNER DEMANDS AN INQUIRY.

Private bills as a rule do not receive the attention they deserve, but the Board of Trade report, recen- tly published, on the bill promoted this year by the 1 trustees of the Weaver Navigation &multi have the effect of drawing more than usual attention to the conditions and history of that very remarkable Trust. The Board of Trade has indeed no particu- lar objection to the bill this year, but thinks it aivisablo to remind Parliament of the history of the Weaver Navigation. This little reminder, only extend- ing over five pages, is well worth perusal. The Weaver is, or rather was, a natural stream in Cheshiirenwavhiiacahbilne some of its turns is even now hardly inferior to the Thames in beauty. The idea of making t appears to have first occurred to three Cheseire 'gentle- men in 1720, who received powers under an Act of Parliament for that purpose, the cost of the undertaking to be defrayed by tolls. The surplus of the tolls, after paying debts and expenses, was to be applied to the repair of bridges and highways in the county of Ches- hire. Fourteen gentlemen under these conditions agreed to lend among them £9,000, a debt which has long since beeo paid off. Several other Acts were passed at differ- ent times, generally at the instance of the trustees, regulating the conditions of the Trust, and by one of these-47 Geo. lll.—the trustees were empowered to fill up vacancies in their own body. Being thus rendered permanent and irresponsible, they proceeded to act, with a full sense of their new character. Thousands of pounds a year—rarely less than fifteen, and often double that sum, amounting in all to over a million and a half—were paid by them as surplus to defray the Cheshire county rate ; this notwithstanding that they were themselves burdened with a debt not far short of £250,000, and that all the money they obtained was from tolls, i.e., from navigation. In 1840 a bill was introduced empowering the trustees to expend £6,000 on the erection of churches and the endowment of ministers. All this beneficient work of mending roads and repairing bridges of building churches and endow- ing ministers, was paid for by those using the naviga- tion of the Weaver,'in other words by those who did not use either the roads 'or bridges—except in very few cases—or the churches or the ministers. This body of gentlemen—the Weaver trustees—still exist. They still continue a self-elected body of Cheshire gentry, squires and clergy, to his place in which a Cheshire peer succeeds as naturally as to his seat in Parliament. They still continue to levy tolls, the principle of which Parliament has again and again condemned. They still held annual inspections of the Weaver, described as " lunch all the way up and dinner all the way down and they still every now and then promote private bills. One of these having passed through its stages in the UpperounmHoele it willto thesliortlayttecnotmioen boeffotrehatthme Commons. We vire e , inquir- ing body. ' Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., evidently intends that there shall be the fullest inquiry, and he has addressed the following letter to the President of the Board of Trade: —"Dear Mr.Mundella,—l beg to draw your attention to the fact that the trustees of the River Weaver Naviga- tion are promoting a private Bill this session, and then, first, to a report of the Board of Trade, Harbour, &c., Bills, River Weaver Navigation, February, 1857. Secondly, to Mr. Gladstone's speech on Earl Grosvonor's , motion. 3 Hansard, vol. 197-1817. Thirdly, to the Brine Pumping (Compensation for Subsidence) Act,lB9l. I propose to move on the second reading of the above private Bill—(1) to commit the Bill to a hybrid com- mittee of nine ; (2) that all petitions presented five days before the meeting be, referred to the committee, and that petitions he heard, &c. ; (3) power to send for per- sons, papers, and records ; (4) five to be quorum ; (5) that it be an instruction to the committee to inquire into and report upon all matters connected with the con- stitution, powers, finance, and management of the trus- tees of the Weaver Navigation,and on the provisions and administration of the Act relating thereto, and that the committee have power to insert in the Bill such provi- sions in connection with all or any such matters as in their jndgment are expedient. I appeal to you to sup- port my motion. The Board's report of 1857 is, I think, amplejustification for my appeal, and I have not the smallest doubt that after you have read it you will agree

with me. I may further point out that the arguments against the continuance of the tax levied upon the traders on the river Weaver—almost all brine pumpers— is indefinitely strengthened by the Compensation Act of 1891. This Act, as von are aware, compels pumpers of brine to pay for the damage they do, and takes away every shred of excuse for taxing them for the relief of the county rate.

div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS AT RUNCORN.

In aid of the Wesleyan Home Missions, special services were held in St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday. There were good congregations at each service, and the Rev. Thomas Hind, of Birkenhead, preached two admirable sermons. On Monday after- noon a fairly good audience assembled to hear the 'Rev. John Pickup, of St. Peter's Mission, Leeds. IThe annual meeting was held in the evening in the chapel. There was a large congregation. Mr. F. Wig- wall presided, and there were present the Rev. John Pickup, Miss Morley, and Miss Barraclough, workers in connection with the Leeds Mission ; Revs. T. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmith, and J. Hanby: Messrs. T. Simister, W. Rawlinson, E. Taylor, F. J. Norman, A. R. Norman, S. Pope. After the singing of the hymn " Jesus, thou all redeeming Lord," the Rev. W. irrowsmith offered up prayer. The Chairman in the course of his speech, said he was in thorough sympathy with that Home Missionary Society, and with any object of kindred nature, and with all objects for the welfare and amelioration of the masses of the people. It was pleasing to find that great attention was being paid to this movement, and there was no doubt that the Wesleyan Home Mission was doing a good work. The ladies and gentlemen who were devoting themselves in this movement with noble self sacrifice, to uplift the degraded masses, came across much misery. He sometimes thought that a great deal of it might be prevented, in his opinion the introduction of destitute aliens was a great drawback to the masses of the people in this country. He had read of one gentleman who visited Tilbury Dock, and saw an emigrant ship with some hundreds of English emigrants on board. On the same day he saw a large foreign steamer land as many destitute aliens. That was an awkward state of things and was a difficult problem to deal with, and he was glad that the attention of the Government had been called to it. The English Govern- ment had been the protection of the foreigner at home and of the Englishman abroad, and it was a question whether this had not been carried too far. He drew attention to the horrible mode of life of the Jews in some parts of Manchester, which he contended must have a detrimental effect upon our own people,and much as we blamed our own people for their condition and indiffe- rent mode of living, there was still some consideration due to them, and it would not do to leave them to them- selves, as many people were inclined to do. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. J. Hanby, referring to the Chairman's re- marks, said he honed that there were some Wesleyan Methodists and more Christians in that emigrant ship going to colonize and Christianize other countries. He would not then object to some destitute aliens coming to England, for they might, too, be made Christians. (Ap- lause.) The report showed that the income during the past year had been £36,899,and theexpenditure £36,761, so that the debt due to the treasurer of £609 twelve ' months ago had been reduced to £470. Towards that amount toe Runcorn circuit contributed £B6 18s. 6d., made up of collections in the schools, chapels, and public meetings. Of this the Camden Juvenile Association raised £2l. The particulars of the collections were—yearly collec- tion, £8 ss. ; congregational collection, £26 55.; public meetings, £23 3s. Bd. ; Camden Juvenile Association, £2l Be. 7d. ; Messrs. W. Collier 55.,8. Crosby 2s. 6d., R rosnett 103. 6d., John Simpson £2 25., P. Speakman £l, collected by Miss Massey £3 15s. 3d. It was pointed out that the society employed 96 home mission ministers, an increase of 12 on the year ; there were three connex- ional evangelists, and three district missionaries. There were 400 circuits assisted by the fend. Missions in London and large towns were assisted by it ; and Methodist work was carried on in the army and navy. In London there were six branches, the Liverpool mission was presided ever by the Rev. Chas. Garrett, and there were missions in Manchester and Salford, Birmingham, and Leeds, and from the latter three, workers were present to advocate the needs of the society. (Applause.) Miss Barraclough explained that she was not a" sister of the people," that was she was not set apart altogether from the work. She lived at home and had home duties to attend to, but she was able to give a little time each week, to the work of the mission. She narrated her experiences in the slums of Leeds, described the misery and wretchedness there, and the difficulties met with in attempting to lead them to a better and higher life. During the past winter a soup kitchen had been a great help, and their Girls Club had been a remarkable success in reclaiming girls from their sordid surroundings. Miss Barraclough made an appeal to those present to join in similar work in Runcorn, where no doubt they had the poor and wretched though perhaps of a different class to those in Leeds. (Applause.) Mrs. Morley in the course of an interesting speech, spoke of the value of the lessons that were learnt by the workers, and of the great benefit that they themselves derived from their offorts. If they were to succeed there must be fewer temptations by reducing the num- ber of public-houses, by providing for the people innocent recreation, and in other ways looking after the interests of the very poor as their fellow citizens and fellow creatures.

The Rev. John Pickup gave a:sketch of his own life, which was listened to with much interest,and occasional flashes of humour caused much laughter. On the motion of Mr. Hope seconded by Mr. Rawlin- son a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, the deputation and the singers. The collection amounted to £26 ss. 7d.
During the evening the choir and scholars sang several hymns under the leadership of Mr. J. Birkett,and their efforts added brightness to the proceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOA RD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOA RD.
The montMy meeting was held on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. T. Handley, E. lint- son, and G. Moss (clerk).

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The School Attendance Officers had reported that the percentage of attendance during the past month was 80.7 as compared with 823 in the corresponding period last year. The School Attendance Committee (Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, chairman) had ordered proceedings to be taken against a number of parents. THE SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. Dr. McDougall, chairman, recommended that the salary of Mr. E. W. Rosser, assistant master at Green- way-road school be increased to £65 ; and that a sum not exceeding £5 to purchase prizes for the Greenway-road evening school.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Handley. CHILDREN IN THE STREETS. Dr. Gastaldi said he saw from the last month's return that some schools were better attended than others. He failed to understand why it should be. At whatever time of the day he was in the town he always found children of school age in the streets, and it was very seldom he met one of the officers in those streets. The greatest patt of the officer's time was taken up in clerk- ing which was not practical. He suggested that the officers should change districts every six months, and that this might result in an improvement.—The subject was referred to the School Attendance Committee.

div.head: INSUFFICIENT ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: INSUFFICIENT ACCOMMODATION.

Mr. T. Handley drew attention to the fact that no re- ply had been received from the Education Department with reference to the application of the Board to provide temporary accommodation for girls,there being a greater number in attendance than there was accommodation for. He proposed that a cpmmunication be sent,request- ing a reply.—Mr. Imison pointed out that last month there were only 11 more girls in attendance than there was accounted for.—Mr. Handley remarked that the number on the rolls was greatly in excess of the ac- commodation, and if attendance were only attended to, they would not have room.—The Chairman asked if' some provision was not being made P—Mr. Imisun did not think they should take into account any provision that might be provided in the future. If there was not sufficient accommodation, it was undoubtedly the duty of the Board to provide it.
APPLICATIONS.

Mary A. Simkin, assistant mistress, and Mr. Albert E. Parr, assistant master, at Greenway-road School, made applications for increases of salary.—The applications were referred to the School Management Committee.—lt was decided to purchase a clock for the Boardroom.

SCIENCE AND ART COMMITTEE. The Clerk read the report of the Science and Art Com- mittee for the Session ended April 1892. He also sub- mitted the statement of accounts for the year ended Sept. 492. Atter recapitulating the circumstances which led to the School Board to take up Technical Edu- cation, the report stated that the Committee had pro- vided mechanical and scientific apparatus,art examples, and plaster castes for the use of the classes.—The resuito of the science examinations may be considered satisfac- tory on the whole. It would be the p,licv com- mittee to foster and encourage all branches of study which were appreciated by stadents and were likely to be of permanent benefit to the town. of the
