The Chief Constable said that "Johnny" had told him that he would work hard if peopkr would be civil to him. Mr. Garnett: "What do you db for a living?" Prisoner: "I get it as best I can." Mr. Garnett : "Do you live anywhere ?"Prisoner: "I sleep out always." Mr. Hunt asked him where he slept, but "Johnny "de- dined to commit himself. Mr. Taylor, P.C.M., said that he could get him a place in the firewood factory at Bootle, and as prisoner promised to go there he was discharged.

THOSB TRUANTS AGAIN. Elizabeth Deakin' Percy-st., was charged on Wednes- day at the Borough Court, at the instance of Mr. Riley ' (school attendance officer), with not sending her son Herbert regularly to school. The case had been re- manded horn Tuesday, in order that the lad might be apprehended. Mr. Rilev said it was a case from St. Barnabas' Schools, and the boy had already made his fourth appearance in court, and he hoped the magis- trates would make a settlement of the case by sending the bey to the ship "Clio," as his mother said the boy was utterly. unmanageable. The boy was apprehended at Monk's works the night previous at eight o'clock. The magistrates decided to send him te the "Clio," where he will be detained until he is 16 years of age. A SWEET-TOOTHED "BILL &HES." At the Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, Frederick Burke, alias John Haines, an old offenaer, was charged with burglariouslv breaking into the shop of Wm. Henry Crosby, 173, Orford-lane, on Wednesday, the I Bth inst., and stealing a quantity of sweets and an egg, valued 3d. Fred Crosby said that he saw everything safe on Tuesday night. At four o'clock in the morning he was knocked up by the police, and found a window pane broken,and the contents of the window disarranged. A small quantity of sweets was missing and an egg. P.C. Forster said that on the above date he saw prisoner in Orford-lane,and saw him then go to Mr. Crosby's shop. Witness ran towards the shop and heard a smash of glass. When he arrived at the shop he found prisoner with his hand and arm inside the window. When he withdrew his arm he had an egg in his hand. Prisoner said, "lam nobbled this time." He then put the egg in his mouth, and swallowed part of the contents, and spat the rest aut. Prisoner was brought to the Police Station and P.S. Cheeny said that when he met him being 'brought down" he was masticating the sweets. He said that be had found the window broken and had taken some sweets. Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A LUCKY" BOBBY." On Saturday, at the Warrington Borough Court, before Mr. John Burgess (chairman), and Mr. L. Voisey, George Whitney, and George Bradley, were charged with being deserters from the East Yorkshire Regiment. The two prisoners were seen in Buttermarket-St., by P.O Turner, who brought them to the police station, and examined their clothing, when he found on one of their socks the words " E.Y.R. The prisoners on being charged with being deserters admitted their guilt. They were remanded to await an escort. The constable then asked for the usual reward which was granted. This made three cases during the week for the constable for which he would receive a reward of £1 each. I BICYCLE" IN CUSTODY." On Saturday, at the Borough Court, a representative of Messrs, Jones and Co., bicycle dealers, Liverpool, asked permission to take possession of a bicycle then lying at the police station. It appeared that the machine had been purchased on the hire system from Messrs. Jones and Co, in 1892 by Mr. Pendlebury, then in Warrington, who had paid about £4 by monthly instalments, on account, it being a £lO machine. But for some time he had not paid anything, and the repre- sentative called on Friday at Mr. Pendlebury's house in Pierpoint-at., and took the bicycle away. This action did not seem to be appreciated by some of the neighbours and a" scene "ensued. During the melee the represen- tative was roughly handled and taken to the police sta- tion with the bicycle. Whilst there Mr. Hunt tried to settle the matter and it was agreed that it a:lc-mid be brought before the magistrates for settlement the fol- lowing morning. The bicycle was therefore kept at the police station for the night. Mr. Pendlebury did not put in an appearance on Saturday. Messrs. 'Jones and Co., therefore asked for the machine. After examining the agreement, which stated that in default of payment the bicycle should be forfeited, the magistrates allowed the representative of the firm to take the machine, and Mr. Pendlebury could take any action he thought pro- per afterwards for its recovery. STREET ROBBERY. At the Berough Police Court on Monday, Joseph I Burke, alias &molly alias Teesdale, and Elizabeth Flem- ing were each charged with robbing George Hill with violence in Cocklaedge-lane on Saturday night, and taking a sum of £1 4s. in money and an Irish £1 note.—Mr. Hunt said that complainant lodged in a model-lodging house in Old-road, Latchford, and the male defendant also lodged at times in the same lodging house. The female defendant is a well-known character and lives anywhere. On Saturday night, complainant and male prisoner went out for a walk and called at several public-houses. They then went across Town Hill and met Fleming, who went with them to Cockhedge-lane. When they got near the Alexandra, Burke asked Hill how much money he had. Hill replied that he only had 14d. in change. Burke said " That's not good enough. "That's no use." Complainant pulled out his purse, when the two prisoners seized his hand. Complainant struggled very hard but he was forced to the ground. He shouted Police! Police! Help! Help! upon which Fleming ran away up Cockhedge-lane, but complainant kept hold of Burke, and they struggled together until they got to Buttermarket-street, when a young man named Albert Snelson ran and informed the police. Inspector Spinks and Detective Monaghan then came up and teok the prisoner into custody. When they got to the police station, complainant made a statement from which the female prisoner was arrested. Nothing was found on the prisoners.—The case was remanded until Thursday. The two prisoners Joseph Edward Burke and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming,were again brought before the magistrates On Thursday. The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), appeared for the prosecution. Complainant aeorge Hill, repeated his evidence given on the previous Monday.— Albert Snelson, Lythgoes-la,ne, said that on Saturday night he was going home along Scotland-road, when he heard complainant shouting for help in Cockhedge-lane. He heard the male prisoner say to Hill " Come on, your money will be all right." The male prisoner then knocked the complainant to the ground and ran off, but he was caught in Buttermarket-st. Witness went for the pelice and prisoner was taken to the police station.— James Henry Sanson, Orford-lane, corroborated last wit- ness.—Detective Monaghan said he and Inspector Spinks were called out by the witness Snelson,and they went to the scene of the scuffle. They brought the com- plainant and male prisoner to the police station, and when charged with the theft the prisoner said " I have not the purse, a young woman snatched it and ran away." Complainant also complained of prisoner assault- ing him. Fleming was arrested the same night.—Pri- soners were committed to the Liverpool Assizes. ANOTIBR FOWL ROBBERY. Emma Lane, 178, Battersby-lane, and Jane Briars, 28, Dickenson-St., were each charged on Monday, at the Borough Police Court, with stealing two fowls, the pro- perty of Wm. Carrington, 5, Leonard-St., on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Hunt (chief constable), said that Mrs. Lane was seen by a witness, Mrs. Cooke, inducing two fowls into her yard on Thursday. On Satarday night, Carrington reported the matter to P.C. Evans, and they searched the ashpits and excreta tubs about Leonard-st, &c. They found the heads or the fowls in the excreta tub of Mrs. Briars, and at once charged her with the theft. The police officer walked through to the back kitchen and found the fowls dressed up ready for cook- ing. From a statement by Mrs. Briars, Mrs. Lane was also taken into custody. When charged with the theft Mrs. Briars said that Mrs. Lane had enticed the fowls into the yard, and she (Mrs. Briars) had killed them.— Wm. Carrington, Margaret Cooke, and P.C. Evans cor- roborated Mr. Hunt's statement, and the magistrates, in consideration of their previous good character, fined them 10s. or seven days. Trim OF A SHAWL. Eliza Brady, 5, Buckley-st., was charged on Monday, 1 at the Borough Police Court, with stealing a shawl from Harriet Brown, 45, Foundry-st., on Saturday afternoon I in Puoner's Brow.—Harriet Brown said that on Saturday afternoon, she had been to the butcher's, when prisoner, with whom she used to lodge, met her and took her Shawl off her. Witness went home and told her hus- band, and the matter was reported to the police. Detec- tive Monaghan and Inspector Cox arrested the prisoner on the same day. Prisoner admitted taking the shawl, but said the complainant owed her some rnoney,and she took the shawl as part payment of it. Prisoner was fined ss. or 7 days, the Magistrate's Clerk saying that the County Court was the place to settle debts. JORN WARRINGTON BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES AGAIN. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, John Warrington was charged with being a convicted thief, and with frequenting the Market Place with intent to committ a felony on Monday night. P.C, Clarke said that on the previous night he was in Horsemarket-st., when he received a complaint of prisoner being in the I ket Place. Witness proceeded thither and saw pri- 'Marsoner trying the locks of the different stalls. Prisoner: " You're a liar ! " Witness proceeding said that prisoner when he saW that he was watched,but he was ran away w .staMl r. Ever since I caine out ot prison I watching , tolen anything, and lam jolly sure that I •have never Mr. Garnett : You hale only tried. Pri- xaevee

div.p: MINOR. CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
• • - MONDA.Y. —Before the Mayor (in the chair), and Messrs. S. Wright and J. W.Hayward.

- DESERTER.—Wrn. George Dickens was charged with being a deserter from H.M.East York Regiment,staticned at Preston, osk February 28th. P.C. Wheatley proved the case, and prisoner was remanded to Strangeways Gaol, to await an escort. P.C. Wheatley received the usual reward. DEUS% L\n DISORDERLY.—John Callaghan was charged with the above offence, which was proved by P.C. Hollingworth, and was fined ss. and costs, or seven

days. - Ass...nix ON THY POLICE.—John Shields was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, in Dial-st., and also with assaulting P.C. Liethwood while in the execution of his duty. Julia. Shields was also charged with assaulting P.C. Liethwood at the same time and place. The Chief Constable said that it was characteristic of the male prisoner to have a '•go" at every new psliceman. The Bench dismissed the female prisoner, and sent the male prisoner to gaol for three months' hard labour.

A Stsriczons Ozer/tem.—Michael Cunningham was charged with being a suspicious character and with fre- quenting Cockhedge-lane on Saturday night. Detective Monaghan said that prisoner cc-habits with Elizabeth Ellen Fleming,who was brought up on a charge of street robbery on Saturday night. He gets his living by fol- lowing Fleming who robs drunken men ,and on Saturday night he was found it, company with Fleming when she was arrested for the robbery. Prisoner was sent for a month's hard labour. DISORDERLY WOMRN.—Martha Brown and Hannah Walton were charged with being drunk and with inde- cent behaviour in Sankey-street on Sunday night. P.S. Smith proved the case, and prisoners were dismissed on promising to leave the town. SMASHING HIS OWN FURNITURE.—John RUMP WES charged with being drunk and disorderly in Lythgoe's- lane,on Sunday morning. P.C. Evans said that prisoner was drunk at his mien house on Sunday morning, and was smashing all the furniture he could lay hold of with an axe. He afterwards gave chase to his wife, and wit- ness with the assistance of P.C. Turner, was obliged to lock him up. Prisoner said that he had been teetotal for , some time, but had broken down. He dlcl irt know what he was doing. The magistrates.. on his promising to sign the pledge, dismissed the case on payment of the costs. CHIMNEY on FIRE .—For this offence Tohn Rushes, 25, Bank-st., was fined is. FOOTBALL IN THE STRRETS.—John Edwards, Thomas Brown, Richard Horton, Thomas Pendlebury, and James McGuire were each charged with playing football in Lythgoe's-lane on the 26th ult. P.C. Chrinies said that on the above date he saw defendants playing football in Lythgoe's-lane. Be caught Edwards and from him got the names of the rest. Edwards said that he gave Pendlebury's name by mistake. Pendlebur7 was accor- dingly dismissed and the rest fined in the costs 3s. 6d. Tnarr AT THE BARRACES.—Pred Smith was charged with stealing from a sleeping room in Orford Barracks, ' during the night of Tuesday, February 28th, 4s. belonging to John Ward, is. 9d. from James Walker, is. 101 d. tobacco and a penknife from Thomas Pendle- bury andothers. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said prisoner and complainants were in the Liverpool Militia,and slept in the same room in Orford Barracks on the above date. The complainants next morning missed the money, tobacco, and knife, and reported the case to Colour-Sergeant Buller, who from information he obtained handed prisoner over to the civil authorities. Private John Worral said that he awoke during-the night of the above date, and saw prisoner feeling his pockets. Witness told him to leave his pockets alone. Prisoner said he was only looking for some tobacco. Prisoner then felt the pockets of the rest of the inmates of the room, and then offered to share the money with witness, but wit- ness refused. Next morning witness found the pen- knife on the ground outside the window of the sleeping room. John Hartley, Michael Crivins, and Henry Mc- Grevin also gave evidence to seeing prisoner feeling the trousers pockets of complainants. Prisoner was sen- tenced to 3 months hard labour. ASSOONDING FROM THE WORICROUSE, HIATT PENALTY.— Thomas Troy was charged with being a convicted thief, and with being found in the enclosed premises of Walkers Botanic beer premises,. Froghall-lane, and also with absconding from the Warrington, Workhouse, and with taking the clothes, the property of the Guardians, on Saturday night. P.C. Bell said that on Saturday night he saw prisoner climbing over the palings of Walker's premises. He said that he had been to get some coffee. Witness knew him to be a convicted thief and took him to the police station. Mr.. Curry, Werkhouse janitor, said that prisoner absconded from the Work-

AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHIC 50C JET Y. A SUCCESSI'UfseEXHIBITION.. • The sixth annual exhibition of lantern slides, and maeical entertainment given by the Warangton Amateur Photographic Society, was held on Tuesday, night, in the Co-operative Mall, Sankey-street. There was a large attendance. The chair was. oc cupied by Mr. T. J. Down, president of the society, who,ein his opening remarks, said that he could hardlyrealise that IL was six years since he first had the honour to be on that platform as presidebt of the-Warrington Amateur Photographic Society. Then the society wit* in its infancy, and it was perhaps-a somewhat feeble thing, but now, -thanks to the careful nursing it had received from Mrs Houghtone.Mr. Harding, Mr. Dalton, their very energe- tic secretary Mr. Pritchard, and others ..it had become a strong,erigorons institution, which had. already done some good-work, and had a little property of its owre Month alter-month the meetings had been regularly held. and they had lways been interesting and instrnetive,and one very interesting feature of these meetings was, that there had been always a batch of fresh aniiearees for .ad- mission to te.e..society. The Secretary informed him that elisire had • been 15 new members elected during the past twelve months. He might say that the work of the society was tbierouOly appreciated. With regard to the property ofthe society, they had detective cameras, a tri-unial lantern lime- light and other apparatus, and also a good: library of books on photographie subjects, all of which were lent out on certain conditions to the members of the society. This was a greatiboon,as scientific apparatus was costly, and there were- men naturally clever,. who. were pre- vented from working according to their ability, for want of proper tools. They had helped these meia,as far as. their funds permitted the-ii to do.. There was muck more they could do if they had the money, but they had made it a rule to keep out of debt. (Hear hear.) But he/ be- lieved, that satisfactory as the position of the-society was at the present moment, it was nothing towahat it would become: He felt &wee that it had come-to steer, and that year by year it wouli become more usefutaed more firmly established. He knew of no more deserving society than theirs.. He hoped that the audience-we:Ad enjoy the entertainment, and that they would go away convinced that the society was- at least trying to, cany out a good and useful work. The society felt consider- ably indebted to their musical friends who had kindly promised their assistance on that occasion. (Apeelause..) They had lent their help on more than one of the-pre- vious exhibitions, and their assistance was very cheer- fully given, and it certainly added to the pleasure of the entertainments. On behalf of the society,. he begged to tender them. their warmest thanks. The programme of the evening was then entered upon. It consisted of exhibitions of photographic slide views— the work of members of the Society—agreeably alterna- ting with items-of vocal-and instrumental music of more than ordinary . interest. Mrs: Pearson's two song* "Stars of the Summer night "(Palmer), and" 0* that we two were Al/Lying."' (Growled), were both well sung. and deservedly applauded. Tke first—an entirely new and pretty setting of•Longfellow'S favourite verses—is especially adapted I. Mrs. Pearson's voice and style. Both songs were enhanced in interest by the scliAir, accompaniments sustained. by Mr. Pearson and. Mr. Bond. Mr. W. H. Vi.allington sang Matti's ever-popular " Oh, hear the wild winds blow" with spirit and a dee regard for the strong contrasts-of efieet for which., this. song gives scope. Butehiarentiering of " Thou'rt pass- ing hence,"—a song much; more. difficult of artistic Mter- pretation—was the more pronounced success, andoeini response to the demeetetration of the audience's approval- which followed it, Mr. Wallington was constrained. to. bow his acknowledgements, Messrs. R. H. Pearsonille Bond, and W. H. Payton played a couple of trios cet two movements each- for violin, 'cello,. and piano reepect- ively which contributed considerably to the varietyiot the musical part of the entertaintment,and Mr. Payton further officiated as accompanist to the songs and/dis- played good taste and judgement in supporting; the vocalists. The photographic slides consisted of views-of local and distant sceneryegroups,. Am., many csli them. "lump shots" from tile detective camera now pretty well indispensible in the etuipinent of members- on, holiday tour. Thouelea large propowtion of the views. embodied tit-bits of wood,riwereglen or sea charmingly reminiscent or pleasmat. " outings„' the photographs-as a whole were scarey up, to- the /standard of all-round excellence attained in sernivot the Society's past work. The following members- contributed slides :Messrs. .J W. Cavanagh, James Hardiage H. N. Hous • Ce. W.. Aylward, J. Smith, Graham,. Hallows, Kirby, i/Velsby, Pritchard and Miss Williamson. The lantern wee- ably manipulated by Messrs. J. Harding and W. Lawson, The exhibition closed with the singing of the National Anthem after which/ a dance was- indulged in be. those members and friendswhocared to remain.

PRESENTATION TO SIR GILBERT GREENALL.: The long talked of presentation to Sir Gilbert Chemin, Bart., was made on Saturday afternoon. at the Conservative Club. The present took the form of a silver bowl, and. in 'addition to this a, diamond star was presented to Lady Greenall. Sir , Gilbert was unable to attend, but Lady Greenall, I accompanied by Mr. Gilbert Greene'', and the Misses Greene'', was present. Mr.-Robert Pierpointy the Mayor, (Alderman Greenall), Rev. F. Slater, , Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Alderman Wright, Alderman Sutton, Dr. Cannel!, Councillors Hill, Hatchinson,Eleaton,Smethurst,ancl,Mr.Jenkins,were ale. present. Alderman Francomb3,who was in the Chair said that the testimonial had,been subscribed for by the workingmen Conservatives of the town, and was a token of the respect in which that class ' held Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall.—Mr. Robert Pierpoint and made the presentation to Sir Gilbert through, his son, ;. and Mr. Mills made the presen- tation to Lady Greenall. Mr. Gilbert Greenall •and Lady &menial acknowledged the gifts and :short speeches were made by several of those

'present.. . ANNUAL MEEPLIII% OF THE ASSOCIATION. The same evening the annual meeting of Conserve- tive.Assoeiation was held. in the dub. Mr. John White psesided, and amongst. those present were Mr. R. Pier- point, M.R.,,Aldermaa T.Mutton, Alderman Franconab, Mc, J. Fairolough,„ Alderman Wright, Mr. Jenkins, Mr. Jain Roberts, and Mr. Wm. Diggle. JOHI4-WHIT3. in a. short speech, warned the party that they would probably be in the midst of another election in a-few months, and that it was necessary they should not become ksthargiaaud thus risk losing the seat. He pointed out that Lancashire had done its duty to the Unionist party, for, said he, "The number of votes given in Lancashire for the Unionist cause at the recent election exceeded those given or the Separatists by 20,040eand in-Cheshire by 65000. It should be further take* into consideration that in those two counties there were 25,000-Irish votes." Mr. -JOH* Baimmonsau then moved the following reso- lution That this meeting has heard with great alarm and dissatisfaction that a bill to create a separate legislature in Ireland has been introduced into the House of Commons, and hereby records its conviction that the creation of such a legislature will jeopardise the lives a:Ai property of the loyal inhabitants of that country, will cause oppression and foster crime, and in all proba- bility result in anarchy and civil war, and further that if the bill should become law it will be a cause of con- stant and-grave danger to the welfare and stability of •Great Britain and the Empire." Mr. Btoomentuaseconded the resolution. I Mr.-41..Pranv0urx„ M.P., in supporting the resolution sr rid since the opening of Parliament he had noticed several bills which had been brought before the notice of Parliament during the past few weeks. He had that evening had an interview with a deputation of the Lou- du n and North-western Railway men with reference to th employers' liability bill, and they had stated their I vie we. Some parts of the bill were praiseworthy, but nth ers required condemnation. It contained a deliberate at tmpt tnabolish freedom of contract, and would serve to ; lonrote hostility between directors and their em- plos vs. The local veto bill the speaker described as a kite, ,to be flown for a time and for purpose, but not. ;Berk usly intended to be passed into law. Ho would like to know what a three years' grace for purposes of !tram ler would be worth? The bill offered no compen- Betio nto the publican, who was exercising a perfectly !lawn ii trade. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Gladstone had con- tencld d that a man had a legal right in a slave, and if 'therd was a. legal right in human flesh and blood, Surely there was an equitable one in a publican's 1111)si- • nese 1? (Hoar, hear, and cheers). The registration bill ,be (M r. Pierpoint) objected to, as the three months' resi- demi +clause he did not consider gave them a chance to know theirkvoters. div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.
TWO MEN KILLED.

About half past five on Saturday evening, por- tione of a tall chimney in the yard of Sullivan's works,.Widnes, of the United Alkali Company. fell and caused the death of two men. The chimney, which•was 90 feet high, was connected with the saltcalre department, and the gases had eaten away the mortar and some of the bricks of the upper por- tion; and the high winds that have recently caused doubts to be felt as to its safety, and accordingly Messrs, J. Whitehead and Co.,steeplejacks of Liver- pool, were engaged to repair the structure. To put the chimney in thorough and safe condition it was deemed necessary to remove about six feet of the old brickwork at the top and replace it with new. Seven men were employed in carrying out the job, and after placing ladders on each side of the chimney, they constructed.a scaffold in the usual way with poles and planks, On, Saturday afternoon a large iron band was removed and all went well antil half-past five when the defective portion suddenly collapsed, carrying with it several stages of the scaffolding and two men named Boden and Mains. The men fell about 85 feet to the ground •, Beclan was killed out right,but Mains survived his terrible injuries until he was conveyed to the hospital. One man who was on the ground had a narrow escape from .being buried in the debris-. Three other men, who had fortunately descended the chimney just prior to the accident, otherwise they might have shared the fate of theirtomrades. Roden was 29 years of age, and had lived in Warrington-road, Widnes ; and Joseph Mainse, 31 years of ,agediad his home at Stamford-St., Warring- ton.

THE INQUEST. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquest at the Moss Bank Hotel, Widnes, on Tuesday. Mr. T. Minton, manager of the works, and Mr. J. W. White- head (Liverpool) were present, and the proceedings were v;atchdd by Superintendent Keighley, on behalf of the

police. William Soden, Derby, identified the body Gf George IBoden as that of his brother, .who was 29 years .of age. .He had followed his employment as steeple- jack for about nine years. It was not true that he was married. The body. of Joseph Maines was identified by his widow' rg, Maaret Maines, residing at 10, Stamford- street, Warrington. Dora Jones,assistant-matron at the Widnes Accident Hospital, said the deceased, Joseph Maines, was admitted into•the hospital at 7.15, and died at 7.45 the same night. He was- uticonscioull when he was admitted, and remaiaed in that condition up to his

death. Frederick William Londsdale, foreman to Messrs. J. W. Whitehead,, contractors, Liverpool, said his firm had been engagolto repair a chimney 35 yards high at the before-mentioned works. They had to take 12 feet of the top partof the chimney down, and for this purpose the chimney was laddered on both sides, and a pole scaffold erected upon the top. They had taken three- fourths of ,the defective portion down, and at half-past five o'clock on Saturday afternoon the remaining portion Collapsed lie had been 22 years employed as a steeple- jack, and the scaffold was similar, and the material of the same quality as those be had erected in previous work.--In reply to-the coroner, witness said he sub- contracted from Messrs. J. W. Whitehead.—The Coroner: .oh,, I see. You do work by the price. The- sooner youdo the work, the more money you get.—Wit- ness coatinuing, said when he came down, a few minutes, before the accident happened, he thought they had got the unsafe part done, 4nd be expected the men he left working would finish *the remaining work of demolikinnin about ten minutes. In reply to a jury- man, witness said he had served his time as a steeple-

jack: John Monne Blaynan, inthe employ of the last wit- ness, said he had- had twelve years experience in climb- ing chimneys. Having explained in detail the construc- tion of' the scaffold, he considered that he with other. men had made a, scaffold as safe as they could for them— selves. They had taken the whole of the top off with the exception of about a yard and a half, which was' about two feet deep. The scaffold would not be strong enough in the probability of any of the brick work failing but that they did not anticipate. Witness came down the chininey Inca hammer,. and a few minutes later he beard a crash. ne, had examined the chimney; that morning,.and found one bolt and tyro planks broken by the,fallen bricks. N they could have worked ten mimu,. tea longer, they would have pulled all the defective brickwork. &mu. Robert )3enry lEennedg said he helped to 'Woo the. brickwork down. About half-past four on Saturday afternoon,he, along with five other men, pulled off the iron band, encircling the brick work. The accident hap- pened in consequence of some of the brick work the band had been lying upon falling upon the scaffold. None of them expected the brick work would fall. lionsdale, the foreman, recalled, said he took upon himself the responsibility of pulling down the -chimney. ' When they took off the iron band early in the,afternoon a few bricks fell and broke a poll, but thia.one was. spliced -and was now intact. The taking oWof.the iron band was far more dangerous than taking down the , brickwork when the accident happened.—A. Jurycsa.n, said the scaffold could not have been a bad one when it held ten men and the iron hand, which weighed lewt.— This was all the evidence, and the Coroner, in address- ing, the jury, pointed out that they had nothing 'to do with any civil liability. The question for them to de- cide was N anyone was criminally liable.-.7The jury re- turned a verdict of accidental death, no,..blaine was. at- tarlied to anyone. •

MORS GUARDIANS FOR RUNCORN. The Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board respecting the proposal that three additional Glardians should be assigned to the township of Runcorn. The Board had carefully con- sidered the matter and were of opinion that having re- gard to, all the circumstances, two additional Guar- dians might properly be assigned to the township of Runcorn-, but they regret that they are unable to concur in the view that in connection with this assignment of additional Guardians to that township, the representa- tion of other townships should not be taken away. The Board would, therefore, proceed to issue an order provid- ing that for the future the township Runcorn should be represented by seven Guardians, and that in pursu- ance of the provision in the 31 and 32 Viet. cap. 1.22., . sea. 8, the township of Aston Grange shall be united with the township of Aston-by-Sutton, and the township of Seven Oaks with the township of Whitley ,StiPerior, for the purposes of election of a Guardian for the united township io each case.—Mr. Heywood said the Commit- tee recommended the increase in the representation without any wish to deprive, the townships of their members,,and he moved that the clerk write'and ask the Government Board to reconsider the matter.—Mr. 'W• Whitlow seconded.—Mr. A. SATURDAY.--The Court charged with the trial of the flomestead poisoning case to-day terminated its proceedings, and sentenced the prisoners Dempsey and Beatty to seven years' penal servitude each, Gallagher and Davidson being condemned to five and three years respectively.

div.head: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COM-
div.p: THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COM-
PANY.

The report of the Prudential Assurance Company for 1892 states that in the ordinary branch the number of policies issued during the year was 56,912, assuring the sum of £5,886,889, and producing a new annual pre- mium income of £319,948. The premiums received during the year were £1,665,611, being an increase of £222,865 over the year 1891. The claims of the year amounted to £418,367. The number of deaths were 2,932, and 117 endowment assurances raatured. The number of policies in force was 301,643. In the indus- trial branch the premiums received during the year were £3,849,157, being an increase 'of £160,819. The claims of the year amounted to £1,602,816. The number of deaths was 178,231, and 1,230 endowment assurances , matured. The number of free policies granted during the year to those policy holders of five years standing, who desired to discontinue their payments, was 47,395, the number in force being 288,493. The number of policies in force was 10,105,877 ; the average duration of them is seven years. The total assets of the company are £16,309,652, being an increase of £1,686,025 over those of 1891. A complete valuation for the past year has been made with the following results :—The total sni- ping of the two branches is £664,109, out of which it is proposed to carry forward £270,000 (£70,000 from the ordinary branch and £200,000 from the industrial), leaving £394,109 for distribution among the participat- ing policy-holders and shareholders, in accordance with the regulations of the company under ito special Act of Parliament. By the adoption of an annual declaration of bonus, policy-holders will attain each year a vested increase to the sum assured and will nit have to wait until the end of a Quinquennial period. This advantage is emphasized by the fact that reversionary bonuses can Ile surrendered for cash. The directors desire to record their high appreciation of the efforts of the staff of the Company in carrying out the work of the valuation, which, under the improved methods, was accomplished in less than ens month from the close of the year. The balance sheet has been submittpd to Messrs. Deloitte, Dever, Griffiths and Co., whose- certificate is appended to the accounts.
COLONEL SAUNDERSON ON THE WARPATH. LIVELY ENCOUNTER BETWEEN M.P.'s..

The London correspondent of the Manchester " Guardian " says ;—" Na more amusing incidents have been witnessed in the lobby for many years than the rehearsal in petto of the coming encounter between Ulster and her " hereditary foe." I believe the history of the episode is as follows. In Angust last Mr. William Redmond made a very excellent speeeh in reply to Colonel Saunderson, in which be assured ti A pouse that the Colonel was perfectly harmless. Nor thia he , received the compliments of Mr. Punch, and ever since he has considered himself the natural antagonist of the member for North Armagh, Thg other day colonel satuAierooo. in biUstial liieaSant way, said something in the Clare debate which Mr. Willian Redmond took to mean that he and all his colleagues were murderers. Mr. Redmond thought it necessary to challenge the Colonel to repeat the words outside, and it is said Colonel Saunderson did actually lie in wait in the lobby for some time, ready, with characteristic courage, to call Mr. Redmond anything. To-day, with still more ex- traordinary indiscretion, he actually despatched to Mr. Redmond a message, saying that after the division he Would be prepared to repeat the stale abuse in the lobby. As soon as the division was over Mr. Redmond, accompanied by Mr. O'Kelly and followed by a police- man, came to confront Coionel Saunderson, who was accompanied by Colonel Waring, and followed by another policeman. For twenty minutes, surrounded by some 150 members, they challenged each other to say something or other—what no one seemed clearly to undepstand. Mr. Redmond was evidently very anxious for a fight. Colonel Saunderson assumed an air of coldness. But somehow, whether it was on account of the policemen or from a reawakening sense of the ridiculous there was no fight but a tongue fight, and each went away with the air of a disappointed man. I venture to prophesy that Colonel Saunderson never will fight much in the presence of the police. Mr. Redmond's conduct was not perhaps altogether discreet, but after all he has only himself to consider. The funny thing is that quiet and otherwise sensible people in Ulster look upon Colonel Saunderson as a kind of leader."

div.head: "HEAVEN ON EARTH." PROTEST FROM A WORKING MAN TO DR. FARRAR.
div.p: "HEAVEN ON EARTH." PROTEST FROM A WORKING MAN TO DR. FARRAR.
THE ARCHDEACON'S REPLY.

In his sermon on Sunday morning, at St. Margaret's, Westminster, Archdeacon Farrar mentioned with sym- pathy an interesting letter which he had received from a stranger, a working man, with reference to a previous sermon which the '6 Westminster Gazette" reported a fortnight ago. In that sermon he had quoted a saying of the Bishop of Derry that "the road to Heaven lies through Heaven, and all the way to Heaven is Heaven." . . _ •

The working man, a stranger to the Archdeacon, wrote as follows : " Venerable sir,—ln my " Westminister Gazette " this evening I have just read a sketch of your sermon on the text " For ever. ' I am a hard-working labourerd and I want io know where is this heaven upon earth '

you tell us of. I use by five a.m. in the miming, any turn out in the winter's bleak and bitter cold to earn the few miserable shillings that are doled out to me as wages. Many a curled darling in the West End spends more on his weekly cigars than I received for my week's toil. Do I strive for success ? Yes all my life I have striven for a measure of prosperity and happiness, but neither the one nor the other falls to my lot. What keeps me in a miserable solitude ? It is the dread of married poverty. Rev. sir, I can suffer poverty myself, but I refuse to inflict this curse upon others. Have I any social life ? None whatever ; not the ghost of an atom of human sympathy, love, friendship, or any sort of social intercourse. Yet lam an honourable, honest- living, and God-fearing man, with no vice, no gross sin of which my conscience can accuse me. Do I ever pray to God ? Yes, very often and earnestly. I pray to God to send me a little earthly happiness and prosperity, but what I get is plenty of hard drudging toil. That is my heaven on earth, and as I am so are thousands of other men and women in the land. Like Hamlet, I lack ad- ' vancement. On every side I see the unworthy prosper. •Am I selfish ? lam not. To those of my people who are in want I give away tar more than I can really afford, and if I had a fortune to-morrow, my greatest happiness would consist in helping many who have no claim or friendship upon me. No ! dear sir. Take it how you will. There is evidently not much heaven upon earth for " YOUR WEARY AND HARD-WORKED INDUSTRIAL SLAVE." .

The letter was only quoted to illustrate thoughts' that may be in thousands of minds, and in commenting upon it the preacher said : "The writer's errors all turn on this fundamental misconception, that by a heaven upon earth, I mean prosperity or comfort, or freedom from trial, or im- munity from sorrow, sickness and disappointment. In that sense, to speak of a heaven upon earth would be an effeminate falsity for which I should blush. The writer says with perfect truth, that there are thousands —he might even, more acJurately have said millions—of men and women,and not in the so-called working classes only,whose lives are lives of struggle, anxiety, hopeless- ness and want. In addition to those who find tueir way to our hospitals there are men and women,' it has been said, who lie and die day by day in these wretched gngle rooms, sharing all the family trouble, enduring all the hunger and the cold, and waiting without a single ray of comfort until God curtains their starving eyes with the merciful film of death." Think of parishes in the East und South of London, with their ugly squalor and horrible monotony rendered more horrible, and not only horrible but fatally destructive by the flaring bale- fires of the gin palaces, which are to them as the gates of:hell—apart from the indescribable curses which men draw on their own heads by betting, fraud, theft, un- cleanness, drink ; think of the inevitable miseries of a pauperism the result of our crowded cities, our compli- cated civilisation ,our deathful competition,our antagoni- tic forces of greedy and rutkless selfishness. Look at the horror of deleterious trading, blighting, and debas- ing the human form divine. I have talked to fishermen, weary and old who have told me of the days and nights that they spent drenched through and through by clammy mist and blinding spray with scarcely a moment now and then to snatch a mouthful of even the coarsest food. I have talked to a man who had spent the years of a lifetime, ten hours a day or more, going up and down a lift from morning to midnight without a holi- day. I have seen men sweltering naked in the blazing heat and roar and glare of the furnace-mouth in iron and steel factories. And to such and to millions of every race and climate we might well seem to be like mockers if by talking to them of a heaven on earth we meant anything which resembles the elements which are usually accounted fortunate. Might not such talk seem to them no better than that of the Queen of France,who, when told that the people were starving for lack of bread, wondered why they did not eat cakes? Might it not look like pushing to the miserable a sponge full of vinegar on a dry hyssop staff of spurious comparison ? But the notion that by heaven on earth one meant com- petence, advancement, popularity, social ease, and a comfortable home, becomes at once absurd when we re- member that, if any have ever enjoyed it, they have been the saints of God—men who, for the most part, had none of those things, but were homeless and hated, unknown, despised, and poor."

RELEASED AFTER TWENTY YEARS' IMPRISONM,ENT.

A LANCASHIRE MURDER. Some twenty years ago a sensational case was heard at Lancaster. Mary Davidson, a domestic servant, 21, was convicted of the murder of her illegitimate child, aged about fourteen months. The case aroused wide- spread interest at the time, and is still remembed by many people in various parts of the county. The pris- oner, who resided in the neighbourhood of Manchester, , left her place of residence to go to Carlisle, taking with ber,the child. She broke her journey at Lancaster, and left the child in the grounds of Mr. E. B. Dawson, Aldcliffe Hall, where it was afterwards found drowned in:a pond. Numerous petitions for the commutation of the capital sentence were got up and were successful. Though the circumstances of the case relate tog time so distant the unfortunate girl has been remembered, and in the belief that she had suffered adequately for the crime, efforts have recently been put forward in the prisoner's interest. Mr. T. H. Stirzaker, of Lancaster, has been very active in endeavouring to secure the woman's release, and through the member for the Lan- caster division, Mr. James Williamson, the Home Secre- tary's attention has been called to the case, with the result that the prisoner was liberated a few days ago. Mr. Stirzaker, in view of her release, had written to the prisoner's friends asking them to give her attention, and on Monday received a message that she was liberated and was with her relatives. Mary Elizabeth Davidson was convicted at Lancaster Assizes on Tuesday March 11, 1873.

THE GREENALL PRESENTATION.

I read the letter of" One Disgusted "in your issue of Saturday last, with considerable surprise. I was always under the impression that Alderman Francomb, who was the Chairman of the Testimonial Committee, was a most unassuming gentleman, one who never pushed himself forward, nor sought honours, not even mayorality. In fact I thought all his honours had been thrust upon him—perhaps I may ,be wrong—what a disappointment to a man when his, idol, is dashed down. I see his remarks were full of the workingman " this " and the wotkingman " that." I wonder how often he has assisted or recognised the workingman. Well, the great presentation is over, and all who were present who had subscribed a copper or two, were treated to " Refreshments " afterwards. Oh why didn't I hear of this ? lam sure the subscription list would have been ten times larger had the touters for coppers only had instructions to hold the " feed " out ae an inducement to subscribe. Liberals, remember! Refreshments ! always ! !—Yours &c. HUNGER.
THE WARRINGTON GUARDIANS AND THE RELIEVING OFFICER.

Sir,—What was the meaning of the Guardians busi- ness a fortnight ago when the relieving officer was appointed ? Why was there no advertisement? And why should a Committee decide a question of so great a moment, and which concerned the whole Board ? Wer- they ashamed of the choice which they had previously made, and dreaded the public knowing the result ? Or had they a little scheme to hatch which required haste and secrecy ? The worthy clerk informed the Board that seven former selected candidates had been written to, but why ? There was no need of putting the six candidates to the trouble of getting references,Acc. That might have been dispensed with, and the gentleman elected might have been put into office without the farce that was gone through. All other points being equal surely priority of claim should have been given to a person of experience, and who as a ratepayer had sus- tained the funds of the union. But, no, the appoint- ment was virtually made before the meeting, and the sooner the business of the Board is done in the board- room the better will it be for the reputation of the town I wonder by whose authority, or under what circum- stances it happened that the elected gentleman was on the premises, and ready to be called into the boardroom when the other applicants had not been asked to attend, and did not think of doing so. The guardians must not think they are not noticed, and that their actions pass unchallenged, and some of them may find that, when they again appeal for sup- port, they have been weighed and found wanting. A RATEPAYER.

div.head: INFIR.HARY AND DISPENSARY.
div.p: THE INFIR.HARY AND DISPENSARY.

Sir,—ln reading the report in one of our local news- papers, of the annual meeting of subscribers to the Infirmary and Dispensary, I notice with regret that there has been:a loss in the year's accounts to the amount of £l3 89. 11d. I learn that for many years past the contributions received from the workingmen and the philanthropists of the neighbourhood have more than covered the working expenditure of the establishment, although I am not in a position to say how the figures have stood in past years, with respect to the amount received from both sources. According to the present report the workingmen have contributed about £4OO, while, on the other hand, the gentry have kindly sub- scribed £1,361 19s. 3d. Although there seems room for an increase of subscription in the direction of the work- ingman, still there are plenty of gentlemen and tradesmen who are in a position to help us more who do not desire to subscribe to schools or places of worship, but would. I perhaps, be willing to allow their names to be entered as subscribers to the Infirmary. But as to the suggestion thrown out by one of the speakers to approach the employers with a view of put- ting into operation a scheme whereby each man would I consent to a deduction of a penny per week from his wages, and each boy a half-penny, I feel sure such a system, if adopted, would not meet with that approval that the committee imagined. In the first place the good spirit that has hitherto existed between the Working- men's Committee and ourselves would be broken down. I am now speaking from personal knowledge as a work- man in connection with the largest works in the town, and knowing as I do the dispositions of the workmen, and:thcse at the head. Although we are quite willing to contribute voluntarily and do all we can to help the Institution, we would not be compelled or coerced by any employer into contributing to whatever they may think proper. The amount may seem simple to the suggestor but the idea would be obnoxious to the major- ity of English workingmen. Again is any such amount as the subscrintion would realize required. And supposing we accepit it, what room would there be left for the philanthropic spirit that exists in our midst? It the committee would approach the neglectful ones in the form of a notice sent to the workingmen, and not to the employers, appealing to their sympathy and showing the increase of patients during the past year, and the extra expenditure caused by making more accommodation for inside patients which necessarily takes more to support, I am certain the committee will do more good and the response will surprise even the despairing ones.—Yours, &c., A WORKINGMAN.

div.head: BUDDHISM AND CHRISTIANITY.-SOME POINTS OF RESEMBLANCE.
div.p: BUDDHISM AND CHRISTIANITY.-SOME POINTS OF RESEMBLANCE.

Sir,—What a pity it is that Mr. Dignum cannot imitate the courtesy and fair-mindedness of his great authority Max Muller. I can only regret the attitude of bitter and uncompromising hostility that has characterised his letters so far. Either the statements advanced by me are correct or they are not. If they are not correct they ought to be easily disproved—and they have not been so far—but if correct, why not honestly and candidly admit the fact? Saul ! Saul ! it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. But I should like Mr. Dignum to read my first letter again. He will then find that he has persistently misrepresented what I said. My letter was not an attack on Christianity, but a plain state- ment of remarkable and well-known facts, a knowledge of which of which is now been widely diffused by emin- ent clergymen themselves, as witness the recent address of Archdeacon Wilson, at Rochdale.

lam in no way concerned with " Eclecltc "but am prepared to defeud my own statements. I never said that the Christian gospels were copied from the Bud- dhist ones. What I said was that the accounts given of Chrishna were almost word for word like the accounts given of Christ in the Christian gospels. I took the statement from Mr. Laing's " Problems of the Future," a work much more recent than Muller's " Science of Religion." I will now give other authorities. In the chapter " Hindu Religions" in Clodd's " Childhood 1 of Religions " occurs the following passage :—" Vishnu receives the worship of millions, and has great hononr paid him as Krishna, one of the forms in which they believe he came on earth. The Avatars of Vishnu are his descents to this world to save it when ruin threatened at the hands of king, giant, or demon, and he then comes under the disguise of man or animal. As such a divine deliverer the brightest memories crowd round him under the myth of Krishna. A mighty demon-king, Kansa had rule over the world, and when he heard that a child was born who would grow up and destrQy him, he ordered a general slaughter of young boys, hoping thus to kill the child. But it was sent to a place of safety and grew up beautiful Krishna, god of love, and slayer of Kansa." I Your correspondent " Eclecltc " referred th Peeble's " Seers of the ages." The ninth chapter of this book deals largely with Chrishna, and although the author takes up an attitude of hostility to Christianity, and makes the deliberate statement that the Christian gospels are copies of the older Hindu Scriptures, :he certainly hacks up his statements with quotations from numerous and weighty authorities—authorities that are not to be dismissed in the light and airy manner affected by Mr. Dignum. Peebles asserts that all the wonderful stories that cluster round the name of Christ, cluster also round the older Hindu god Chrishna, who is described in the most glowing language as being beautiful, merciful, pure, loving, and just. Some of these wonder!ul re- semblances are alluded to in the " Encyclopedia Brit- tannica " as existing between Buddha and Christ ; also remarkable resemblances between Buddhist books and the Christian gospels, as quoted by me the other week. As I stated Max Muller speaks of Christina as " the lovely shepherd god." How do all these various accounts fit in with Mr. Dignum's statement that Chrishna was " the trickiest rogue and the foulest debauches of the Hindu pantheon ?"

In his first letter Mr. Dignum speaks of the anachron- ism of the Bhagavad-gita beiAg the source from which our gospels were derived, seeing that the former were the production of the 2nd or 3rd century of our era, whilst the latter were the production of the Ist century. Now Mr. Dignum must be well aware that the date of our gospels is a very debateable subject. About two emineat scholars assign their date to the let century.but a great many of the finest scholars of the day fix their date at the latter part of the 2nd century. And, be it remembered, these scholars are christian ministers— great dignitaries in their different churches, and they further say that their authorship is anonymous—a mere tradition. I have read a good many books dealing with the Hindu Scriptures, and have never read in one of them that their date is anything like so recent as Mr. Dignum supposes. They all an. 511411 a date much older j than the oldest Christian Scriptures.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH_ IL 1893. NOTES ON GAMES AND AfIILETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH_ IL 1893. NOTES ON GAMES AND AfIILETICS.

Touching M. Jacolliot's book Mr. Dignum gives but a very garbled account of Max Muller's reference to it. From Max Muller's own words one may fairly infer that M. Jacolliot ought to be an authority. He was president of the Court of Justice at Chandernagore, India, and devoted the leisure left to him from his duties to study-

ing Sanskrit and the holy books of the Hindus. Max Muller then goes en to say—speaking of a beautiful extract from M. Jacolliot's book—" I must warn niy readers, lest the extract should leave too deep an impres- sion on their memory, that what M. Jacolliot calls a simple translation from Sanskrit is, as far as I can judge " (italics are mine) "a simple invention of some slightly mischevious Brahman, who, like the pundits of Lieutenant Wilford, took advantage of the zeal and credulity of a French judge." Observe, Max Muller I does not prove any forgeries, nor does he make use of any offensive adjectives, but merely says that "as far as he can judge " M. Jacolliot has been imposed upon. So much for the scorn and derision poured upon this episode by Mr. Dignum ! I repeat my first statement, that the various mirac- ulous incidents related of Christ are likewise related of Chrishna, and are firmly believed by the Hindus. Further, that according to the highest authorities, there is in many respects a wonderful similarity between the Hindu and the Christian Scriptures. But I have never said, nor do I now say, that the one account is copied from the other—though it looks very like it. I may have a further letter next week, in which I shall give the opinions of Gerald Massy one of the most learned men of this century. HARRY ESMOND.
FOOTI3ALL.

Our jewel of la P.D. sends a note to say that he is in- disposed this week, consequent upon a difference which occurred between him and his mamma on Saturday: He laid the whole of his wages upon Warrington in the the match against Salford. He was a victim to the blessed uncertainty. I should recommend him to take the Dean of Manchester's advice and never bet—that is unless its on a certainty, then its a bit excusable for a weak boy. He was not the only one I believe, who was rash enough to " lay money " on Warrington on Saturday ; some particular reason had induced many, who pretended to ' be in the "know," to believe that it was a" dead snip." Dead snips are good things, maybe, but I would prefer to hold a good stake.

I notice that our contemporary the " Athletic News," states that when our team reached Salford they had no watches! Is this meant to account for the wirepullers late arrival, or—can it be that they inferred that the noble opponents of leather punching in Warrington were unable to reach Salford without having visited that philanthropic friend—"me uncle." I would shed tears of reproach upon that paper if that dark suspicion were ever.to gain a firmer grip upon my credibility.

Jesting aside—or rather more correctly, not jesting at all—Warrington, although suffering defeat by a try, played an excellent all round game, and it is conceded by the most hypocritical critics, that the game provoked more genuine interest than any game that has been played at New Baras,the Salford ground,for a long time. A try which Warrington gained was disallowed or con- sequently tl.e match would have been a draw. The try gained by Salford was the result of asmart piece of work tor it entailed a fair race down the field between Webster and Miles the scorer. Good runner as cur tall athlete is, one Mile in so few minutes is to tall for him.

There was much scrimmaging in the game, and this brought our forwards into test, and the steady consist- ent style of their packing was just a pleasant surprise, after the recent defective shows at which we have had occasion to growl. The tackling, too, was fine. Nevins, Jolley, and Lawless all did some good tackling; but Webster never had any chance at his favourite delecta- tion, scoring. His fame had preceded him—he was looked up to there as a try snatcher,and was consequent- ly shadowed all through the game. The two Bates and the Turners made a firm quartette. Boscow had a consider- able demand made upon his defensive prowess. Especi- ally in the second half. But he repulsed every on- slaught upon his territory with a dexterity and litheness which had a mystifying effect upon his opponents. Just when one of them—like a horse I knew—was smiling up Iris sleeve, because he had cornered Boscow—whizz ! the merry little back had dodged 12 yards away and was punting into touch at the centre.

The Salford men are playing Swinton on Saturday,and they flatter themselves now that they have " humped " Warrington, they will have a chance with the leading team in the competition. Well, as a prophet of my ac- quaintance used to say, " One cannot say, unless one knows." The blessed uncertainty is likely to crop up at any moment now. Just take Saturday for instance. Swinton, who have never before been beaten in the com- petition, were overthrown by Wigan, a team which was only recently fetching up as the rear guard in the com- petition list. As the famous Molly remarked, " Lawks, aint it scrumps," which just hits the nail on the heaa ; although I don't know what it means.

Tho great question asking for settlement now is, "Who is going to win next Saturday—Warrington or St. Helens Recs." If the forwards in either of the teams prove to be wrecks which isn't a "goak"—then there "aint no chance in that direction." During the season St.Helens team have played 30 matches, won 22, lost one, and drawn seven. They have scored 241 points against 26. The Recs. have an almost equally good record to show. So now, then, Warrington,don't be modest and generous like you have been during the season, because "there aint anything in the club worth winning" this is a team worthy of your steel—figuratively speaking, of course.
At present the results in the cup competition stand thus:—

For. Agst. Phi. Won. Lost. Drn. G.T. G.T. Pts. Swinton l2 9 . 1 . 2 ...15 26... 1 5 ...20 Salford Tyldesley St. Helens Recreation 12 ... 5 ... 4 ... 3 ...11 11... 7 7 ...13 Oldham Warrington Wigan Rochdale Hornets 13roughton Rangers Broughton l4 . 1 11. 2 .. 3 3 ...13 30... 4

Warrington A. team met Salford A. team and had better luck than the first team. They were winners by 1-4-4. There was great interest taken in the match. Neither team had been beaten before, and as may be expected the struggle to maintain a unbroken record, was a tough one. Our A. team well merit commenda- tion, and there are few teams that hays a better record to show this season, than they have.

H. Bradshaw, of Bramley and Yorkshire, was one of the finest forwards on the ground in the International match at Leeds. He is a thick-set, powerfully built player, and is wonderfully quick for a man of so mas- sive a make. His style of play is borne out by his appearance, being remarkable for his bulldog rushes and tenacity in sticking to the ball. He is at any time a good handful for any four opponents. He first played for Yorkshire against Durham last season, and gained his International cap without taking part in the trial match He only received his cap against Wales this season by a fluke, but he was so conspicuously the pick of the English pack that the Bugby Union could not leave him out of the remaining matches.
STILL THEY COME.
BY MR. B. -IVIIITHAM.

Yes,still they come. More Warringtonians, Whit- tington like, turning out to seek their fortune in this "great country." I am now writing at the close of a fairly happy day. It is Sunday,Feb. 12th, and after spending a few hours in the company of Mr. and Mrs. Butler, I feel more disposed for a chat about them than anything else.

So far, we have had, here in New England, a terribly cold winter. Snow and King Frost have held the fort, making it altogether impossible to do any- thing in the shape of pedestrianism. A change, and a welcome change, in the weather, made me suggest to the dame a walk to the church at Green- dale, of which our son-in-law is pastor. This being readily agreed to, five of us were soon out of doors, to find the sun shining warmly upon us, and just enough frost under foot to make it pleasant walk- ing. I very seldom leave my books on Sundays, so that I must confess to being no authority as to what an American Sunday is like, but when I do, I must confess to feeling that there is something wanting—a sort of veid in the air, and invariably my mind wanders in a dreamy fashion to that old home of mine in Manchester-road, where I used to stand and listen with pleasure to the old church bells clanging forth to the people their summons to church. I guess I am rather a weak supporter of the church, and if I were a resident in a large city I fear I should not subscribe much in support of the art of " campanology," but I do love to listen to a peal of bells when there is no rivalry. A something else is wanting. We miss, as we walk over the two miles that stretches out between home and church,something that is especially sweet in dear old Eng- land,that is the song of birds. 011,you English folk have a lot to answer for, you have not only sent your Irish con- victs here, but you have sent the domineering, spiteful, fightiug. sparrow as well, and if you couldn't conquer and hold the laud, the sparrow has taken and holds the air against all comers, and so we have no sweet singing birds to cheer us on the way.

But dreaming is over—here we are at the church. We don't deal in chapels here—nothing so common as that— churches or nothing. Bless us all, what a lot of friends we have. One can scarcely believe it. " How are you, Mr. Whitham ? We haven't seen you for quite a time," is heard all around, and it is with much ado we get in- side and comfortably seated. Here another surprise was in store for us. Seated on the platform was a stranger, one whom I had not seen before. An explanatio:a came when Mr. Ellison announced Mr. Butler as the preacher for the morning service. So this was the gentleman to whom I had seen reference made in the "Examiner,"and I was doubly pleased with myself at having displayed so much courage in turning out on that bright sunshiny morning, as it had brought me in contact with the most recent arrival from the inland port of Warrington. I think he was fortunate in his congregation. There was more than an average attendance, and I know he was listened to attentively. His text was the parable of the Prodigal Son, and I think he brought out the good points pretty effectively. One lady sitting beside me said at the close, " Well, Mr. Whithatn, I like lain very much, if he is an Englishman." So several friends expressed themselves as having had very much pleasure in listen- ing to the Englishman.

I am sure Mr. Butler's first Sunday in America would be quite an experience for him. Re had the opportu- nity of seeing a little of the ways and doings in church management. Of course, after church we had the hand shake, and one or two words together. Only time for that, no going home yet. Immediately following he church service dames the Sunday school. Usually 1 find a few of the deacons standing at the church doors after service inviting all, the young, the old, and the stranger to stay for Sunday school. So it was here, a good por- tion of the congregation stayed for the school, and soon we formed into classes. In my class, a pretty large one, were several considerably older than myself, and all were well on in years. Now reader, don't smile, I couldn't help it. If I wasn't the creature of circum- stances that Sunday morning, what was I ? There was only one little matter I could control. I would not be led into any discussion. Reading a verse in your turn, and giving the teacher an explanation is all very well in the ordinary way of things, but here was something rather extraordinary. How could I explain the mean- ing of such hard words as prayer, and faith, without getting into trouble, especially as I noticed Mr. Butler gliding quietly round and seating himself at my elbow. You give it up, same as I did, only I had the wife there enjoying my discoinfiture or twitting me about being " bested." Now I think this is a pretty good days' work. Church service commences at eleven, Sunday school at twelve, closing at two. Three hours straight on. Once a year of that will ba enough for me, I was glad to get my knees under somebody's mahogany. There will have to be more sorts of cramming than one to enable the martyr to go through the ordeal.

Well all things come to an end, and at last we three got together. A parson, a sort of a parson, and quite another sort of a parson in myself. I had asked myself very often, while listening to Mr. Butler, why had .6. come to America ? Was there no work for him in Eng- land ? Well, now, I think there were lots of work for him, and are lots for all who have studied the social problems of tke day as I find he has. In our conversa- tion I was pleased with the questions he put. They evinced a desire to know what the people think about matters. I found in Mr. Butler a perplexity as to how work for the people's amelioration could be done effectively. We want the preachers to get hold of the .• social condition" question, and to help to make this life worth living. So many, so very many of us think it a dismal dream. Among other questions Mr. Butler put the following : flow is it flesh meat is so very dear here in America ? How is it flour is so dear ? America grows flour. Well, I couldn't answer, I could put ques- tions also. How is it good bacon' and hams cannot be bought here ? It is fed here, mad is good when it gets to ngland, but it is simply detestable stuff bought here. Hew is it house rent is so high, when there is so very much land lying around?

"But, now, Mr. Whitham, don't you think the work- ing man very much better off here than in England ? " " Well," I said, " perhaps, at least, he appears so, yet I know the great majority of the men I work amongst are living from hand to mouth. Rent settles the business." " Oh," Mr. Ellison put in, "you don't see such abject poverty hers, shoeless, and stockingless children." Well, I can only put the following extract in for answer, taken from the " Boston Herald :—" A most pitiable sight was witnessed in the South Boston court yesterday morning. Seated on a bench were nine children, boys , and girls, the oldest being six and the youngest four. They were singularly garbed. Two of them had shoes without stockings, and the others were without either shoes or stockings. They looked as if they had not Used either water or soap for months. Their clothes were ragged." I think there are quite a number of good people in this world who will not see misery ; they are so optimistic in their views that they refuse to look on the dark side of humanity.

Mr. Butler loaned me two books, "Warrington as it is, was, and might be," and "The Dream of an Eng- lishman," of which I shall have something to say in a further letter. In the meantime I may give a short extract from Mr. Butler's contribution to the first of these works. "There is suffering and forsaken poverty enough in Warrington to sets angels weeping for very pity." Yes, that's it, the people are forsaken and those who know it leave the cAuntry, carrying with them flannel petticoats for the Hottentots. Well, I don't want to tire anyone with moralizing in this letter. I understand Mr. Butler and his good wife had rather a rough :wo weeks voyage of it. He has a trade in his hands which is in great request here, and I feel confident of his future success. Clarence-Street, Worcester.

div.head: BUDDHISM AND CHRISTIANITY.
div.p: BUDDHISM AND CHRISTIANITY.

Sir,—Your readers who have given any attention to this discussion will have now been able to estimate the value of your two correspondents' insinuations that our gospel narratives of the facts and incidents in the life of Christ, are indebted to the legends of Buddha or Chrish- na. Such an assumption has been proved on the testi- mony of the best scholars to be utterly enfounded and false. Brahmanic legends of Christina are of too late a date to be pressed into this service. On the contrary evidence of any parallelism, except of the most trifling and insignificent character points decisively to the in- fluence of christianity, in the early periods of its exis- tence, upon Brahmanic literature. It is equally estab- lished with respect to any assumed Buddhistic parallels whether of facts and incidents, or of doctrines'and teach- ings, that the consensus of opinion of our best scholars, amongst whom ranks pre-eminently Dr. Rhys Davids tes- tifies directly against any evidence of copying by our Evangelists from Buddhistic sources. Let us understand, therefore, exactly where we are. It is something, indeed enough, to have established ins, contention that the flourish with which both your cor- respondents set out was mere " sounding brass ;" and that the attempt to prove that our gospels are either copies, or are in any way indebted to the ancient reli- gions of India has not the slightest basis of truth. Any rebutting evidence to the contrary is so far nil, the one correspondent being reduced to absolute silence, and the other practically yielding the point by falling back upon the moral and doctrinal teaching only of Buddha. To cover his defeat" HarryEsmond " has recourse to a very I quixotic piece of logic. Let us sift the method by which he arrives at the conclusion that" Mr. Dignum is climb- down." Climbing down from what may I ask ? Where have I moved one jot from my contention that our gos- pels owe nothing to either Clarishna or Buddha as to their facts or incidents ? Truly enough, I said that " I am most heartily ready to admit that there are w ful points of comparison between the moral teachings and conduct of Buddha and the character and teachings of Christ "—but no more than in the case of facts and incidents did I either imply or admit—that there was any borrowing in the case. Where then was the " climbing down ?" But notice further there is some- thing worse to come. "Harry Esmond" quotes my words " The string of ordinary insigai Gcent parallels cited by your correspondents (I refer here to facts or in- cidents) should merely excite one's derision or contempt. The fleeting features of most of the coincidences noted vanish the moment you come to trace or compare them." And then by an absolute twist of my sentences he follows on, to say according to his own inverted ar- rangement " these ordinary insignificant coincidences are now admitted to be truly wonderful points of resem- lance "—an utter misrepresentation, for I neither said nor admitted anything of the kind. Any appearance of climbing down" then is due merely to his own inven- tion. I reject absolutely the assumption so confidently made at first with respect to the fact and incidents in the life of Christ, and with equal emphasis as to his doc- trines and teachings being borrowed from Brahmsn or Buddhist sources. But we are Seriously asked now (of course in the moral and spiritual side of the subject) would Christian- ity "be any the worse for its indebtedness" to the ancient religions of India. I rather think it would " Harry Esmond ?" But why ask such a question, as foolish as it is profane ? Foolish for what need had Christ to learn aught of Buddha? Just as much as the sun need to borrow light from a waxen taper. Again is it profanely assumed that the person and the authority of Christ stand on no higher level than Gautama's ? We know rather more of the credentials—of the one than of ' the other to admit of any comparison. The divine mis- sion of Christ is established as an historical fact—if his- tory can establish aught. He came with a message from the Eternal Father proclaiming the divine love for man. His own love for the race, and the Father's com- mand to the world that it should " Hear Him." Of Buddha whatever we know of his assumed mission to men we know that he was neither priest nor prophet of God—for God inspires no man to proclaim to the world so infamous a lie as the denial of His own existence. Buddhism is essentially atheistic, and is no religion at all. Its aspect Godward is a blank negation, and in its relation to man it is merely a moral system, blending with a wretched, false, philosophy. Whatever elements of truth or goodness we may i discover in its human as- pect find their explanation n that natural law of kind- ness more or less written everywhere on the human heart and conscience, and which in its higher manifes- tations may be referred to that" light which enlighten- eth every maa that cometh into the world." As to whatever good of this nature may be found in Buddhism, Christianity possesses it in a transcendently higher, and more perfect form ; but soars infinitely beyond it into its rich, eternal provisions for the human soul. "Budd- hism with its ghastly Nervana and the utter hopeless- ness of its highest good" has been well described to be "an exceeding great and bitter cry for what Christian- ity has to offer." And now a word as to my authority Max Muller. I was quite sure that this eminent scholar was not likely to stultify himself. I cannot understand the compre- hension of" Harry Esmond " in applying the passages he quotes as having any relevancy to my main conten- tion which is now finally disposed of. Nor do these quotations justify him in assuming " Max Muller to be of opinion that Christianity does owe a good deal to the other religions which have preceded it "—that is in the sense of any copying of truths and doctrines on the part of the Great Teacher Himself, or as recorded by the Evangelists and other writers of the New Testament. This is a distinct question from Muller's scientific view of the genesis and growth of religion which is the sub- ject of the passages quoted. The subject discussed in this correspondence has been all along with me a literary and historical one, and not scientific or philosophical. I dissent from Muller's theory in his various writings on the science of religion (and I decline to be drawn into any discussion upon this subject), but he entirely sup- ports my contention on the literary and historical side —that the writers of the New Testament owed neither their facts and incidents, nor their doctrines and teach- ings to the ancient religions of India. Another line or two in conclusion. "Harry Esmond " wonders if I have read Sir Edwin Arnold's ' Light of Asia." Indeed, I must own to the mild impeachment. I was moved like the rest of the " excited" multitude,curious to witness how the dignified Christian official could make his ob- sequious bow to Buddha, and found that I had gone out into the wilderness only " to see a reed shaken by the wind." If it should be worth while to continue this correspondence, I may have something further to say which may not grate very pleasantly upon the nerves of " Harry Esmond" or other admirers of what has been styled in a very trenchant criticism " this weak and sentimental poem."—Yours Zsc., JOHN DIGNUM. Penketh, 9th March, 1893.

div.head: SCENE ON A FOOTBALL FIELD.
div.p: SCENE ON A FOOTBALL FIELD.

On Thursday afternoon during the progress of a football match. between an Orford barracks team, and the Earlestown shop assistants, on the Mesnes field, one of the Earlestown players named Worsley received a severe kick in the face, whilst placing the ball in position. The spectators rushed forward with the intention of severely handling the Orford team but the latter wore got away, and the game came to an abrupt tenni iation.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday at the Town Hall. There were then present Messrs. R. Heaton (chairman). BaMarry, Wm. Houghton, Turton, J. Jolly; Pilling, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Dignum, J. Houghton, Owen, Mather, Auckland, Davies, Hill, A. J. Jolly, Longton, Fair- dough, Muir, Shaw, and Dr. Pattison, and Messrs. J. C. !Sutton (clerk), S. The Clerk men- tioned that he had received a letter from the. Liverpool Blind Asylum, in which the Board bed patients, replying. to a request made by the Guardians for perouswm to visit the institutions The permission was granted providing the' visit. were not made on either Saturdays or Wednesdays. Mr. Frank Auckland was formally appointed relieving officer, and vaccination officer for the No. S district. completed the business of the Board.

div.head: THE" GYM."
div.p: THE" GYM."

If ere we have some more " blessed uncertainty." A few weeks ago our local" eight "met an " eight "from the Manchester Simpson Memorial Gym. They beat them by a fair number of points. On Saturday the two eights met again at Manchester and Warrington were defeated by nine points. They were beaten in the horizontal bar, and parallel bar exercises, but came out of the Indian club exercise 18 points a head. The de- feat was attributable to two things. First, G. W. Vernon was disqualified in the horizontal bar exercise, after scoring two points, because he fell. It isn't con- sidered a very sportman-like thing to disqualify a man for an accident, and had Vernon gone on he would un- doubtedly have pulled off another ten or eleven marks. That would have stamped" victory "on the other side of the programme.

--- The second reason is that the Warrington eight were im very poor condition. That is the result of the want of practice—due to indolence and too-much self-estimation. There are men in our" gym " who might shine if they would only stick to their practice. Ishould hope that this defeat would bring them to a sense of their fallen powers.

These are the indiyidual scores of the two eights : Warrington—the first figures are for horizontal bars, the second for parallel, third, total :—A. Dickens, 8, 10, 18 ; F. C. Bennion, 6, 15, 21; A.
