div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. CHA.RLES CHORLEY.
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. CHA.RLES CHORLEY.

At noon on Saturday the remains of the late Mr. Charles Chorley, borough treasurer of Warrington, were interred in the cemetery. The ceremony was witnesied by a large concourse of people. About eleven o'clock the funeral eortege consisting of the hearse and three coaches containing the deceased's relatives and friends, left the house in Lodge Lane. A large public procession had been formed opposite St. Paul's Church, and joined the cortege, in its solemn journey. The procession was headed by the Mayor, in his civic robes, who was followed by the various members of the Town Council and the Corpora- tion officials, and there was a body guard of police consisting of Inspectors Spinks, Bowen, and Cox. Bewsey-road was thronged with hundreds of onlookers, right down to Horsemarket-at. At the cemetery the coffin encased in black cloth was borne on the shoulders of six men, and followed by Mrs. J. Chorley, the Rev. H. Gibson-Smith, Mrs. Gibson-Smith, and the deceased's two nephews. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. H. V. Pigot. div.head: LY MM.
div.p: LY MM.
LOCAL BOARD.

At the monthly meeting of the Board, on Tuesday, there were present—Mr. James Gregson (in the chair), Messrs. Hugh Harrison, James Holt, William Brazen- dale, John Perrin, Alexander Mclntyre, Samuel Apple- ton, F. Swallow, Mr. Ridgway, (law clerk), Dr. Fox (medical officer), Mr. William Mullard (clerk), Mr. James Mort (surveyor), and Mr. William Severs (gas manager).—Dr.Fox, medical officer, presented his annual report as to the health of Lymm, in which he stated that, in spite of adverse circumstances, in only two re- corded instances had the rate of morality been lower than in 1892. They were 1881 and 1886, when the deaths were 52 an 62 respectively, and the general death rates 11-7 and 12-6 per thousand. In the year 1892 the total number of deaths was 65, and the annual death rats 13 per thousand exactly, which was lower by 3.1 per thousand than the average of recent years in Lymm, and 6 per thousand below 199, given by the Registrar-General as the death rate of England and Wales in 1892. This was a gratifying fact alone, especi- ally when associated with another equally gratifying, circumstance, namely, that the zynaotie death rate was but for one imported disease, under a unit, or '6O per thousand. The number of births in the year was 142, giving a birth rate of 27-4 per thousand, somewhat , lower than the average, which was a regrettable circum - stance as suggesting a depressed state of local industry, but unregrettable as indicating that there had been a fall in the early and improvident matrimonial market. The infant morality was 11.6 per 1.000, and that for Eng- land and Wales 14.8. The report was adopted.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board stating that an inquiry would be shortly held with re- gard to the application to sanction the borrowing o 3,000 for sewerage purposes at Heatly.—lt was re solved t hat the sniall;vx; hosp:tal h Closed on the 11th init., and the [Writs and Lartei. relieved of their duties.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS WELCOME A NEW MEMBER.
div.p: THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS WELCOME A NEW MEMBER.

During the fortnightly meeting of the Warring- ton Board of Guardians on Wednesday morning, Mr. Rateliff introduced Dr. Pattison, who made his first appearance on the Board as the successor to Mr. Hood Wright. Mr. Heaton (the chairman) said: I am sure we are all very pleased to see you amongst us, Dr. Pattison. I am also sure Lora your personal appearance—if that has anything to do with it,that your electors have made a very good selection. Your face is one which denotes charity and that is what is required here. (hear, hear.) .Mr. Ratcliffe: He is almost as fine a man as you, Mr. Chairman. (Laughter.) Several of the mem- bers expressed their pleasure at seeing Dr. Pattison amongst them, and Mr. Shaw complimented him upon the majority by which he won his seat.—Dr. Pattison acklowledged the greetings, and was afterwards appointed to the Committees upon which his predecessor had sat.

div.head: BANK PARK LSIPROVEMETS.
div.p: BANK PARK LSIPROVEMETS.
A PROSPECT FOR THE SUMMER.

Now that the spring has come, there is an imme- diate prospect of the Warrington public enjoying the benefit of a number of improvements, that have been made in the Bank Park during the winter. A new hot house has been erected near to the Infir- mary wall, and it contains no fewer than 2,000 new plants. Several hundreds of _other special plants have been procured, and these, when in season will be placed in the new hot house, which will be thrown open to the public on Sunday after- noons. Formerly there was a considerable amount of stagnant water in the park ; there was no flow in the pond in the aviary, and for a long time the pool near the collection of Roman remains has been so dirty and stagnant as to prevent fish living in it. This has been altered. A large pipe has been laid between the aviary pond and the large lake, and this causes the water to be constantly running from the former place through another new pond behind the lawn, in which fish have been placed, and through a new water-cress bed near the path at the south end of the lake. Here this flow of water is serving another good purpose ; it is rapidly reviving a number of beautiful aquatic plants, which for two seasons have lain stunted, at the top end of the lake owing to the stagnance of the water. Last year it was attempted to cultivate water lilies in the lake, but various injurious chemical ingredients, which fell from the smoky atmos- phere prevented this. So that now we cannot have lilies, the committee are thinking of placing on the lake a collection of fireign ducks. A stroll through the grounds shows that on every hand the gardeners have been busy re-modelling the flower beds in a manner which should have a charm- ing effect upon the grounds when the Rowers are in bloom. Improvements of many kinds are to be seen all over the grounds. Improving hands have beta busy in the recreation ground, too, and have ac- complished a task which will be fruitful of benefits. The large expanse of grass, which, after a shower of rain, hag hitherto been unpleasantly swampy, has now been drained, and a grave objection to allowing the little folk to-gambol on it, has thereby been removed. New paths have been constructed in many places ; old trees have been felled, dark corners of the shrubberies have been cleared and lightened, and taking everything into account, it may be safely said that—given suitable weather, the grounds will look prettier this summer than ever they have done before. At the present time ' the place presents a pretty appearance in consequence of some eight or nine thousand variegated crocus's being in bloom on the edges of all the beds.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
"HOME RULE DISCUSSED."

The meeting of the Society on Thursday night was a more interesting and livlier one than that last week. Mr. H. ff. Hutton had arranged to open the debate in support of Home Rule, as against Mr. London's opposition to it last week. The pub- lic were again invited to attend ; and they did 50 in such numbers that accommodation could not be found for them all. All the principal deba- ters of the society were present, whilst amongst the " public" were several well-known champions of both the Home Rule and Unionist 'cause. Mr. Percy Silcock was in the chair, and Mr. Hulse who had occupied the position last week, took his place amongst the Unionist speakers of the evening. At eight o'clock Mr. H. H. Dutton opened the debate, with what was admitted by all present—Unionists included—to be a dexterous and masterly handling of the case. It was a speech which, to speak figuratively" opened the eyes" of Mr. Dutton's acquaiatances. It lasted half-an-hour, and was delivered with an earnest eloquence which made the meeting lis- ten, whether they bad been inclined or not. He dealt with all the principal aspects of the case, and he quoted Mr. Gladstone's Bill to prove that Ulster could not suffer from religious tyranny at the hands of the Nationalists. He referred to the times of the famine and distress in Ireland, and showed that the Roman Catholic Priests had come forward and been the saviours of the people. He contended that priestcraft was no more rampant in Ireland than parsoncraft in rural England, and he also made allusion to " the canting humbug," of certain Ulstermen who had threatened to fight if the Bill was passed. He attached no importance to that, but to show , its logical worth, lie contended that as the Nationalists of Leland were in the majority, they would be equally I entitled to fight if the Home Rule Bill was not passed.— The leader of the opposition was Mr. Hulse. He was very brief, terse, and emphatic. He alluded to Mr. Gladstone's measure for re-distributing the 80 Irish seats at Westminster. He took the six counties of Antrim, Down, Armagh, Tyrone, Fermanagh, and Londonderry. They had an aggregate population of 1,236,000 with 162,000 registered county electors. They were repre- sented by 19 members, 14 of whom were Unionists. Mr. Gladstone meant to take away five seats and that would leave fourteen. On the other hand Galway Mayo, Donegal, Leitrim, Sligo, and Roscommon, had 38,000 electors, represented by 18 Nationalist members, which number Mr. Gladstone meant to reduce to 15. That was scandalously unequal, he contended. Then again, Belfast and Londonderry were to be represented by five members for 41,000 electors, and Cork,Limerick, Waterford, Galway, Newry, and Kilkenny, with 25,000 electors, were actually to be repreeented by seven mem- bers. He considered that alone was a parody upon Mr. Gladstone's measure to "redress inequalities."—Mr. C. ' Lyon followed in support of Home Rule, and after him came Mr. Nield, who spoke very hotly against both Mr. Gladstone and his measure, and dubbed the former an "oratorical acrobat," with an elastic principle which he had made to fit the fads of all his motly supporters. This assertion was met with uproariods cries of disapproba- tion, and the feelings of the meeting were worked up to a warm pitch when quite an exciting oratorical assault- at-arms took place between Mr. Donnellan (Home Ruler) and Mr. Hawthorne, an Ulster anti-Home Ruler. The debate between these two gentlemen became so warm the the Chairman had to call both to order. Mr. Kirby and Mr. Harrington both took part in the debate, and the meetingclosed at half-past ten.

PADGATB SICK CLUB. The balance sheet of the club for the year 1892, shows that it is in a very flourishing condition. At the end of 1891, there was a balance of £246 181. 9d. in hand. The payments of members during 1892 amounted to £26 2s. and bank interest to £5 14s. 41, making a total of £278 15s. 81d. The ex- penditure had been rather heavy, amounting to £35 19s. 61,-d., thus leaving a balance in hand of £242 16s. 2d.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
A SHIP CANAL STEAMER WRECKED. HEROIC DEED BY THE CAPTAIN.

An exciting wreck is reported on the Cornish coast.. the steamer Gustav Bitters, of Newcastle, 614 tons register (Captain Bull, South Shields), from London for Manchester Ship Canal, with a general cargo, went ashore on the Sky Rocks, off the Lizard, during a dense fog and rough sea about six e'clock on Saturday morn- and soon became a total wreck. The captain ordered the men to launch the boats, but only the punt was lowered. Directly it touched the water several of ' The crew jumped in and put off. The captain jumped': into the sea, swam after the boat, and tried to get the men to turn back, but without effect. The second mate (Oliver Cowans, of Greenock) then jumped into the sea. The men then put back to pick up the mate, but they " were too late, for, being unable to swim, he quickly went under and was drowned. There were then four , men left in the rigging. The cries of these and of the • other men, attracted the attention of the outlook of the Lizard, and the Lizard and Cadgwath boat rescued three out of the four men in the rigging. The remaining man was George Goss' chief engineer, of Swansea, and he was so much disabled that he could not move. Captain Bull was determined, however, that he should not remain thereto perish without a great effort being made to save him, so despite the heavy sea then running be jumped off the lifeboat on to the rigging, climbed up to Goss, lashed a rope to him, got him down on deck, assisted him along a little way, and then threw him into the sea and followed himself. The crew of the lifeboat picked both up safely. The conduct of Captain . Bull was in every way admirable, and praise is due to the men who ,t manned the lifeboat for the splendid way they behaved, as undoubtedly they were the means of preventing a much greater loss of life. The rescued men were cared < for on being landed and provided with clothes. They then went to Falmouth and were received at the Sailors' Home, with the exception of Captain Bull, who remained behind pending an inquest on the second mate, who, it should be stated, leaves a wife and six children, and whose body was picked up on the beach late in the day.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. RABIES ORDER, 1892. ATUZZLING OF DOGS.—Notice is Hereby Given, I_ll_ that at a meeting of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the CreweArms Hotel, Crewe, on Thursday, the 2nd day of March, 1893, it was ORDERED that the exemptions set out in the Special Regulations as to Dogs, made by the said Local Autho- rity, on the 9th day of December, 1982, be extended to Dogs which have on a collar with the name and address of the owner of the Dog legibly engraved thereon, THE EFFECT OF WHICH ORDER IS THAT DOGS NEED NOT BE MUZZLED PROVIDED THEY HAVE ON A COLLAR AS HEREIN MENTIONED, but subject as aforesaid, the regulations of the 9th dag of December, 1892, will continue to remain in operation until further modified or revoked. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 3rd March, 1893. The District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, does not include the City of Chester nor any oi the Boroughs either wholly or partly within this County.

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED. Chief Office: HOLBORN BARS, London. SUMMARY of the REPOET presented at the FORTY- FOURTH ANNUAL MEETING held on 2nd March, 1893. The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their re- port and accounts for the year 1892. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The number of policies iesued during the :year was 56.912, assuring the sum ot 25,886,889, and producing a new annual premium income of £319.918. The premiums received during the year were £l,6e 5,611, being an incre :se of £222,855 over the year 1891. The claims of the year amounted to £418,667. The number of deaths was 2,932, and 117 endowment assurances matured, The number of policies in force was 301,643. INDUSTRIAL BRANCII.—The premiums received during the year were £5,849,167, being an increase of £160819. The claims of the year amounted to £1.602.816. The num- ber of deaths was 178,231 and 1,230 endowment assurances matured. The numl-er of free policies granted during the year to those policy-holders of five years standing. who have desired to discontinue their payments, was 47,395, the number in , force being 289,493. The total number of policies in force was 11,105,877 ; the average duration of them is seven years. The total assets of the company, as shown in the balance- sheet, are £16,309,652, being an increase of £1,686,025 over those of 1891. The directors have since 1885 been considering a plan whereby the great labour and expense attendant upon the quinquennial valuation might be lessened, and have now matur.d a system of rccordiug and classifying the risks in both branches front day to day in such a manner RS to make the work of actual valuation possible at any moment at a comparatively small cost. The directors therefore determined to exercise the power recently conferred upon them by the shareholders, and a complete valuation for the past year has been made with the following results : ORDINARY BRANCH.— The valuation of this branch has been made upon the same principle= as those of the preceed- ing quinquennium, namely, a net premium valuation on the Institute of Actuaries' (lm.) Table Of Mortality for the life risks, and Mr. Fiulaison's Government Annuity Table, 1884, for the annuities, the rate of interest in both cases being 3 per cent. The surplus assets over liabilities amounts to £369.600. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.—The valuation of this branch has also been made on the basis of a net premium valuation at 3 per cent. interest, the table of mortality being Dr. Farr's "English Life Table," No. 3. The surplus of assets over liabilities amounts to £294,609. The total surplus of the two br. riches is £664,109, out of which it is proposed to carry forward £270,000 (£70,000 from the Ordinary Branch and £210,000 from the Industrial), leaving £394,109 for distribution among the participating policyholders and shareholders, in accordance with the regu- lations of the company under its speCial Act of Parliament. It may be thought that in carrying over so large a sum as £270.00) the directors have acted with unnecessary caution; but although ample provisioa has been made for every known contingency, it must not be forgotton that in so extensive a business the working of a single year cannot be taken as the measure of the average profits over a series of years. The processes and results of the valuation, which has been carried out by the actuary, Mr. F. Schooling, have been approved by Mr. E. H. Bailey. By the adoption of an annual declaration of bonus policy- holders will obtain each year a vested increase to the sum asaured and 'will not. have ,to wait until the end of 'a quit'. qtiennial period. This advantage is emphasised by the fact that reversionary bonuses can be surrendered for cash. The directors desire to record their high appreciation of the efforts of the staff of 0-1.1 company in carrying taut the work " - which. under the improved methods, was _ . . Of the

balance sheet has been submitted to "Messrs. Deloitte, Dever, Griffith. and. Co., whose certificate is appended to the accounts. EXTRACT FROM the REPORT of Mr. F. SCHOOLIN4,the Actuary to the Company. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The number of life policies in force at 31st December, 1802, was 381,643, assuring with bonus, £33,971,264, and producing a premium income of £ ,707,488 perannum. After providing for all liabilities, there remains a surplus of 069,500, which includes the sum of £50,000 brought for- ward from last year. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.—The number of policies In existence at 31st December last was 10,105,877, including 288,493 free or paid up policies, and the amount assured £98,214,167. The weekly premiums receivable in respect of these policies amounted to £78,05.1 per week, or £4,058,600 per annum. After providing torahl liabilities there remains a surplus of £294,609, y, hich includes the sum of £150,000 brought forward from last year. Dating the year £77,000 has been aided to the sum assured , by policies completing their fifth year of existence, and £85,0. 0 to the sum assured by policies completing their tenth year. The present cash value of these increases, and of the sums assured under free policies granted during the year is 2140,000. WARRINGTON UNlON.—Persons willing to CON- TRACT for the supply of any of the undermentioned articles from Lady Day to Michaelmas next, to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or at the Industrial Schools, Psdgate, at such times and in such quantities as the Board of Guardians shall direct, are re- quested to send in TENDERS, properly sealed, endorsed,and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians, before four o'clock p.m. on Tuesday, the .21st day of March. The following are the articles for which tenders are re- quired : Groceries and Provisions Shoes and Clogs Beef and Mutton Glazing „ Joints for Officers Brushes Milk for schools Coffins Flour and Meal Best Oakum Rope for picking Loaves of Bread Best Peninaenmawr Stone Beer and Porter for breaking purposes Straw and Potatoes Leather Drapery, &c. Wood for cutting into Fire- Cord and Twill wood Coal and Slack Earthenware Samples of any of the above may be seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse. The Coal and Slack supplied muSt be to the satisfaction of the Rouse and Schools Commit- tees. The Pit and quality of Coal must be named in the Tender. Forms of tender and full particulars as to the prob- able quantities of each article required may be obtained at the Clerk's Office. Each tender must be made upon the prescribed forM, and properly enclosed and endorsed with the name of the article tendered for. Each article tendered for must be of the size, material, and quality shown at the Workhouse or Schools. No Tenders for other articles will be accepted. Each contractor , must be prepared (if required) to enter into security for the due performance of his contract. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. All contract accounts will be paid quarterly - By order. JAMES CLOWES SUTTON, Clerk to the Guardians. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, March 9th, 1893.

CMARGE AGAINST A FINANCIAL EDITOR- At the Okl Bailey, on Thursday, Henry Louis Waller- stein,, of the "Daily Bourse," was indicted for an assault upon Isabella Ilizmby, aged 18 years. Com- plainant, who lives with her parents at Poplar, an- swered an advertisement,, and eventually accepted a situation, in the prisoner' S office as lady clerk. She alleged that on goiag to commence her duties she was taken into Wallerstein's private office,vvhere he squeezed and kissed her, and otherwise misbehaved. The girl made complaint to her mother, hence the present pre- , ceedings. Wallerstein was found guilty, and sea- -1 tamed to Mae months hard labour. BET. STEPHEN GLADSTONE AND THE SUSPENbORY BILL. • The Rev. Stephen Gladstone, rector of Hawardenotc- kaowledging the receipt of a circular from his charch- wardens convening ameeting to discuss the Suspensory Bill, says that had it been the desire of the parishioners be meet him to discuss the subject he would willingly have met them, adding, "It is not, in my opinion, desirable or proper for me as a parish priest to attempt, unasked and unsought, to inflame the political feelings and opinions of my parishioners. THE OVERDUE STEAMER NARONIC. The White Star steamer Britannic, which arrived in the Mersey from New York yesterday morning, went about ninety miles south of the usual course, but saw nothing of the Naronic. • THE END OF THE COITON STOPPAGE. It is stated that with the exception of a few minor points it is now confidently held that an end of the prolonged dispute in the cotton trade at Oldham has been reached. Work is likely to be resumed immedi- ately.

ANOTHER RUMOURED ELECTION PETITION __- ALLEGED BRIBERY AT PONTEFRACT. General excitement was caused at Pontefract, yester- day, by a rumour, that a petition was being lodged against the return of Mr. Beckett, the Liberal member for the borough. It is alleged that there are thirty cases in which bribery was resorted to in outlying districts of the borough. A KENT RAILWAY MYSTERY. -- STRANGE DEATH ON THE LINE. On the arrival at Hastings on Thursday night of the last train from Loudon the window of a third-class car- riage was found smashed and glass scattered on the seat. Yesterday morning a body, identified as that of Mr. Mercer, manager of the Hastings Electric Light works, was found on the line between Frant and Tunbridge Wells. He left Hastings on business on Thursday,and is supposed to have opened the door and fallen out.
